name: Regional government working group, first brainstorm
summary: Synthetic sample. Six colleagues at a regional government in Germany with about five thousand staff record their own first planning session with dembrane, in English so a new data colleague can follow. Katrin from the citizen participation unit chairs; Jonas from IT, Ute from mobility, Felix from HR, Selin from youth and culture and Ravi from the data team join. They list possible uses (bus network evenings, staff dialogues on hybrid working, a youth council, the yearly meeting with municipal participation officers, open survey answers) and worry out loud: is this just another tool next to Teams, will people treat summaries as facts, what will the privacy officer say about the legal basis, and will the staff council accept recordings of colleagues. They park anything internal and anything with minors, pick two low-risk pilots with real deadlines, make the participation unit the workspace owner with IT as admin, keep the workspace invite-only, agree a project naming convention and a sandbox project for tests. At the end they ask the assistant what they decided. It turns a maybe into a decision, and they catch it by opening the cited source.

chunks.text: Okay, the screen says recording, there's a little green dot. Good. So, hello everyone, and hello to the phone. This is the working group, first proper session. I thought, if we are going to tell five thousand colleagues whether this thing is useful, we should at least try it on ourselves first. I set the project language to English because Ravi is with us today, so the summaries come out in something he can read.

Does that matter, Katrin? I thought it just hears whatever you say. It does, Jonas, the transcript follows whatever people speak. But the summaries, and the screens residents see when they scan, come in the project's language. So the bus evenings would be German, this one is English. Anyway. I also wrote a small project context last night. Five sentences. Who we are, that this is a brainstorm, that nothing said today is a decision, and the names of our departments so it spells them properly. Mobility, not mobile tea.

Sorry, sorry, the lift is broken again. Is this the dembrane thing? Are we being recorded? We are, Selin, it was in the invite, and it's our own project, nobody outside this room can see it. Sit, there is coffee, there are those dry biscuits. Right. Can we start with a list? Just throw out every place in this house where people talk to each other and nobody keeps what they said. No judging yet. Ute, you start, you're the one with the buses.

Okay, the obvious one. The bus network redesign. We have four resident evenings this autumn, one in each district town. Last year we did sticky notes and a colleague typing on a laptop at the back, and the report took seven weeks. Seven. By the time it went to the committee the plan had already changed twice, and residents wrote to us asking if anybody had read their notes. Which, honestly, some of them nobody had read.

Mine is staff. The new hybrid working policy. In spring we want round tables with maybe two hundred colleagues across the buildings. And, um, exit interviews, I was thinking. We lose people and we never really know why. No, Felix, not exit interviews. Not in a first round. Why not? Because it's one person, it's sensitive, and it's not a room with many tables, which is what this is good at. Fine, I take it back. Write it down as taken back.

From youth and culture I have three. The youth council, which meets every month and their minutes are, let's say, short. The culture funding round, where we have sessions with artists and they always say we don't listen. And the yearly meeting with the participation officers from the municipalities, thirty-two municipalities, six or seven tables. That one is interesting because they are our critical colleagues, they will tell us very directly if something is rubbish. Ravi? Data side?

For me, the open answers in the citizen panel survey. We get thousands of free text answers and we read maybe a sample. I understand you can upload text, so we could put them in and ask questions across all of them. Upload is only for audio files, Ravi. Text goes in through the portal's text option, you paste it in and it becomes a conversation. Then I'd paste them in one conversation per question, clearly named, not one giant text. And Jonas, you wanted to say every meeting. I did want to say every meeting, but please, please not every meeting. I'm the one who gets the tickets.

Okay, that's actually my worry, so let me say it now. Is this just another tool? We have Teams, which already transcribes. We have the survey tool. We have the participation platform which, be honest, nobody logs into after the first week. Every year someone comes with a new tool and in eighteen months I'm the one switching it off. So what is different? Why is this not just a transcription app with a nicer logo?

Fair. The way I understand it, it's not for meetings at a laptop. Teams is fine for that. It's for rooms with many tables at the same time, with one phone in the middle of each table. The transcription is only the start. The point is that afterwards you can ask across forty conversations, what came up about the night buses, and every answer points back to where it was said. And the residents never need an account, they scan a QR code.

And that's my worry, from the data side. Not the tool, the people reading it. If a department head reads a summary that says residents want fewer buses, and in reality two tables said that and six said the opposite, it becomes a fact in a slide. I've seen it with dashboards. So for me there has to be a rule. Nobody quotes anything from it without opening the source and reading the actual transcript. Yes. Write that down. That's a rule.

I like that rule, Ravi, but who checks the rule? Us. The pilot owners. Okay. Next worry. Privacy. Selin, you said youth council. They are fifteen, sixteen years old. Then not as a first pilot, I think. Agreed? I agree, it's a pity, but agreed. And for everything, before we start, Hildegard has to see it. She will want to look at the legal basis setting and at the consent text that participants see before they record.

There's a setting for that? There is, the legal basis is set for the workspace as a default and you can change it per project, and it changes what participants are told when they scan. I clicked around last night. I didn't change anything, I just looked. I'm not going to decide that, it's Hildegard's call. Good. Hildegard will be happy we asked before, for once. Normally she hears about our projects from the newspaper. That was one time, Jonas.

Okay, and the staff council. Anything with staff, the staff council has to agree. That's not optional. Recording colleagues talking about their working conditions, even with names removed, they will ask who can read it, can managers read it, can it be used to assess people. And they're right to ask. So internal is not pilot one. My suggestion is we invite the staff council chair to watch one of the external pilots, see it in a real room, and then we talk.

That's smart, Felix. Show, don't present. Okay. Small tangent. How do we even say the name? Dem brain? It's dembrane, all lowercase, I wrote it with a capital in an email and got a very polite correction. Lowercase like a whisper. Okay. Back to work. We have, what, seven possible uses on the board, and we need two pilots. Not five. Last time we did five pilots and we finished zero. Criteria first, before anyone falls in love with their own idea.

Criteria. One, a real process with a real deadline, not a demo. Two, someone who owns it and will actually read what comes out. Three, low sensitivity, so no minors and no staff for now. Four, a room with several tables at once, because that's the thing it's built for. And maybe five, people who will tell us honestly if it was bad. Okay, by those, the bus evenings and the municipalities meeting. Both. Ute, Selin, are you willing?

I am willing but I'm also nervous, Katrin. If it fails in front of residents, it's my evening that fails, not yours. Then we take that seriously. We test the QR on our own phones before printing. We do a rehearsal with colleagues. There's a printable host guide that goes on every table. And for the first evening we keep the sticky notes on the tables as well, so if a phone dies, the table is not lost. Belt and braces. Okay. Two of the four towns, then. Altheim and Brunnfeld.

And the municipalities meeting in November, I can do that. Thirty-two people, six tables, already on the calendar. I'd like to keep it small, though, and say openly at the start that we're testing something and want their opinion of it too. Good. That's honest. Next question, and this one will be awkward. Who owns the workspace? Me, I assumed. IT owns tools. Hmm. Can I argue against that, Jonas, without you getting offended? You can try.

If IT owns it, it becomes a system, and a system gets a ticket queue and a change board. And then Ute waits three weeks to create a project for an evening that's in ten days. I think the participation unit should be owner, because it's about how we run processes, and you are admin, for accounts and for the procurement side. Hmm. Okay. As long as I'm not the one people call when the phone at table four is locked. Deal.

And visibility? I would not open it to the whole organisation yet. Invite-only for the pilots. Ute and Selin as members, plus one buddy each, because I don't want one person in the whole house who knows how it works. Mehmet for me, he's good with this kind of thing. Then project structure. The rule of thumb I read is, if you'd write one report about it, it's one project. So the bus evenings, one project or two? I want to compare the towns.

Then one project for both evenings, with tags per town and per table, because as far as I know you ask questions inside one project, not across projects. But the context would be different per town. Then write both in the context, Ute, it's a shared programme anyway. And the municipalities meeting is its own project. And naming. Department, topic, date. Mobility, bus network 2027, resident evenings. And one sandbox project, called Sandbox, do not analyse, for every test recording. Tests never live in real projects.

Yes, Ravi, and delete tests after. I've seen shared drives. What does success look like, quickly, each of you? For me, a summary for the committee in days, and residents recognising what their table said. For me, the staff council chair saying, okay, let's talk. Every point traceable to a transcript. That it works for people who don't scan QR codes. There's a type instead option, and paper. Okay. Open questions list. Cost and procurement, Jonas. Youth council, parked. Staff dialogues, parked. Accessibility, Selin.

Shall we ask it? About this. Our own brainstorm. I'm curious what it makes of us. Go on, Ravi, it's your idea, you do it. Okay. Laptop. I open Ask in this project and select this conversation. It will only have what's transcribed so far, so maybe not the last minute. I'll type, what did we decide today, and what did we leave open? Short and plain. Katrin said start small, it usually gives you more than you asked anyway.

Here. Decided: two pilots, the bus evenings in Altheim and Brunnfeld and the November meeting with municipal participation officers. Participation unit owns the workspace, IT is admin, invite-only, sandbox for tests, a naming convention. Open: legal basis with the privacy officer, procurement, accessibility. And then, the group agreed to start internal staff dialogues after consulting the staff council. Wait. No. We didn't agree that. We said parked. Can you click the source? Where does it get that from?

It's you, Felix. Your sentence. We could start staff dialogues after we talk to the staff council. You said could, it wrote agreed. Ha. Okay. So this is exactly the rule. If I had pasted that into the minutes, the staff council would read that we already decided, and we'd have a very different first meeting with them. Good catch. That's the best demo we could have had, honestly. It was mostly right, and the one wrong thing was the important one.

Can I ask one more? Which worries did nobody answer? Go. It says the question of residents without smartphones was raised but not resolved, apart from a mention of typing and paper. That's fair, actually. That was me and nobody really answered me. Okay, it goes on the open list with your name on it, Selin, sorry. Ute, for next time, draft the context for Altheim, like a briefing to a friend who's coming to help. Same time in three weeks. I'm stopping it now.

name: Coaching call before a first 40-person evening
summary: Synthetic sample. Tomás, a programme coordinator at a small-town public library in Ireland, records a coaching call with Ingrid, an experienced process facilitator, ten days before his first evening with dembrane: about forty residents at six tables talking about a planned new library building. Ingrid turns his one-line project context into a briefing (who comes, the rounds and their questions, what is fixed and what is open, which provocations come from the organisers), has him fill key terms with local names, and explains what the language setting does and doesn't change. She uses the name field as a table label, adds a line to the editable host guide so table hosts type the same format, and sets portal tags per round. They decide on anonymise transcripts before collecting, ask for email only because the report will be sent back. Ingrid insists on testing the QR on his own phone after the last portal edit, Do Not Disturb, auto-lock off, a colleague on the Monitor all evening, a planned five-minute Verify moment or none, and paper on every table in case the technology lets him down.

chunks.text: Is it, okay, it's going. Ingrid, I'm recording this, is that alright? I thought if I record you, I'll stop panicking at two in the morning, I can just listen back. Fine by me, Tomás. And it's quite nice, the very first conversation in your account is you being nervous. Very honest data. Right. Tell me the evening. Thursday week, the reading room upstairs, forty people signed up, six tables. It's about the new library on the old creamery site.

Lovely. And what's the question? What should the new library be. The council has bought the site, the budget is set, the building is happening. What's open is opening hours, the rooms, what services, whether there's a café. Good, keep that sentence, we'll use it. Before we touch anything else, read me your project context. Um. Library consultation evening. That's it? That's it. Okay. That's a title, Tomás, not a context. It's alright, everybody does that the first time.

The context is what the language model reads before it does anything with your conversations. The summaries, the answers when you ask questions afterwards, the report, the questions it asks participants if you use that. So write it like you're briefing a curious friend who's coming to help you on the night. Who is in the room, what you're asking in each round, what's already decided and what's open, and the local words people will use. A paragraph or two. Not an essay, not a slogan.

Can you give me an example? I'd write something like: this is an evening with about forty residents of Kilbarra about the new library planned on the old creamery site on Mill Lane. People sit at six tables with a table host. Round one, what do you use the library for now and what's missing. Round two, imagine a Saturday in the new library in a few years' time. The site and the budget are fixed. Opening hours, rooms and services are open for discussion.

And then I'd add the things you know will come up. Many people will talk about the mobile library van and the Tuesday knitting group. And this one is important: if you read out provocations, say so. Are you planning any? Three statements, one per table card, like the library should open on Sundays. Then put in the context that those statements come from the organisers, so it treats them as prompts, not as what residents think. Otherwise your own provocation comes back as a finding.

Oh, that's sneaky. It is. Next, key terms. That's a separate field and for transcription it's the one that pays off most. Names of places, people, schemes, anything a stranger would misspell. Kilbarra, Mill Lane, the creamery, whatever the van is called. The van is called the Bookmobile, no, it's called Rosie, actually. Then Rosie. Your head librarian's name. The councillor, Siobhán, if she speaks. And add dembrane itself, because people will say it and it gets written in strange ways.

Okay, typing. Rosie, Bríd, Mill Lane, creamery, Kilbarra. Siobhán. Good. Language. What language will they speak? English. Mostly. There might be a table from the Polish Saturday school, the parents asked if they could come together. Okay, so the project language is English. That sets the welcome screens and the language of the summaries. The transcript itself follows what people say, so a Polish table gets a Polish transcript. But Polish isn't one of the portal languages, so somebody explains the screens to them in Polish. Test it with one of the parents before. I wouldn't mix and hope.

Don't trust me on mixed rooms, by the way. Ask the assistant in your dashboard or ask dembrane before you promise anything to those parents. I only tell you what I've done. Now, the tables. Forty people, six tables, so six or seven a table. That's on the edge for me. I like five or six per phone. I have a colleague who swears by trios, three people per phone, nobody can hide. For an evening with table hosts, I'd keep your tables, one phone in the middle.

How do I know if the room is too loud? My rule: if you can sit at a table and follow the conversation without straining, the phone can too. If you can hear the next table better than your own, move the tables apart. The reading room, is it echoey? A bit. Wooden floor. Then spread the tables out, use the corners, and ask hosts to keep the phone in the middle, not in front of the host's own mouth. Don't put a table beside the tea urn.

Now, naming. In the portal you can ask for a name. I turn that on, but I don't use it for people's names. I use it as a table label. So when the table host starts the recording, they type Table 3, Round 1. Otherwise you end up with Table3, three, T three, and one called Mary's table. And on the Monitor and in your list later, you can see straight away which table is which. You type the format on the host guide.

The host guide is editable? It is. You print it, it goes next to the QR on every table, it reminds the host what to do. I always add one line at the top in big letters: in the name box, type your table number and round, like Table 3, Round 1. And I set portal tags for the rounds, Round 1 and Round 2, so they just tap one when they start. Then afterwards you can ask about round two only, or compare the rounds.

Okay. And anonymise? Decide now, not on the night. Anonymise transcripts removes names from the transcripts, and it also turns off playing back and downloading the audio. It only works on what you collect after you switch it on, it doesn't go back. For a library evening, what will people say? Bríd. Everyone will say Bríd fifty times, they love her. Ha. Then think about the report. Do you want Bríd in it, or residents' neighbours, or the man who complained about the parking?

Probably not the man with the parking. He's my uncle. Then I'd switch it on. You lose the audio, but you're not going to sit there listening to six hours of audio anyway. And if you leave it off, write in the context, do not name individuals in summaries. Either way, decide before Thursday. Next. Ask for email? Only if you'll actually write back. I will, I want to send them what we heard. Then turn on email and the updates, so the report reaches them.

And the finish text, the last screen they see, say what happens next. Something like: thank you, we'll send what we heard to everyone who left an email within two weeks, and it goes to the library committee in October. People want to know their talk goes somewhere. Okay. Now the most important bit of this call, so listen. Test it on your own phone. The whole thing, like a resident. Scan, consent, mic check, talk for a minute, stop, finish.

Then go to the dashboard and check that it's there, with a transcript. It should show up within a minute or so. If it says empty, it didn't hear you. Then delete your test, so it's not sitting among the real tables. And do your portal edits before you print. A host I know changed the portal language the night before her event and the QR code changed, because the language is part of the link. The old printed ones still worked, but she didn't know that, and she didn't sleep.

So, edit, then print, then scan the printed paper with your phone, and then don't touch the portal. Got it. Edit, print, scan the paper, hands off. And the phones on the night. Who's holding them? The table hosts, library staff and two volunteers, on their own phones. Fine. Brief them half an hour before. One sentence for the table: scan this, allow the microphone, and just talk. Then the host guide does the rest. And the phone settings, which is where it usually goes wrong.

Charged, or a power bank on the table. Wifi or good mobile data, check the reading room. Microphone allowed. Do Not Disturb on, because a phone call in the middle can stop the recording. And the screen has to stay on. Change auto-lock to never for the evening. The most common failure I've seen is a phone that locked after two minutes and recorded nothing for half an hour while everybody talked beautifully. Screen on. Say it three times at the briefing.

Now the Monitor. Open it on a laptop at the back of the room. It shows each phone as it goes from scanned to setting up to recording. And it flags things like audio stopped or screen locked. Who watches it? Me? No. You're facilitating, you'll be at the front with the microphone. Ask a colleague whose only job that evening is the laptop. Aoife would do it. Then Aoife. When she sees screen locked, she walks over quietly, unlocks it, checks the dot, walks away.

Don't stop the table, don't make a scene. And record your welcome and the closing round too, as their own conversation, called Plenary. That's where you explain what happens next, and it's useful in the record. What do I say at the start about the recording? Plainly. The tables are recorded on the phone so we don't lose what you say. Names are taken out. It's optional, you can type instead, or use the paper. You can stop any time.

What about Verify? I read that people can check their own summary. They can. For a first evening, either you plan a proper five minutes at the end of round two, in the running order, with the host reading the outcome out, the table saying what's not quite right, pressing revise, and only approving it when it's right. Or you skip it. Don't do it as an afterthought while people are putting on coats. Then it's just one more screen and nobody remembers why. Okay. I'll think. Probably skip.

That's a fine choice for night one. Afterwards, close the conversations for new recordings in the project, so nobody adds a stray one from the car park. Don't analyse that night. Go home. Next morning, tidy first: delete tests, look at anything marked empty, check the table labels and tags. Then ask your questions. Start broad, what were the main themes, then zoom in, what came up about opening hours, then ask for quotes, and open the transcript before you copy one.

And what if it just doesn't work? At all? Then you have paper on every table, Tomás. Pens, sticky notes, the questions printed. The evening is the evening. On the first night the recording is a bonus. People won't remember the technology. They'll remember whether somebody listened to them and whether they heard back. Okay. That actually helps. Write it on your hand if you need to. Screen on, paper out, Aoife on the laptop. Now stop recording and go and fix that context.

name: Solo consultant, voice memo walking home
summary: Synthetic sample. Morag, an independent organisation consultant in Scotland, records a voice memo to herself while walking home in the rain after her first workshop with dembrane: twenty-six staff and volunteers of a community arts centre at four tables, talking about the next five years. She records it into a separate notes project so it never mixes with the client's conversations. What surprised her: people forgot the phone within minutes, the Monitor caught a locked screen at one table, and transcripts were readable during the break. What went wrong: a one-line project context and empty key terms mangled local names, a table of eight ran two conversations into one phone, an everyone-scan-now moment left empty rows, and with anonymise off the summaries named people. Her plan for tomorrow: tidy first (delete tests and empties, add key terms, retranscribe each table into a named, anonymised copy and delete the originals), then Ask from broad to narrow, ask explicitly for what only one table said and where tables disagreed, open every source, and write the client note herself rather than have the model write the board's recommendations. Next time she will decide anonymisation beforehand and ask for email.

chunks.text: Note to self. Thursday, about twenty to nine, walking home from the arts centre. It's raining, obviously. I'm recording this into my own notes project, not the client one. I checked twice before I pressed the button, because that would be a lovely thing for the board to find tomorrow. Okay. First workshop with dembrane. Twenty-six people, four tables, the five-year plan. I want to get this down now, before my head tidies it all up into a nicer story than it was.

Surprise number one. They forgot about the phone. Properly forgot. In the intro, Elspeth asked, is it listening to us forever then, and I explained, it's this table, tonight, you can type instead, you can stop. And twenty minutes later she was holding the phone like a microphone and passing it to the young lad from the box office when he spoke. I didn't tell her to do that. I'm not sure it helps the sound, to be honest, but it helped the mood.

Surprise number two, the Monitor. I had it open on my laptop at the front, mostly because the coaching notes said so, and I glanced at it maybe every five minutes. About twelve minutes into round one, table four said screen locked. I walked over, and the phone was lying under a programme leaflet, black. Unlocked it, checked the dot was going, walked off. Lost a few minutes, not half an hour. Without that I'd have found out tomorrow morning with my coffee.

So, change for next time. Auto-lock off, Do Not Disturb on, and I say it out loud at the start, not only on the paper. Nobody reads the paper until something goes wrong. Surprise three. The transcripts were there. During the tea break I opened table two, just to see, and I could already read it. They'd spent ten minutes on the café closing at four. And I almost reframed round two around the café. I didn't. But I could have.

I don't know how I feel about that, actually. It's useful. It's also me steering the room with a peek nobody else had. Maybe next time I say it openly. Here's something I heard at the tables, does it ring true for the rest of you? That's fairer. Okay. Things that went wrong. My project context. I wrote one line. Arts centre five-year plan workshop. That's it. And key terms, I left completely empty. Big mistake, I could see it already.

Inverbrae came out as in a brae, several times. The Wee Stage is the wee stitch in one place, which is quite sweet. And the funder's name was wrong everywhere. So first thing tomorrow, key terms: Inverbrae, the Wee Stage, the Loft, the funder, the two show names, front of house, get-in. Then retranscribe the four tables. I can do that because I left anonymise off, so the audio is still there. Which brings me to the other mistake.

Names. Anonymise was off because I didn't think about it. And table one's summary says Callum argued the café should be run by volunteers. Which he did. But I'm handing a note to a board who are Callum's managers. Not a scandal, but not what I promised in the room either. I said, what you say goes in as the table, not as you. Switching it on now won't touch these four. I can retranscribe each one with anonymise ticked, which makes a new copy without names, and then delete the originals. Key terms first, though. Lesson. Decide before, every time.

For tomorrow, I'll put don't mention names in every question I ask, and in my own note I'll write table one said, never Callum said. And I won't share the raw summaries with the client, only my note. Other thing that went wrong. Table three had eight people. Two conversations started at once, the end of the table and the middle, and the phone in the middle caught both. When I read a bit at the break it was like listening to a radio between stations.

Next time, six maximum per phone, or a second phone at the far end. Someone in the coaching group says trios, three per phone, and I'm not sure for a board and staff mixed. Maybe for a round. Actually, maybe for a round. Write that down, Morag. Trios for one round, try it. The other thing, the start. I said, everybody, take out your phones and scan the code, just to see what it looks like. Twenty-six people scanned. That's twenty-two empty conversations sitting in my list now.

Well, maybe not twenty-two, some of them pressed stop very quickly. Either way, it was a stupid instruction. Only the table host scans, one phone per table. If people want to see it, show it on the screen. Okay. A dog has just barked at me, ignore that. Tomorrow morning. Coffee, and then tidy before I analyse anything. I want to write the order down because I'll want to skip it. One, delete my test from the kitchen on Tuesday, the one where I read out a recipe.

Two, the empty ones. But I check each one is actually empty. Open it, look for the empty badge or no transcript, not just a short time, because one of the short ones might be a person who said one sharp thing. Three, key terms. Four, retranscribe the four tables with anonymise ticked, and name the new copies Table 1 to Table 4, because I left the default and they're all called participant. Five, check each copy, delete the old one. Then and only then, Ask. An hour of tidying. Fine.

Then the questions. Start broad. What were the main themes across the four tables? Then zoom. What came up about the café and the opening hours, per table? Show me the quotes. Then two questions I'll ask on purpose, because I was told the minority stuff doesn't surface unless you ask for it. What did only one table raise? Where did the tables disagree with each other? Table two and four definitely disagreed on the Loft, and I want to see whether it notices.

And every quote I use, I click the source and copy it from the transcript. Not from the answer. The answer paraphrases, sometimes nicely, but I'm not putting a nice paraphrase in quotation marks in front of a board. When I've got the map, I'll do a Specific Details chat on just the four tables, for exact claims. And I'll add, don't mention names, keep the language plain. Because the board chair hates consultant words. So do I, to be fair.

What I won't do. I won't ask it to write the recommendations. It's very tempting at eight in the morning. But the board has to decide what the next five years are. My job is to tell them what their people said, honestly, and where it was thin, and where they disagreed. If the model writes recommendations, they're the model's, and then they're kind of mine, and they're not the room's. So, I write the note. I use Ask to check it.

Actually, that's a good one. When I've drafted the note, I'll paste it in and ask, compared with the transcripts, is there anything a table said strongly that's missing here? Is there anything in here no table said? That second question is for me, because I'll have my own opinions creeping in. I know I will. Oh, and I want to ask it how much the facilitator talked. It can't tell who's who, there are no speaker names, but I sat in on table three.

And I know I talked too much at table three. I'll read that transcript myself and count my own interruptions. That's not analysis, that's penance. Okay. Sharing back. I didn't ask for emails. So the twenty-six people who gave me their evening get nothing directly, unless the board passes it on. Next time I turn on email with the updates, so they get the report. And I offer the board a half-hour conversation about it instead of just sending a document.

I'm nearly at the door. Let me do the list. Change: a real context, written like a briefing, key terms before, not after, decide anonymise before, six per phone or trios for one round, no mass scanning, screen on said out loud, email on. Keep: the Monitor on the laptop, the paper at every table, the honest intro, the break peek but said openly. And tomorrow, tidy first. Right. Keys. Bye, me. Well done, mostly.

name: Privacy officer, works council and project lead agree the rules
summary: Synthetic sample. At a public agency planning ten staff listening sessions about a new appointment system, the project lead Kwame, the privacy officer Liesbeth and the works council member Dorota meet to agree the rules before anything is recorded. They record the meeting in a sandbox project and agree to delete it once minutes exist. They disagree on the legal basis (Dorota wants consent, Liesbeth worries about consent in an employment relationship and will decide in the impact assessment; a workspace admin then sets it for the workspace and the project). They agree anonymise transcripts is on from the first session, accepting the loss of audio, and note that it removes personal names but not team or office details, so tags go by region and the project context forbids naming small teams. Access is narrow: an invite-only workspace, a project for three analysts, the works council member as a member so she can check the synthesis against sources, no managers in the workspace, the board gets an exported PDF. Verify becomes a planned five minutes. They draft what to tell staff and refuse to put storage or deletion promises in the script that are not checked in writing.

chunks.text: Okay, it's recording. Before we start, Dorota, you asked whether recording this meeting is fine. It's in my sandbox project, the three of us agreed in the invite, and once I've written the minutes I delete it. Is that okay with both of you? It's okay, Kwame. I just think it's funny, we are recording a meeting about whether we are allowed to record meetings. It's also useful, Dorota. If we disagree later about what we agreed, we can look. Fair. Go on.

So the plan. Ten listening sessions, one per regional office, about twenty to twenty-five front desk colleagues each, about the new appointment system. Tables of five, one phone per table. Two questions, what works today and what worries you about the new system. And the output is a synthesis for the programme board in December. That's the plan. Liesbeth, you said you have three things. I have three things. Legal basis, what participants are told, and who can see what. In that order.

Legal basis first. In dembrane you set a legal basis as a default for the whole workspace, and you can override it per project. It changes what participants are told when they open the portal, so it's not just a box for me to tick. If we go with consent, there must be a link to a privacy notice in the portal, and the dashboard actually warns you if there isn't one. I like that. I haven't decided which basis yet, and I won't decide it in this meeting.

I'll tell you what the works council wants. Consent. Staff must be able to say no, and it must be real. Not consent on paper and then the manager looks at you. I understand, Dorota. My worry is exactly that. Consent between an employer and an employee is a difficult thing, because of the relationship. Someone who says yes because their team leader is standing at the door has not really freely consented. So consent can look stronger than it is. I'll write my reasoning in the impact assessment.

But then you'll choose something where they cannot say no. No. Whatever the basis, nobody is forced to sit at a recorded table. That's a separate promise and it goes in the script. There's a paper table in every session, and the portal has a type instead option for people who don't want to talk into a phone. And they can stop at any time and ask us to remove their contribution. Okay. I want that in writing, not just said. It will be.

Second, who sees what. Dorota, I know your position. My position is simple. No managers at the tables, and managers never see transcripts. Only the synthesis, the one we agree. Hmm. Can I push back a little? If the programme board only gets a synthesis, the first question will be, where does this come from? The whole point of using this instead of me writing notes is that every point goes back to what somebody actually said. Traceable to the record, yes, Kwame. Traceable to Jan from Eastgate, no.

Those are different things, I agree. Then the question is anonymisation. Liesbeth? Anonymise transcripts takes names out of the transcripts, and it also turns off audio playback and download. And it has to be on before the first session, because it only applies to what's collected after you switch it on. It doesn't go back. If we forget for session one, session one stays as it is. Without audio I can't check whether it misheard something. That's my problem with it. That's a real cost.

It is a real cost, Kwame, and I still want it on. Colleagues talking about their own work and their own managers. For me it's not a hard choice. Okay. I'll live with it. Then I need key terms filled in properly before session one, the system's name, the office names, the jargon, so the transcription is right the first time, because I can't retranscribe later. Good. But there's something else. Anonymised is not anonymous. It takes out names. It doesn't take out who you are.

If someone says, on the night desk in Eastgate there are three of us, everyone in the agency knows who that is. It's personally anonymised, not organisationally. Okay, that's a very good point. So what do we do? Tags by region, not by office. North, South, Coast, not Eastgate. The project context says, do not name individuals, teams or offices in any output, refer to regions only. And in the opening we ask people, please say a colleague, not a name. They'll forget. Some will. Fewer will.

And the names on the phone? In the portal there's ask for name. Turn it off, or use it as a table label. A table label is fine, as long as it's Table 2 and not Eastgate night desk. And email? Off, except the updates. If a colleague wants the report, they can leave an email and they get it when it's published. I actually like that, Dorota. Staff get the same document the board gets. Same day. Yes. That I like very much. Write that in big letters.

Now, access. Workspace invite-only, not open to the organisation. The project itself private, me and two analysts as members. Liesbeth, you don't need access? I don't want access. I want to know who has it. And I want access. Dorota, as the works council, to check. Hmm. Raw transcripts for the works council, is that okay for privacy? Hold on, Kwame. If Dorota is named in the assessment, under the same confidentiality as your analysts, and her purpose is checking that the synthesis matches what was said, I can work with that.

Only for that, Dorota. Not to read what a particular office said and bring it to a meeting. Of course only for that. I don't want to read two hundred colleagues' complaints in my evenings, believe me. I want to open the report, click a point, and see that it's really there. That's exactly how it should work anyway. Okay. Then you're a member on that one project, with a role that lets you read and ask. Managers, not in the workspace. Not even read-only. Agreed.

And how does the board get it? Not a published link. I'd prefer an exported PDF, sent internally, so I know where it went. Fine. Now. Dorota, you wrote Verify on your list. Yes. I want colleagues to check their own table's points before anything leaves the room. If they say we didn't say that, it doesn't go to the board. Kwame? I'm worried about time. The sessions are ninety minutes, and people need to get back to the desk.

From my side I like it, by the way. It's their own words, they get a say over what's taken from them. That's good practice for me, not only for Dorota. Okay. Then five minutes, planned, at the end, in the running order, not an afterthought. The table host reads the outcome out, the table says what's wrong, they revise or edit it, and they approve it only when it's right. And if they never approve it? Then it isn't verified, and I won't use it. The transcript is still the transcript.

Okay. Next. What do we tell participants? I want to draft the opening script now, while we are together. Go. We're recording the table conversations on a phone so we don't lose what you say. No video. The transcript doesn't record who said what, and names are taken out. It's your choice: there's a paper table, and you can type instead of talking. You can stop at any time, and if you want your contribution removed afterwards, you write to the project mailbox. Good so far.

Then who sees it. Three analysts and one works council member read the conversations. The board gets a summary, and you can get the same summary by email if you leave your address. It won't be used for anything else, not for assessments, not for anything about you personally. That last sentence, Liesbeth, can you stand behind it? Purpose limitation, yes, that goes in the assessment and in the notice. What I won't put in the script is anything about storage or deletion periods.

Why not? People will ask. They will, and the answer will be in the privacy notice that the portal links to. I have the processing agreement and my questions to dembrane, and I'll write it from those, in writing, checked. I'm not having a table host say a number in a room that turns out to be wrong. If someone asks, the host points to the notice. Hmm. Okay. That's actually more honest than what we usually do. We usually say don't worry.

One more worry from my side, and it's not about privacy. The language model. Will it make things up? Will the board see, the AI concluded, and that's it? No. The synthesis is a draft. Every point gets checked against the sources it cites. We ask explicitly for minority views, because they don't show up unless you ask. And nothing goes to the board that one of us hasn't read against the transcripts. You can check that yourself, that's why you have access.

And no, the AI concluded, in the slides. Staff said, at so many tables. Yes. Agreed. And no managers in the building at all? Dorota, the regional manager opens the session. It's their office. Then they open and they leave before the tables start. And the welcome isn't recorded. We start recording at the tables. Fine, compromise. One more thing, Kwame. You will not put these transcripts into other tools. No connecting other systems to this project, no exports except the agreed report.

Agreed. No connections to this project, and the only export is the PDF for the board. Liesbeth, write that as a rule, not as a promise from me. Already writing. Okay, actions. Liesbeth: impact assessment and the legal basis decision, which the workspace admin then sets for the workspace and the project, with the privacy notice linked. Kwame: anonymise on before any test, key terms, portal text, script, and a test session with two works council colleagues pretending to be staff. Dorota: brief the works council, review the script, check the first synthesis against sources.

And for the record, I still think it should be consent. I know, Dorota. I'll write down why I might decide otherwise, and you can disagree in writing. That's how it should be. Okay. Good meeting. Kwame, stop the recording, and delete it after the minutes. Like you promised. Like I promised. It's in the minutes that I'll delete the recording of the meeting that produced the minutes. Very Kafka. Stop it, Kwame.

name: Municipal pilot evaluation after three months
summary: Synthetic sample. Five colleagues at a mid-sized Danish municipality record their evaluation of a three-month dembrane pilot, in English so they can share it with a Nordic network of municipalities. Henrik ran the pilot; Mette (planning), Aisha (youth work), Lars (communications) and Birgitte (department head) take part. They used it at two park redesign evenings, a youth club session, a batch of online form answers pasted in through the portal's text option and the Monitor once it arrived in August. Ask the morning after was the big win. Reports were rewritten by hand: the generated one was too high-level for the council and missed the allotment holders' objection until Mette asked what only one table said. Verify was barely used because it was placed at the end of a long evening, though the one table that used it corrected a key point. Failures included confusion over the language setting (Danish is not a portal language, so screens and summaries came in English while transcripts were Danish), a portal language change after printing that changed the QR code, empty rows from an everyone-scan moment, and one giant pasted text. They renew for the next programme with conditions, and list advice for other municipalities.

chunks.text: Okay, it's recording, the project is set to English for once, because Birgitte promised the Nordic network a write-up in English, and I'm not translating my own notes again. So this is the evaluation of the pilot. Three months, it ends Friday, and we have to decide if we continue. I want this honest. If it was bad, say it was bad. The network is asking because three other municipalities are thinking about it, and they don't need another success story. They need the truth.

Let me say what we actually did, Henrik, because I've lost track. Two evenings for Engparken, the park redesign, in July and September. One session at the youth club. The online form answers from the spring consultation, we pasted them in as text through the portal's text option. And our own team day, which was mostly to practise. Around seventy conversations in total, if you don't count the empty ones. Which we'll talk about. Yes, we'll definitely talk about the empty ones, Aisha.

Then I'll start with what worked, because for me it's clear. Ask, the morning after. After the July evening I sat down at eight with coffee and asked, what did people say about the playground, and in a few minutes I had the broad picture that normally takes me a week of reading sticky notes. Then show me the quotes, and I click and it's there in the transcript. For me that alone was worth the pilot. Mette is in love. I'm not in love. I'm impressed. Different.

Okay, and the report, because that's the part I'm least happy with. We generated the report for the park after the first evening. And it read well. It read like a reporter writing an article about our evening. Nice, smooth, a bit too polished. And for the council it was too high-level. Nobody could find their own table in it. And the thing that made me nervous: the allotment holders. One table, very strong, against moving the path through the allotments. Not in the report.

Not at all? Not a word. I only found it because I asked Ask, what did only one table say? And there it was, top of the list, with quotes. So the report was not wrong exactly. It was the majority. But the council needs to know the allotment holders are furious, because they will be at the council meeting, I promise you. So in the end we wrote the participation report by hand. Well, not by hand. With Ask open on the other screen.

How did that work, Lars? I used Ask to make the map. Main themes, then per theme, which tables, then what only one table said, then where tables disagreed. Then for the exact claims, the Specific Details chat on the conversations from that evening, so I knew precisely what it was looking at. And every quote I copied from the transcript, not from the answer. The report took two days instead of three weeks. But it wasn't the report button. Be honest about that in the write-up.

I'll be honest about it, but I'll also be honest about us. We never gave the report any instructions. You can write your own instructions for a report, and you can have several reports in one project. We just pressed the button and were disappointed. I'd like to try a report shaped per question, the way the evening was, with the minority views asked for in the instructions. Before we say the report doesn't work, we should try it properly once. Fair. Put it on the list.

Verify. Barely used. Let's say it. We tried it once, at the September evening. At the end. People had their coats on. Two tables did it, the others didn't bother. But one of those two tables, Birgitte, wouldn't approve it. The outcome said they want to close the car park at the north entrance. They said, no, we said move it, not close it. They said so out loud, pressed revise, and it changed. If that had gone to the council as close, we'd have had a very angry evening. So, is it useless?

No. We put it at the wrong moment. At the youth club it was the same. It was one more screen, and they were done with screens. That's what they told me. I think Verify is good, but you have to give it its own five minutes in the running order, and the table host has to read it out loud. Not, oh, by the way, if you have time. Okay. So we didn't really test it. We tested it at the worst moment. Exactly.

Now the failures. Lars, you start. Why me? Because two are yours. Okay. The first evening. Danish isn't in the language list, so the project was on English, and the welcome screens were English. The transcripts were fine, Danish, it writes what people say. But the summaries came out in English and a bit flat, and I panicked and almost told Henrik it doesn't work in Danish. It works in Danish. You have to know which parts follow the setting, and write the welcome and finish text in Danish yourself.

And the second one is the QR. I printed the table cards. Then, the same week, I changed the portal language to see if it helped with the Danish. It didn't, and the QR code changed, because the language is part of the link. The old printed codes still worked, as it turned out, but I didn't know that for twenty minutes and I was printing new cards in the copy room at six o'clock. Rule now: all portal changes before printing, then scan the printed card, then nobody touches it. Even small ones. Especially small ones.

Mine is the youth club. I said, everybody scan, let's see. Thirty young people scanned. We got thirty rows, and nineteen were empty. Some opened it and closed it, some pressed record and then just put the phone on the sofa. And it's a mess to clean up, because you have to open each one to be sure it's really empty. Next time, one phone per sofa group, and only the youth worker at that group starts it. And honestly, several of them liked typing instead. That surprised me.

And the form answers. The online form, three hundred answers. We pasted it into the portal's text option as one giant text, and it was slow and the answers were vague. We split it into one text conversation per question, named by question, and then it was useful. So don't paste in one huge text. Split by question. Henrik, the Monitor? We only got it in August. In July, one table recorded nothing, a screen lock, and we found out the next morning. In September I had Mette's colleague on the Monitor laptop all evening.

Twice it said screen locked, she walked over, it was fixed in a minute. That's the difference between losing a table and losing two minutes. So that's advice number one for the network, one person whose only job that evening is the Monitor. Not the facilitator. And one more thing that worked: sharing back. We only switched on the email updates at the September evening. Forty-one residents left an email and got the summary. Several replied. One corrected something about the bike path.

I'd do that from day one. From the very first evening. That's the bit that changes how people see the municipality. They say something on a Tuesday and two weeks later they get it back. Okay. Now the decision. Lars, renew or not? Renew. Without discussion. Mette? Only if we have a next process. The town centre plan starts in spring. If we renew and then nothing happens until spring, we'll forget how it works and in June we'll say we never used it. I've seen that with other tools.

Aisha? I'm honestly not sure for youth. Some liked it, typing more than talking. Some thought it was weird to talk to a phone. I don't want to force it on the youth club. If we renew, for me youth stays optional. Okay. Birgitte, you decide the money. I'm not going to talk about money in a recording for the network. I'll ask one question. If we hadn't had it in September, would we have missed it? Yes, for the park. Very much. For the youth club, less.

Then we renew, for the town centre plan, with conditions. Two people trained, Henrik and Mette, and they train the others. I don't want everyone booking Henrik. A context template for every project, written like a briefing, with the questions per round and the place names. Verify planned twice properly, its own five minutes, then we decide. A report with our own instructions, per question. Email updates on from day one. And we look at it again after the town centre plan, not after three months.

Agreed. Okay, last part, for the network. What would we tell another municipality? Start with a real process with a deadline, not a demo. Know what the language setting changes before anything. One project per question, or per thing you'd write one report about. Write the context like you're briefing a colleague. Fill in the key terms with street names. Name the tables. Put one person on the Monitor. Don't promise the council that the report button writes the participation report. It doesn't, and that's fine.

Ask for minority views on purpose. Every time. What did only one table say. Where did tables disagree. And read some transcripts yourself, all the way through. If you never read one, you don't know if the summary is right. Budget that time. And send it back to residents. And Birgitte? Don't let it become one person's tool. If Henrik is ill the day before an evening, someone else must be able to set it up. That's the real test. Okay. Henrik, stop it. Stopping.

name: Onboarding a new colleague into the team workspace
summary: Synthetic sample. At a participation agency in Ontario, Canada, Leah walks her new colleague Joaquín through how the team uses its busy dembrane workspaces, recording the session so he can ask the assistant about it later; the analyst Priya drops in. They cover one workspace per client with the client as data owner and observer, the naming convention (client, process, session, date) and a sandbox for tests, and the team's project context template: who is in the room, questions per round, what is fixed and open, which statements are the agency's own, proper nouns, noise and language warnings, and a no-names line. Key terms come from asking the client which words an outsider would misspell. Tags are agreed before and set as portal tags; conversation names are table labels written on the host guide. The core habit is tidy before you analyse: delete tests, handle duplicate recordings, open anything that looks empty, rename, fix tags, add key terms and retranscribe (then delete the old copy), tag what has been reviewed. A story about a report counting the same table twice explains why. Saved Ask templates, report review against cited sources, and reading one transcript in full close the session.

chunks.text: I'm recording this, Joaquín, it's our onboarding ritual. Next week when you've forgotten what I said about tags, you can ask the assistant, what did Leah say about tags, instead of me. Which is better for both of us. That's very efficient. It's survival. So, this is the workspace list. We have one workspace per client, plus our own internal one. And inside each, the projects. And yes, there is a project called Untitled project 3. That's from before the rules. We don't talk about Untitled project 3.

Why one workspace per client? Why not everything in ours? Because the client owns their data, not us. Their workspace is set up with them as the data owner, their people come in as observers, so they can watch what's happening but not chat or change things. And at the end of the engagement it can be handed to them. Also, once a client saw another client's project name on a shared screen during a call. It was nothing secret. It was still once too many.

Okay. Naming. Every project is client, process, session, date. So, Harrowfield Transit, route review, session 2, and the date written year, month, day so it sorts. If you'd write one report about it, it's one project. Two sessions with different questions, two projects. And every client workspace has a project called ZZ Sandbox, which sorts to the bottom. Every test recording goes in there. Not in the real project, ever. If I find hello hello testing in a real project, you buy coffee.

Next, the project context. This is the most important thing I'll show you today. We have a template in the shared drive, and you fill in every heading, every project. Who is in the room. What we ask in each round, word for word. What's already decided and what's open. Which statements on the table cards are ours, so they're read as prompts and not as what participants think. Proper nouns. Warnings, like, dinner setting, expect background noise. And the last line, always the same.

Do not attribute statements to named individuals. Why does it matter so much? Isn't it just a description? It's what the language model reads before it does anything. The summaries, the answers in Ask, the reports, and the questions participants get if Explore is on. If the context is one line, you get generic answers. If the context says the city has already fixed the route and only the stops are open, the answers stop telling you that people want a different route, as if that's news.

Then key terms. Separate field. That's for the transcription. Names, places, acronyms, the client's internal jargon. Here's the trick. On the kick-off call, I ask the client one question: what words would an outsider misspell? They always know. Street names, the name of the programme, some acronym nobody outside their building uses. If you get those right before the first session, you save hours. And if the project is anonymised you can't retranscribe later anyway, it's switched off for anonymised conversations. So get them right first.

Okay. Tags. We agree the tags before the session, with the client. Round 1, Round 2, and the stakeholder groups if we need to compare them, like residents, business owners, staff. They're set as portal tags, so the table host taps one when they start recording. Keep it short. If there are twelve tags, people panic and type their name. Can I add tags afterwards? You can, by hand, per conversation. We have one we add afterwards, called check, for anything that needs a second look.

And names? The name field is a table label. Table host types T3 R1. Table three, round one. We edit the host guide, the printed sheet on each table, so the first line says exactly that, with an example. If you don't, you get table3, three, Tbl 3, and a person's actual name. And then on the Monitor during the evening you can't tell which table has gone quiet. With labels, you see T4 R1, screen locked, and you walk to table four.

Now. The habit. If you take one thing from today, take this. Tidy the conversations before you analyse. Every time. Before you ask a single question. Let me show you on last week's project. It's the library one, session 1, look at the list. What do you see? Um. Some are called participant. There's one called test qr. Two T2 R1 at the same time. A few very short ones. Exactly. That's a normal list after a normal evening. Nobody did anything wrong.

So, step by step. Test qr, delete. It's in the wrong project anyway. The two T2 R1, that's two phones on the same table, the host was being careful. Open both. Usually you keep the longer one. If both are useful, keep both, but when you ask questions, tick only one, otherwise that table counts twice. Then the short ones. Don't go by the time. Open them. Look for the empty badge, or no transcript. We once had a full recording with no duration showing.

And a forty-second one can be someone who said the one sharp thing of the night. Then rename participant to the table label. Fix the tags if someone tapped the wrong round. If you see a word the transcription keeps getting wrong, add it to key terms and retranscribe those conversations. That makes a new copy of each, so check it and delete the old one, or the table counts twice. When one is reviewed, tag it reviewed. And deleting has no undo. Read the name before you confirm. Out loud, if you need to.

And when the event is over, you close the project for new conversations with the toggle. So no one adds a stray recording from the bus home. Why all this? It feels like a lot. Because of the parking story. Do I want to hear the parking story? You do. A while ago we sent a client a report that said parking was raised at a majority of tables. They were thrilled, parking was their whole argument. Then their analyst started counting.

Hi, sorry, are you doing the parking story? I'm doing the parking story, Priya, help me. Okay, so, three of those tables were the same table recorded on two phones, plus a mic test where I said parking, parking, parking, can you hear me, because I was looking at the car park out of the window. That's true. That's a true story. Majority of tables became a third of tables. Since then: tidy first, and we count anything that says most or all.

Okay. I'm convinced. Good. Now Ask. We have saved templates in this workspace, pinned at the top. Type a slash in the question box and they come up. Matrix: groups in columns, themes in rows, an X where it was discussed. That shows you in one glance what everyone talked about and what only some groups did. Tensions and dilemmas. Only one group said. Who's missing, meaning groups people talked about but who weren't at the tables. And a quotes on a theme template.

And every one of them ends with, don't mention names, keep the language plain. The built-in ones are good too, Compare and Contrast, Narratives. The way we work: first map with the assistant, broad questions, then zoom in, now just the business owners, now just round two. When you're drafting something a client will read, switch to a Specific Details chat on a fixed set of conversations, so you know exactly what it's looking at. Filter the list by tag first and select all, it's quicker than ticking boxes.

Reports. For a client report we write our own instructions. Usually sections per question, because people want to find what their table said, not a theme soup. Then review. Every claim with a number, check it. Every quote, click through to the source and copy it from the transcript, not from the report. Every most, many, all, count it. And Priya's rule. My rule. Before you trust any summary in a project, read one full transcript start to finish. One. You'll know straight away how good the summaries are.

Can the assistant remember our conventions? Like the naming? You can ask it to remember things for you, or for the whole workspace. I've asked it to remember our naming convention and the no-names line. It also suggests improvements to the setup, like key terms it thinks are missing. It proposes, it never changes anything itself. You accept or you don't. I'd say read the suggestions, they're often good, and sometimes it suggests a key term that's obviously a person's name, which you do not want.

What about getting data out? For a handover, the transcript zip plus the report as a PDF. Priya sometimes connects her own tools to a project for one research client, through an MCP connection, but only where the client agreed to that in writing. Don't do that on your own. Ask first. Okay. And sharing with the client? The client decides. Some want a published link, some want a PDF, some want us to walk them through it in a half-hour call. The call works best.

Okay. Your first task. Last week's library project, session 1. Tidy it, everything we just did, before Thursday's analysis meeting. Don't ask it a single question until you're done. Then send me the list of what you changed, and I'll check it. Is this a test? Yes. Everyone does it. Priya deleted the wrong conversation on hers. Leah. It's in the onboarding recording now, Priya, it's history. I'll stop it here. Ask the assistant if you forget anything. And then ask me anyway.

name: Museum team debrief after a deliberate failure rehearsal
summary: Synthetic sample. A small maritime museum in Wales is preparing its first community evening with dembrane. Instead of a normal rehearsal, Gwen, the learning manager, ran a failure rehearsal: twelve staff and volunteers sat at three tables in a separate rehearsal project, and each got a sealed envelope with one secret thing to get wrong. This is their debrief. They let a screen lock, put a phone in a coat pocket, phoned a recording phone, spoke Welsh into a project set to English, set two tables too close together, did an everyone-scan-now moment and planted one absurd idea at one table. They learn what each failure looks like, that a green recording pill on the Monitor can hide a phone that hears almost nothing unless you read the latest transcript line, that announcements and neighbouring tables end up in transcripts, and that Ask lists a one-off idea alongside widely shared ones unless you ask how many tables raised each point and open the sources. Popcorn on the café screen was fun but put the planted idea in big letters, so they will use it only as ambience. They write a phone check into the running order and plan for the Welsh tables: a Welsh speaker reads the transcripts, because the summaries come in the project's language.

chunks.text: Right, is it going? Green dot. Okay. This is the debrief, and I'm recording it into the rehearsal project, not the real one, which is the whole point of having a rehearsal project. Hello, everybody, thank you. I think that was the most fun I've ever had in a staff meeting. For the record, because Leila wasn't here at the briefing: we had twelve of us at three tables, pretending to be residents talking about the new galleries in the dry dock building. And everybody got an envelope.

With one secret thing to get wrong. Because, my thinking was, a normal rehearsal tells you it works when everything goes right. I wanted to see what it looks like when it goes wrong, so that on the night we recognise it in thirty seconds instead of finding out next morning. So. Let's open the envelopes, one by one, and say what happened. Robin, you were on the Monitor laptop the whole time, so you saw most of it. Owain, you go first. What was yours?

Mine said, let your screen lock and don't tell anyone. So I put the phone down, didn't touch it, and it went dark after, what, thirty seconds, because my auto-lock is on the shortest setting. I didn't even know that about my own phone. And on the Monitor it said screen locked, for table one, within a minute or so. I saw it, I walked over, I said Owain, your phone, and he pretended to be surprised. Very good acting, Owain. Thank you. Years of practice.

And in the transcript, what does it look like? There's just a hole. It's talking, talking, then nothing for the minutes it was locked, then talking again. So if you didn't know, you'd think table one went quiet. Okay, so lesson one, everyone's auto-lock off before the evening, it's on the table host checklist, and somebody on the Monitor all evening. Next. Leila. Mine was, put the phone in your coat pocket and leave it recording. So I did. In the inside pocket, on the chair.

And this is the interesting one. The transcript is a few words, rustling, one sentence of Ffion's. Fifteen minutes of that. Robin, did the Monitor show it? The pill said recording, the whole time, happy green, no warning. The level meter flickered, from the rustling. The transcript line under it would have shown me, but I was only watching the pills. So a green pill means it's recording, not that it can hear the table. That's important. What do we do about that?

The mic check at the start, when it shows the level, the host has to actually look at it. And the host guide says phone in the middle, face up, screen on. And Robin, ten minutes in, you go down the Monitor and read the last transcript line for each table. Is there actual talk coming in? Not reading it properly, just looking. That's a good one. A phone check moment, ten minutes in, in the running order. Write it down. Ffion, yours. Mine said, speak Welsh for the whole of round one. Which I would anyway, honestly.

So the project is set to English, and table three, Ffion and Dafydd and the volunteers, did round one in Welsh. And the transcript is in Welsh, mostly. Ffion read it at the break. She says most of it is right and the place names are a mess. Dry dock became try doc. Ha. But the summary is in English, because the project is, and it's very confident. Ffion says it got the gist and made one thing up. And none of us on the English side could have told.

So what do we do on the night? We'll have Welsh speakers, maybe two tables. Welsh isn't one of the portal languages, so the screens will be English, but we write our own welcome text in both. Welsh key terms. And a Welsh speaker reads the Welsh transcripts, not the summaries, before anything goes in a report. I don't know how good it is over a whole evening. I'd rather find out next week with Ffion than on the night with the town. And I'll ask dembrane directly. Fine. Next.

Dafydd, yours? Mine said, when the phone at table two is recording, ring it. So I rang Bethan's phone, which was table two's phone. And it stopped. Well, the recording paused, and on the Monitor it said audio stopped, with a question mark. And I didn't hear the phone ring, because it was on silent, but it still took the microphone. So that's Do Not Disturb. Not silent. Do Not Disturb. Silent is not enough. That's exactly the kind of thing I wanted to learn today.

Then the room envelope, that was mine, Robin. My envelope was for the furniture. I put table two and table three about a metre apart, by the café machine. Too close, on purpose. And when you read table two's transcript, there are whole sentences from table three in it. Ffion's Welsh turns up in it too. And the coffee machine is just a roar. So: spread the tables, use the whole gallery, and nobody near the café machine. If you can hear the next table better than your own, move.

And my announcement is in there too. I said five minutes left, very loudly, and it's in every single transcript. That's fine, actually, it's useful, you can see where round one ends. But if I say something about the evening, like, the council has already decided the roof, that's in there too, and the summary might pick it up as if a resident said it. So I'll keep my announcements short and boring. Five minutes left. Thank you. That's all.

Then the start. My envelope said, at the start, tell everybody to scan the QR just to see what it is. Which, I'm sorry, everybody did. Twelve people. And now there are nine extra conversations in the list, empty, or with three seconds of somebody saying oh, is it on. Imagine that with sixty people. Sixty empty rows and you have to open every one to check. So, only the table host scans. If people want to see it, I show it on the screen. Agreed. Never again.

Okay, and the last envelope. The planted idea. Table one was told to say one ridiculous thing, once, and then never again. Which was? A submarine café. In the dry dock. Ha. Owain said it with a very straight face. And then afterwards I opened Ask and asked, what did people want for the new galleries? And it listed things, the boat-building workshop, more about the women who worked in the yard, a children's corner. And submarine café. Just there in the list.

Like it was one of the themes. It didn't say how many tables. It didn't say one person, once, maybe joking. And then I asked a follow-up, how many tables raised each of these, and show me the quotes. And then it was clear. The workshop came up at all three tables, the women of the yard at two, the submarine café once, at table one, from Owain. So the answer was honest when I asked. The first answer just didn't tell me the weight.

That's the lesson for me. Always ask how many tables, and always open the sources before something goes into a report. Because in the real evening nobody's joking on purpose, but somebody will say something once and it will sit next to things everyone said. And the council will think it's a priority. Yes. And there's one more. We tried Popcorn on the screen in the café, during the break. The live slides. And everybody loved it. People's own words, coming up.

And the phrase in the biggest letters, for about two minutes, was submarine café. Ha. So, Popcorn. It's fun, it made people come over and say, hey, we said that. But it's a beta, and it shows what's being said, not what matters. So on the night, I'd use it as atmosphere on the café screen in the break, and never call it the results. The results come later, after we've read things. I agree. It's a mood board, not a report. Okay.

Then what goes into the running order? Let me read what I've got. Before: auto-lock off and Do Not Disturb on every host phone, on the checklist. Key terms for the town, the dry dock, the yard, the ships' names. The Welsh tables tested beforehand, with a Welsh speaker reading the transcripts. Tables spread out, nobody near the café machine. Portal edits finished before we print the QR cards, then scan the printed cards. During: only hosts scan. Robin on the Monitor all evening. Phone check at ten minutes.

After: close the project to new conversations, tidy first, delete the tests and empties, then ask, and always ask how many tables and open the sources. Popcorn in the break as atmosphere. Did I miss anything? The rehearsal project. We keep it? We keep it separate, and we delete it after the evening. It's full of submarine cafés. And Owain's acting. It's a historical record, Gwen. It is not. Delete it. Okay, last thing. Would we do this again? The envelopes? Yes. Every new team.

I'd do it before any first event. It took an hour and a half and some biscuits, and I learned more than from reading the guide twice. Although we should read the guide too. Read the guide too, yes. Okay. Thank you, everybody. Ffion, can you and Dafydd do the Welsh test with me next Tuesday? Of course. In Welsh. Only in Welsh. Then I'm stopping the recording now, before Owain proposes the submarine café again. It was a good idea, though.

name: Assembly organisers, day 3 debrief
summary: Synthetic sample. Three organisers of a five-day citizens' assembly on water in dry summers, in an invented German town, debrief in the empty hall after day 3: Birte (project lead at the town), Malik (lead facilitator) and Ines (who runs the dembrane side). The highlight was an unplanned read-aloud loop: a short bullet draft of the day, pulled from all six tables in Ask, was read to the room while the plenary phone kept recording, so members corrected it in their own words and the correction became data for the next morning. They share the exact prompt that keeps disagreements as disagreements, and why they left anonymise off (to keep the audio) and put "do not mention names" in prompts and context instead. They argue one project per day versus one for everything, and settle on per-day projects with their own context, moving conversations into one assembly project before the last day after testing on two. Other lessons: record the plenary and expert talks as separate, named conversations and stop the phone at breaks (a four-hour recording ran through lunch), a naming pattern printed on the host guide, portal tags per round, watching the Monitor for locked screens, moving Verify before the coffee break, and nobody asking the assistant to write the recommendations.

chunks.text: Is it going? The dot's green, yes. Okay. Day three debrief, it's about quarter past six, the members have all gone home and the chairs are half stacked. It's Birte, Malik and me, Ines. We promised ourselves a short debrief every evening, so that the last day isn't the first time we ask how it went. Malik, you have your list face on, so you start.

I do have a list. But first the good bit, because I want it on the recording. The read-aloud at the end of today. Best twenty minutes of the assembly so far, and we nearly cut it for time. For anyone listening later: at four, Ines pulled a draft summary of the day across all six tables, I read it out to the whole room, and the plenary phone just kept recording while they reacted.

And they reacted. The draft said the members "broadly agreed" that farms should get water first in a dry summer. And Gerda from table four put her hand up and said, no, we did not agree. Half of us said drinking water and the hospital first, then farms, and the other half said gardens are food too for a lot of people in this town, and you've made it sound like a decision. And then three others joined in.

Which is exactly what we want. Their correction is now in the transcript, in their words, with their reasons. Tomorrow morning I don't need my memory of what Gerda said. I can go into the day three project and ask the assistant, what did the room correct during the read-aloud, and it has the actual exchange. The critique is data. I didn't really understand that until today.

Can I be the boring one? It only worked because the draft was short. Ines, how long was it? Maybe four hundred words. I asked for bullets, one point per bullet, and I told it to keep disagreements as disagreements. The first version I got was this lovely smooth paragraph where everybody was thoughtful and nuanced and nothing was in tension with anything. That one I didn't read to anyone.

What did you type, exactly? Because I want it in the host notes for the third weekend. Roughly this: summarise what the tables said today about who gets water first in a drought. Use bullet points. Where tables disagree, do not merge them. Write the disagreement as a disagreement, with the main reason on each side and one short quote for each. Do not mention names. Then I saved it as a template, so tomorrow I just type the slash and pick it.

And the "do not mention names" is because we left anonymise off? Yes. We talked about that before day one. Birte wanted to keep the audio, so that if a member says "that's not what I said", we can go back and listen. Anonymising takes the audio away. So it's off, and instead every prompt says no names, and the project context says it too. It mostly holds. Mostly. On day one a table summary called a man by his first name, because the facilitator had said it about ten times.
