Which I caught, and fixed in the summary before anyone saw it. But it's a real trade-off and I don't think we got it entirely right. For the next assembly I'd decide it much earlier, together with the legal basis and our privacy officer. And maybe just turn anonymise on before the first recording, because it works while the recordings are processed. Switch it on later and only the new ones are anonymised; the old ones you'd have to retranscribe one by one into anonymised copies.

Okay. My list. Number one is the thing we argued about in July: one project per day, or one project for the whole assembly. Birte won, so we have one project per day. Day one, day two, day three, each with its own context. And I'll admit it has been useful. But I'm still not convinced, so let's actually talk about it now that we've lived with it.

Go on then. Make the case. The case is the final synthesis. On day five the members want to see how their thinking moved from day one to day five. If it's five projects, I can't ask one question across all of it, because the chat works inside one project. So I end up asking five times and stitching the answers together by hand, which is exactly the work we brought this in to avoid.

And my case is the context. Day one was getting to know each other and the expert talks on groundwater. Day two was the farmers and the water utility. Today was trade-offs. Each morning I rewrite the context for that day: what the sessions are, which experts spoke, the names of the wells and the two streams, the questions on the table cards. If it's one project, I either write one enormous context that's half wrong on any given day, or I keep editing it, and then the day one summaries were made with a different context than day three. That bothers me.

Can I say what I think we do? We keep the per-day projects for the work in the room, because the loops are daily: tables, Verify, read-aloud, next morning. And before day five we move all the conversations into one assembly project, tagged by day, with a context that describes the whole arc, and we make the final report there with the timeline view. You can move a conversation to another project, one at a time, so that's an afternoon. And I'll try it on two first, because I'm not moving a hundred and twenty recordings on faith.

And nothing has an undo, right? Deleting certainly doesn't. So yes, two first, and I'll check the tags and summaries come along. Fine. I can live with that. Number two. Recording the plenary. We recorded the expert talks as their own conversations, which is great. The hydrologist's talk is in there, and a member could ask, basically, what did she say about the aquifer, and get it with a source.

But the plenary phone on day two recorded for four hours. Through lunch. Through lunch, and the coffee machine, and someone's phone call about their car. Whose phone? The plenary phone. My fault. I hit record at nine and walked away. Today I stopped it at every break and started a new conversation after, and named them. "D3 plenary 1 expert Q and A", "D3 plenary 2 read-aloud". Otherwise the lunch chat ends up in the summaries.

And I had the Monitor open on the laptop at the back, so I could see which tables were actually recording. Table two showed screen locked twice. Both times the facilitator had put the phone face down because the light bothered him. We fixed it in a minute each time. On day one, before we used the Monitor properly, we lost twenty minutes of table six and didn't know until the evening.

Which is my number three. Naming. Day one was chaos. "Table 1", "Tisch eins", "T1", and one called "Gerhard" because a facilitator typed his own name. Today every facilitator had the same line on the host guide we printed next to the QR code: D, day number, T, table number, R, round. "D3 T4 R2". And it sorts. I can see at a glance that table four, round two exists and is twenty-eight minutes long.

And tags. We turned on portal tags for the round topic, so when they scan they tap "who gets water first" or "paying for it", and the conversation arrives already sorted. It helps the assistant too. When I ask about paying for it, I filter on that tag first, instead of hoping it finds the right parts of every conversation.

Four. Keeping disagreements sharp. The read-aloud worked because Ines told it not to merge. But the Verify moment at the tables is more mixed. Each table gets five minutes, the facilitator opens Verify, the group reads the outcome and approves it, or says what's wrong and revises it. Table one loved it. Table five said it was pointless because it only said what they'd just said, and they were tired.

To be fair, it's supposed to say what they just said. That's the point. It's not the model's view, it's their record. If it's boring, that's because it's right. Sure, but boring at a quarter to four is a real cost. I'd move it before the coffee break, not after. And I'd tell the facilitators again: you're asking "does this reflect what we said", not "do you agree with it". Table three started voting on the points, which is a completely different thing.

Good. Write that down. Is there a five? Five is about us, not the tool. When I read the draft aloud today, I was tempted to tidy it as I went. Skip the clumsy bit, round off a sentence. I didn't, mostly. But tomorrow I want someone else to read it. A member, maybe. Then it's clearly not the organisers presenting their view of what the room thinks.

I like that a lot. One thing from me, and then we go home. The members write the recommendations themselves on day five. I want to be very clear, in front of everyone, including the three of us, that nobody types "write the recommendations" into the assistant. We use it to find what was said, to check it, and to bring the disagreements back to the room. The words on the final sheet are theirs.
Agreed. I'll put that in the project context as well, so it's said to the model and not only to us. Good. Stop the recording, Ines. Chairs.

name: Multilingual assembly, getting the languages right
summary: Synthetic sample. Four facilitators of a citizens' assembly on school traffic in a bilingual Swiss town talk on a video call after day 2, recorded with a phone next to the laptop speaker. Corinne, who set up dembrane, explains the day 1 mistake: one project set to German, on the belief that giving French tables the French portal link would be enough. The link only changes the welcome and consent screens. Verify and the summaries follow the project's language, so French speakers got German Verify outcomes, and the Albanian-speaking table got a plausible German summary of a discussion that never happened, although its transcript was fine. She fixed it that evening with a separate French project, moving the French tables' conversations one by one and regenerating their summaries. Albanian can't be set as a project language, so Arben reads that table's transcripts himself. Aurélie and Matthias argue language tables versus mixed and settle on language rounds plus a mixed "bridge" round with a tag. Practices: put the language in every conversation name, colour-code the QR codes, test the real language mix and read summaries against transcripts beforehand, read the consent aloud where the portal has no screens in that language, add key terms in both languages, and quote in the original language with the team's own translation marked as theirs.

chunks.text: Can you all hear me? Arben, you're on mute. There. Okay. I've got my phone lying next to the laptop speaker, no headphones, because the last time I recorded a call with headphones on, the transcript only had my half. So this is the facilitators' check-in for the Brennwil assembly, after day two. Aurélie, Matthias, Arben, and I'm Corinne. I want to get down what went wrong on day one while we still remember it honestly.

Honestly is the word. Day one was a mess, but a useful mess. From the French side it was not useful, Matthias, it was a mess. Can I say it? My table spoke French for two hours, and when we opened Verify at the end, the outcome came up in German. In German! Three of my members don't read German well. So they looked at me, and I translated a summary of what they had just said back to them. It was absurd.

That's on me. I set up one project for the day and set the conversation language to German, because German is the majority here and the plenary is in German with interpretation. And I thought, the portal has a French version, so I'll give the French tables the French link and that's solved. And the French link only changes the welcome screens and the consent. Exactly. The link is the intro. The project's language is what Verify and the summaries are written in. The transcript just follows what people say. Different settings, and I mixed them up.

For my table it was different. We speak Albanian mostly, families from Kosovo and North Macedonia, and two younger members who grew up here and switch into Swiss German. The transcript is actually in Albanian, with the German bits in German. But the summary was in German, and it said we talked about parking at the station. We never talked about the station. We talked about the bus stop on the station road. Which is not the same thing at all.

Which is the scary one, because the summary sounded plausible. If you didn't know that table, you'd believe it. How did you notice, actually? Not on the day. On day one the only sign was Aurélie's table and Verify. In the evening I opened each table's summary next to its transcript, and Arben's was the one I couldn't check, because I don't read Albanian. So I rang him. He read me the transcript and said, no, that's the bus stop.

And what did you do? Nothing clever. That evening I made a second project with the conversation language set to French, copied the context across, moved the French tables' conversations into it one by one, and regenerated their summaries, which came out in French. The Verify outcomes from day one stay in German, they were already made. Albanian isn't one of the languages you can set, so Arben's table stays in the German project. Aurélie, your table's summary is in French now. Arben?

For us it changes little. The transcript is good for the younger members, less for the older man from the village near Prizren, strong dialect, he speaks fast. But I can find what he said. The summaries I don't trust, so I read our transcripts myself and write two lines in German per conversation. Verify we skip at my table. One caveat for anyone hearing this later: we added key terms and retranscribed some of day one. That only works with anonymise off, and each retranscribe makes a new copy, so delete the old one.

Can I make my point now? Because I think the fix on day two went too far the other way. Go. On day two we split the tables by language. German tables, French tables, the Albanian table. Clean recordings, two projects, the French tables get Verify in French. Lovely. But the whole point of an assembly in a bilingual town is that people talk across the language line. If the francophones only talk to francophones, we've built two assemblies in one hall.

But Matthias, a mixed table where half the members don't follow half the conversation is not deliberation either. At your table on day one, the two French speakers said almost nothing for the first hour. Because nobody had told them they could speak French. When I said, speak in whichever language you think in, we'll manage, they started. And the recording handled it, more or less. It switches mid-sentence. Not perfectly, but the transcript has both languages in it.

What we agreed for day three, on the record, because the organisers will ask: rounds one and two in language tables, the French tables in the French project, the German and Albanian tables in the German one. Round three is the bridge round, mixed tables with an interpreter at each, and those go into the project of whichever language most of that table speaks, with a tag "mixed" so we can find them. And in the context of each project we write that people at mixed tables switch between German and French, and that quotes should stay in the language they were said.

And the names. Please tell the others about the names. Yes. On day one the names were all over the place. Now every conversation is named with the day, the table, the round and the language. "D2 T5 R1 FR". "D3 T2 R3 DE plus FR". Because when you're in the German project at eleven at night and you see a conversation called "Tisch 3", you don't know if it was a German table or a mixed one that landed there. The language label costs nothing and saves you every time.

And on the printed host guide I'd like the QR codes in different colours. On day two Matthias's table scanned the French one by accident. In my defence, it was very nicely printed. Blue for the German project, red for the French one, and the language written in big letters above each code, in that language. And we tested both on our own phones on Thursday evening, before day two. We should have done that before day one.

We did test before day one. But I tested in German, on the German project. I never tested a French conversation. That's the real lesson for me. Test the actual language mix you'll have in the room. Get Aurélie and Arben to talk for three minutes each in their own language, and once mixed, and read the transcripts and the summaries before the members arrive. Not after lunch on day one.

One more thing about Albanian. The portal screens, the welcome and the consent cards, are not in Albanian. The interface comes in a set of languages and ours isn't one of them. So I read the consent card aloud in Albanian and explained what happens with the recording, and each person said yes or no, and then I tapped through. I think that's fine, but I want it written down that I did it, and how. Good. Write me the three sentences you said and I'll put them in the facilitator pack, so whoever does it next time says the same thing.

And the key terms. On day one "Schulhausplatz" came out as three different things. I've added the street names, the school names, the two bus lines and the name of the bridge to the key terms in both projects, in the spellings people actually use. Including "place de l'école", because the French speakers don't say Schulhausplatz. And the mayor's name, because she spoke at the opening and it came out as a kind of cheese.

Last thing, and then we eat. The analysis. Two projects means two places to ask. For the day summaries I'll ask the same questions in both with the same saved template, so the answers line up, and Arben checks the Albanian table's part against the transcripts. I write the day summary for the organisers in German, but every quote I use I copy from the transcript in the language it was said, and I put our translation underneath and mark it as ours. Not the model's translation. Ours.

Why not the model's? Because if a member reads it and says "I didn't say that", I want to show them their own words, then my translation, and they can argue with my translation. That's an argument I can have. Arguing with a machine translation of a summary of what you said is too many steps away from you. Fair. Okay. Stop it, Corinne, I'm hungry.

name: Planning drop-in, sorting what's fixed and what's open
summary: Synthetic sample. The morning after a planning drop-in in an invented Scottish town, planning officer Fiona and engagement officer Dev record themselves working through the project so a colleague can run the next one. Eight staff with phones held 127 one-to-one conversations at six map tables, using recording links with tag and title prefilled, which broke when staff moved tables. They clean up first: check for a transcript instead of the duration column, retag, add place names to key terms and retranscribe, deleting the old copies. The core move is a project context that spells out what is already decided and what is open, then an Ask prompt that sorts comments into decided, open and outside the council's remit, with sources. Clicking into the sources shows "came up a lot" means three or four, so Fiona never lets the model count, and Dev argues against any numbers because one resident visited three tables. They ask who is talked about but absent (teenagers, shift workers) and, rather than asking the model what teenagers would think, book sessions at the youth club and distribution centre canteen at shift change. Then they build a four-part committee report where every point carries a quote copied from the transcript and the conversation name, published by link and sent to residents who left an email.

chunks.text: Right. Recording. This is Fiona and Dev, it's the morning after the Kilbrannoch drop-in. We're going to sit with the project and work out what we've got, and we're recording ourselves doing it, because Isla is running the next one in Strathcorran and she wasn't here last night. So, Isla, hello. This is what we did and what we'd do differently. Dev, how many?

A hundred and twenty-seven conversations, over three and a half hours. Which sounds amazing until you sort by length. Go on. Nineteen are under a minute. Some of those are fine, somebody saying "I just want the bins sorted" and walking off. But at least eleven are empty. No transcript at all. That's staff pressing start and then the person turning round to talk to their neighbour, or going off to get a cup of tea.

Don't go by the duration column, by the way. I nearly deleted one yesterday that showed no length, and it's got a full six-minute chat about the path by the burn. Open it and look at whether there's a transcript. Noted. So, for Isla, how it worked. Six map tables: housing, getting about, green space and the burn, the high street, the depot site itself, and one called "anything else", which was the busiest table, of course.

And eight of us with phones. Two planners, me, two people from roads, one from housing, two from the community team. No participants scanning anything this time. People came in, looked at the maps, one of us went up and said, can I ask you a few questions about this, and would you mind if my phone records it, it just turns into text, no names. Most people said yes. A few said no and we just talked and wrote a sticky note, which I'll type in later as a text conversation.

The trick that made it work, sort of, was the recording links. Before the evening I made a link for each table with the tag and the title already filled in. So the housing phone opened the portal already tagged "housing" and titled "Map: Housing". Nobody had to type with a resident standing there waiting. Which worked beautifully until people moved. Until people moved. Gordon from roads started at getting about and ended up at the depot table for an hour, and every conversation he did there is tagged "getting about".

So that's twenty minutes of retagging this morning. Not the end of the world. For Isla: either staff stay put at a table, or they reopen the right link when they move. I'd put that on the host guide in big letters. We printed the host guide and stuck it to the back of each map board, which was good. It reminded people to keep the screen on, and I didn't see any locked screens on the Monitor.

I had the Monitor open on the laptop by the tea urn. Honestly, the most useful thing was just seeing that eight phones were recording at once. One phone, the housing one, kept going quiet, and it turned out the officer was putting it in her pocket between residents, still recording. That's the forty-minute conversation that's mostly the inside of a coat.

Right. So. The real work, the thing I care about. What is fixed and what is open. Because at every drop-in about a third of what we hear is about things that are already decided. If the committee report just lists everything, it looks like we're ignoring people. If we leave it out, it looks like we're hiding it. This is why the context was so long. This is why the context was so long.

Read it out, for Isla. I wrote, roughly: this is a drop-in consultation on the Kilbrannoch town centre and depot site development brief. Already decided, not part of this consultation: the depot site is allocated for housing in the adopted local development plan; the junction with the main road is the roads authority's responsibility. Open for comment: the mix and type of homes on the depot site, the path network and the green link along the burn, play space, parking on Mill Wynd, what the high street needs. Then the street names, the abbreviations like LDP, and: do not mention names.

And key terms. Mill Wynd, the Haugh, Strathcorran Road, the depot, Glenmorie Hall. The Haugh still came out as "the hog" in four conversations. I've added it again and I'll retranscribe those four. Each one comes back as a new copy, so afterwards I delete the four old ones, or the hog is in there twice. Note that down for Isla. Done.

Okay. Ask. I'm typing: go through all the conversations. Sort what people said into three groups: comments about things already decided, comments about things open in this consultation, and comments about things outside the council's planning remit. For each group list the main points, with the conversations they come from. Do not mention names. That's a lot in one go. It is what I want, though. Let's see.

It's back. Already decided: people objecting to housing on the depot at all, and worries about the main road junction, which is roads. Open: lots on the green link, parking on Mill Wynd, play space, people asking for bungalows for older folk. Outside our remit: the GP surgery, the bus timetable, the bins. The bins. Always the bins. Right, now click into the sources. That one, parking on Mill Wynd, it says it came up a lot.

Five sources. Let me open them. One, yes, a man who lives on Mill Wynd, very clear. Two, yes. Three is about parking, but on the high street, not Mill Wynd. Four is the coat conversation. Ha. Five is fine. So it's real, but "a lot" is three or four. And that's the thing I keep saying. I don't let it count for me. If the committee report has a number in it, it's a number I got by filtering the tag and reading them myself.

Can I disagree a bit, though? I'm not sure we should put numbers in at all. That man who came to three tables is three conversations. One person, counted three times. If we write "raised in twelve conversations", a councillor will read it as twelve people. Fair. So we write it differently. "Raised at several tables", the quote, and the conversation it came from. And one line in the method section: these are conversations, not people, and one person may have spoken at more than one table. I can live with that.

Now the bit I'm proudest of from the last one, so Isla should do it too. I'm asking: who is talked about in these conversations, but doesn't seem to have been here? And? Young people. Teenagers come up in about a dozen conversations, the skate park, nowhere to go on the high street, and as far as it can tell almost none of the conversations are with a teenager. Also people who work shifts at the distribution centre, mentioned by their parents. That goes in the report as a gap, not as a finding.

And not just noted. I'll ring the youth club this afternoon, Dev. Their Thursday night, their room, phones on the pool table. And the distribution centre canteen at the six o'clock shift change, half an hour either side. Both before Strathcorran. Or, Fiona, we save ourselves the trip and ask the assistant what teenagers would think. Ha. No, Dev. It would write us a lovely paragraph about the skate park and every word of it would be made up. They're down the road. We go and ask them.

And the school session in September on top of that. Exactly. Now the report. For the committee I want four sections. What we heard on the open questions, theme by theme. What people said about things already decided, so the committee sees it and it isn't hidden. Things outside our remit, to pass on to roads and the health board. And who we didn't hear. Every point gets a short quote copied from the transcript, not from the chat answer, plus the name of the conversation, so any councillor can look it up.

Do they get access? We publish the report as a link and walk them through the conversations at the briefing on the fourth. And we had participant updates turned on in the portal, so the residents who left an email at the end get the report when we publish. Twenty-six of them, I think. Then we read it properly before we publish. Out loud, both of us. Last time the first draft said residents "welcomed" the green link. They didn't welcome it. Two people liked it, and one woman was worried it would bring motorbikes along the burn.

Put the motorbikes in. That's exactly the kind of thing that disappears in a summary and comes back as a complaint in two years. Right, Isla, that's us. Stay at your table or reopen the link. Decide what's fixed and write it in the context. Don't let it count for you. Ask who's missing, then go and find them. And read every quote in the transcript before it goes in. Stop the recording, Dev.

name: District team after the share-back evening
summary: Synthetic sample. In the community centre kitchen of a Swedish district, coordinator Johan and community connectors Hodan and Amira debrief after a share-back evening that ended a summer of listening in Somali, Arabic, Tigrinya, Dari and Swedish. A QR poster brought in four conversations, mostly tests. Connectors worked: people who know people, walking up with a phone at the market, the homework café and the laundry rooms. Hodan explains consent aloud where the portal has no screens in that language, and when someone declines she records her own account afterwards, tagged "connector reflection" so it isn't mistaken for the resident's voice. They describe one project per language (none of their languages can be set, so screens and summaries come in English while transcripts stay in the spoken language), a July check where connectors read transcripts while listening to the audio (place names poor until added as key terms), and teenagers choosing "type instead" because they didn't want friends to hear. At the share-back, quotes went up in the original language with the team's Swedish translation and were read aloud in both. A summary that said "unsafe in the district" turned out to mean one path at night. A short Popcorn trial, translated into English, worked until one phrase was mistranslated. Next time they will share back in July, not September.

chunks.text: Is it on? It's on. Okay. We said we'd record a little debrief tonight, the three of us, after the evening. It's Johan, Hodan and Amira, in the kitchen of the community centre in Gärdesvik, and there's still cake, so if you hear chewing, that's Hodan. That's not fair, it's you. So. Tonight was the share-back of the summer listening. About sixty people came, which for a Thursday is very good.

Let me say, for whoever listens to this, what we did, in short. From June to September we collected conversations about the district: the courtyards, the laundry rooms, safety at night, the youth club. In Somali, Arabic, Tigrinya, Swedish and some Dari. Not one big event. Lots of small moments. The Saturday market, the homework café, the Friday women's group, the laundry rooms. The laundry rooms were the best. Nobody is in a hurry in a laundry room.

The first thing I'd tell another district is: don't start with the QR code. We tried that in June. Posters with a QR code, tell us what you think. We got four conversations. Four. And two were Johan testing it. Three were me testing it. Three. What worked was us. People who know people, walking up with a phone and saying, in your language, can we talk for five minutes, it's for the district, I'll explain what happens with it.

At the market I had a phone, I opened the portal for the Somali project, and I explained the consent myself, because the screens are not in Somali. I say: this records, it becomes text, the district team reads it, no names, you can stop any time, and you can ask me to take it away afterwards. Then they say yes or no. Most say yes. The ones who say no, I talk with them anyway, and afterwards I record myself saying what they told me. And I say that in the recording: this is me, telling what a woman at the market told me.

Which matters, because that's not her voice, it's Hodan's account of it. We tag those "connector reflection" so in the analysis we can see the difference. I didn't think of that at first. Hodan did. Because otherwise it looks like I said all those things. And some of the things she said, I don't agree with.

The language thing. We made one project per language. Somali, Arabic, Tigrinya and so on. None of them is in the language list, Swedish neither, so they're all set to English, and the summaries come in English. But the transcripts stay in what people spoke, and each connector has her own project and her own key terms. The Arabic transcripts are good. Not perfect. The older men from my region, with the dialect, some words come out wrong. But I can read it and I know what was said.

And we checked, which I'd really recommend. In July, Hodan and Amira each took ten conversations in their language and listened to the audio while reading the transcript. Just to know how far to trust it. And? For the Somali, the young people, very good. The old women from the south, with the strong dialect, most of it fine, some sentences very strange. Place names terrible until Johan put them in the key terms.

The key terms list is now ridiculous. Every courtyard, the street names the way people say them and not the way they're on the map, the youth club's nickname, and the bus stop everybody calls after the old shop that closed years ago. That last one made a big difference. And "tvättstuga". Everyone says tvättstuga in the middle of Arabic. Now it's spelled right.

Type instead. Tell them about type instead. Yes, that was a surprise for me. The young people at the homework café didn't want to speak. Not because of literacy. Because the café is quiet, their friends are there, and they didn't want to say things out loud. So they pressed "type instead" on the portal and typed. Swedish mostly, some English, a lot of slang. And what they typed was much more honest than anything they'd have said out loud.

About a third of the youth input is typed. And the other way round: for the older women, typing was never going to happen. Some don't read in any language. For them the voice is everything. So the same portal, two doors. You just have to show people both doors. And you have to not make anyone feel stupid for choosing one.

Now tonight. The share-back. We've been promising since June that people would hear back, and it's the part districts usually get wrong. Three months later, a report in Swedish on a website, and nobody recognises themselves in it. So tonight we had the big screen in the hall and showed the results in short pieces, one theme at a time. A quote in the original language, and underneath our translation into Swedish.

And then we read every quote out loud. In the language, and then in Swedish. Because many people in that room cannot read the screen, either because of the language or because they don't read. If you only put it on the screen, you're telling them it's not for them. When I read the quote about the broken light in the courtyard on Kvarngatan, an old man said, loudly, "that's me!" Everyone laughed. And then he said, "and it's still broken." Which was also true.

Which is the other thing. Each theme had three columns: what we heard, what the district is already doing, and what we can't do and who can. Because the light is the housing company, not us. People need to see you've sorted it, not that you're pretending you can fix everything. Most of the work was that second column. And that was not the model's job. That was Johan walking round every department with a printout.

Tell them how you made the slides. The real way. Ha. Okay. In each language project I asked the assistant for the main themes, with sources, then "show me the quotes" for each theme, and I asked it to keep the language simple. Then Hodan and Amira opened every quote in its transcript to check it, and picked the ones that said it best. The model did the searching. The choosing was theirs.

And twice the summary said something the transcript didn't. It said people "feel unsafe in the district". But when I read the conversations, they said they feel unsafe on one path behind the school, at night, in winter. That's very different. "Unsafe in the district" is what a newspaper writes. That's the one I'd warn people about. The summaries go general. The people were specific. Always go back to the transcript.

And the Popcorn thing. Right. At the end we tried Popcorn, the live slides, for about ten minutes. It's early beta, and I said so to the room. It can't do Swedish, so it showed short phrases translated into English, and people liked seeing their own words. But one Somali phrase came out wrong, and somebody laughed in a way that wasn't kind. We stopped, Hodan explained what the person had actually meant, and it was fine. I'd use it again, but with a connector next to the screen.

And next time we start the share-back earlier. Not at the end of the summer. Already in July, a small one at the market: here's what you said in June, is this right? And we record that too, so the "no, that's not what we meant" is in the data as well. That's the plan for the spring. Hodan, do you want the last word? Bring cake. People stay for cake. Stop the recording.

name: Ministry analyst onboarding a new colleague
summary: Synthetic sample. Henrike, a senior policy analyst at a national transport ministry with nearly two hundred projects behind her, onboards Ruben in his second week. She makes the case for boring, predictable setups: a fixed naming pattern, "one report means one project" with tags per region, and a five-part context skeleton (the policy question, who is in the room by role, what is decided and what is open, terms and acronyms, what the analysis is for plus "do not mention names") so outputs from different projects can be compared. She shows four pinned custom templates, including one for tensions and one for who wasn't heard. Each week she schedules a report for Friday afternoon and reads it before publishing it for a steering group, since the time she published one unread with a technician's microphone test in it; a Thursday clean-up hour comes first. Chat works inside one project, so she compares across projects by keeping setups the same, pastes earlier reports into the portal as clearly labelled text conversations (one was once quoted back as if a participant had said it), and pilots the MCP connection only with information security's approval. Her list of when not to use dembrane: casework, simple minutes, decisions already taken, sessions where you can't say what happens with input, and huge single pastes.

chunks.text: Okay, it's recording. Ruben, this is for you, so that when you forget everything I say in the next half hour you can listen again. I'm Henrike, you're Ruben, it's your second week, and I've been doing this for about two and a half years. My workspace has, let me look, a hundred and ninety-one projects. Which is the first lesson. You will make a lot of projects. Most of them should be boring.

Boring how? Boring as in predictable. When I open a project from eighteen months ago, I want to know in five seconds what it is. So the name always follows the same pattern: year, month, the policy file, the kind of session, the number. "2026-09 Rural transport subsidy, expert session 3". Not "Session with the experts". Not "Test". Not "Copy of Copy of Regional". I have about thirty from my first months that look like that, and I dislike every one of them.

And one project is one session? Mostly. The rule I use: if you'd write one report about it, it's one project. A one-off expert session with twelve people is one project. A consultation round where we visit six regions with the same questions over six weeks and write one report at the end is also one project, with a tag per region. If the regions get different questions, it's six projects, because the summaries would be about different things.

Then the context. This is the thing I'm strictest about. Every project gets a context written from the same skeleton. I'll send it to you. Five parts. One, the policy question in plain words. Two, who is in the room, by role, not by name: "eight mobility officers from municipalities, two from the national transport agency, one researcher". Three, what's already decided and what's open. Four, the terms: acronyms, scheme names, laws by their short names. Five, what we want from the analysis, and the line "do not mention names".

Why the same skeleton every time? Isn't each session different? Because then the outputs are comparable. If one project has a two-line context and another has a page, the summaries come out different in ways that have nothing to do with what people said. And my director reads reports from a dozen projects side by side. She doesn't want creativity in my project contexts. She wants the differences that are really in the conversations.

Templates. Same idea. In Ask you can save your own templates and pin them, and then you type a slash and pick one. I have four that I use on nearly every project. "Session debrief", which asks for the main points per question, in bullets, with sources. "Tensions and dilemmas", which asks where participants disagreed and why, and says don't resolve the tension. "Practical barriers", for implementation sessions. And "What we did not hear", which asks which groups or perspectives are mentioned but not present.

And you just run all four? I run the debrief and the tensions on everything, the other two when they fit. But I always read the sources. Always. The first answer is usually a bit, how do I say it, diplomatic. It makes everyone sound reasonable. The tensions template exists because without it the model will happily tell you the room broadly agreed, when actually the municipal officers and the agency people disagreed about almost everything.

Scheduled reports. You'll like these and you'll be a bit scared of them. For the regional round, every Thursday I schedule a report for Friday at four. It's generated on its own with everything recorded up to then, I get a notification, I publish it, and the steering group reads it over the weekend. Why scared? Because it's tempting to publish at ten past four without reading. Once I did. It had two test recordings in it. Somebody from IT checking the microphone. "Testing, testing, is this the right room." The steering group asked whether that region had been sarcastic.

So now? So now Thursday afternoon is my clean-up hour, before I schedule the next one. Delete test recordings, check nothing is sitting there without a transcript, fix tags, tag what I've reviewed. Then on Friday it generates something I'm comfortable with. And I read every word before I press publish. It's a language model draft. If something in it is wrong, it's my name on the email that goes with it.

Can I ask about comparing? You have two hundred projects. Can you ask, I don't know, across all the rural transport ones, what changed since last year? Not in one chat, no. The chat works within one project. People ask me this every week. What I do instead is three things. First, the boring skeleton and the same templates, so I can put two reports side by side and compare them myself. That gets you most of the way, honestly.

Second, when a new round builds on an old one, I paste the old report into the new project's portal, using the text option, so it becomes a text conversation. Clearly named: "Prior report 2025, not a session". Then I can ask in the new project, what's different from last year's report? You have to name it clearly, and say in the context that it's a document, not participants, or it gets mixed into "what people said". Has that happened? Once. A summary quoted my own report back to me as if a participant had said it. Very flattering. Very wrong.

Third, and this is new. Since September there's the MCP connection, so an assistant we're allowed to use can search and read across the projects you have access to. We're piloting it with information security on a handful of projects, and they're looking at what is allowed to go where. I can't tell you yet whether we'll keep it. Don't connect anything yourself until they've said yes. Seriously. Understood.

And access. Who can see what? Our workspace is invite-only. You're a member. Two of us are admins. When we work with an outside research bureau, they get a role where they can work in the projects and generate reports but can't publish, so anything that leaves the building goes through us. And every project has its legal basis set. Usually it's the workspace default, but for the session with people who rely on disability transport we set it specifically, after the privacy officer looked at it. If you're ever unsure, ask her before the session, not after.
Oh, and one more on access. Every few months I go through the member list and take out the people who've left the file. Nobody else does it, and nobody thanks me for it.

When shouldn't I use it? You said that would be part of this. Yes, good. My list. One: casework. If it's one citizen talking about their own case, their own permit, their own complaint, it doesn't go in here. That belongs in the case system, with the people who have a mandate to see it. Two: internal meetings where everyone just needs the minutes. We have a meeting tool for that. This is built for many groups talking at once and for what you do with it afterwards. Using it as a minute-taker is like hiring a choir to hum.

Three: when the decision is already made. If the minister has decided and we're holding a session so we can say we listened, don't. Or be honest in the session that it's about how, not whether. Participants can tell the difference. Four: when you can't explain to people in one sentence what happens with what they say. If you can't, you're not ready to record them.

And five? Five is technical. The written consultation on the road safety plan, fourteen hundred form answers. Someone pasted them into the portal's text option as one enormous text, and it took ages and the answers we got out of it were mush. If you have written input, split it. Per question, or per batch of respondents. Smaller pieces, one text conversation each, clearly named.

Can I ask a stupid one? Online sessions. Not stupid. Avoid them when you can. When you can't: phone next to the laptop speaker, nobody wearing headphones, and two people per breakout recording as a backup. It works. It's never as good as a table. I'd rather do two regional sessions in person than six online ones.

Last thing. Your first three sessions you do with me, and you write your own summary before you open Ask. Then you compare. Not because the model is bad. Because if you never know the material yourself, you can't tell when the summary is wrong. That's the whole job, really. Okay. Stop the recording, and go write a context for Thursday's session. Use the skeleton.

name: Sceptical councillor, committee pre-meeting
summary: Synthetic sample. Before a committee meeting in an invented New Zealand district, councillor Graham questions participation officer Anika about a consultation report on the future of the town pool: how does he know the model didn't make it up? Anika doesn't ask him to trust it. She shows him how to check it. He picks a quote and she finds it in the transcript by search, and explains that every quote was copied from transcripts, never from a summary or chat answer. He challenges "strong support for a covered pool", and she shows the final wording, a count she made herself by opening each source (two "roof" mentions were about the changing rooms). They agree the record shows what the people who took part said, not what the town thinks. She describes asking who was talked about but absent, and how the first draft left out a small group of winter swimmers until she asked for views raised by only a few. He asks to hear the audio and she explains that anonymise was on, so names are removed and the audio can't be played back, a trade-off she made because residents named neighbours. She shows him the project context, which says not to recommend an option, and offers him a seat in the workspace to try catching it out.

chunks.text: Okay, we're recording. Councillor, you said you were fine with that. I said I'm fine with it as long as I get a copy of the transcript. If I'm going to be quoted by a machine, I want to see what it thinks I said. That's fair. So, for the record, this is the pre-meeting for the Harlow Bay pool report. It's Graham and me, Anika, and we've got about twenty-five minutes before committee.

Right. I'll be blunt, because you know I will be. I've read the report. It's well written. Too well written. My question is simple. How do I know the computer didn't make this up? Because I've seen these things. My grandson asked one for a history of the district and it invented a mayor. It's a good question, and I'm not going to ask you to trust it. I'm going to show you how to check it, and then you decide.

Go on then. Everything in that report comes from sixty-one conversations. Forty-four were recorded at the three drop-ins and the session at the college, and seventeen are from people who chose to type instead of talk. Every one of them is here in the project. I can open any of them and you can read the transcript, word for word. So when the report says something, the question isn't whether the model is clever. It's whether it's in the transcripts.

Pick one, then. No, I'll pick one. Page two. "The pool is the only place my kids see kids from the other side of the river." That's a lovely quote. A bit too lovely. Did a real person say that? Let's find it. I'll search the conversations for "other side of the river". There. Second drop-in, the Saturday morning, the conversation called "Pool map table 7". Here's the transcript. Read the bit around it.

"...and honestly it's the only place my kids see kids from the other side of the river, the school bus doesn't mix them, sport doesn't, it's the pool in summer." Huh. Okay. That's a real person. She talks like a real person. She does. And that's a rule I hold myself to: every quote in the report I copied from the transcript, not from a summary or a chat answer. The chat paraphrases, and paraphrase drifts. A quote is either in the transcript or it isn't.

Fine. Now this one. "Strong support for a covered pool." Strong. Who decided strong? Good catch, because that word was in the first draft and I took it out. You're reading last Thursday's version. The final says: a covered pool was raised in eighteen of sixty-one conversations, more often at the evening drop-in and the college session than on the Saturday morning.

And the eighteen. The machine counted that? No, I counted that. I asked the assistant to find every conversation that mentions a roof or a covered pool, with sources. Then I opened each one and checked, because it listed two that were about the roof of the changing rooms, which is a different thing entirely. I don't let it count for me. When there's a number in the report, I counted it myself. Huh. Okay. That's better than I expected.

Here's my real problem, though. Eighteen of sixty-one. That's not "residents want a covered pool". That's eighteen people who turned up to a drop-in. The people who come to these things are the people who come to these things. I agree completely, and I tried to write it that way. The report doesn't say what Harlow Bay thinks. It says what the people who took part said. There's a paragraph at the start that says exactly that, and who we heard from, and roughly who we didn't.

Who didn't you hear from? Not enough people over seventy-five who don't drive. Hardly anyone from the farms out past the junction. I asked the assistant specifically which groups are talked about but don't seem to be present, and those came up, with the conversations where they're mentioned. Teenagers were talked about a lot, but because we went to the college, we actually did hear from about thirty of them.

What about people who disagree? Every one of these reports I've read, everyone's in furious agreement. That's the one I'm most careful about, because it happened here. The first draft didn't mention the winter swimmers at all. They're against a roof, because they swim outdoors all year and a covered pool changes the whole thing for them. It's a small group, it came up in three conversations, and the first summary just didn't have it.

So it buries minorities. It doesn't go looking for them unless you ask. So I asked: which views appear in only a few conversations, especially ones that go against the main themes? And there they were, with sources. Now there's a section called "Views raised by a few, not many", and the winter swimmers are in it, in their own words. One of them says, "you're building a swimming pool for people who don't swim." I thought you'd like that one.

I do like that one. Okay. But how do I know the transcripts are right? You're telling me the transcripts are the truth, and a machine made those too. It did. They're machine transcripts and they're not perfect. Place names were the worst until I added them as key terms. It wrote Harlow Bay as "Hollow Bay" twice, which was a fun morning. Where a quote matters, I read the sentences around it, and if it doesn't make sense, I don't use it.

Can I listen to the recording? The actual audio. No, and that's on purpose. We turned on anonymise for this consultation, because it's a small town and people named neighbours, and staff at the pool. Anonymising takes the names out of the transcripts, and it also switches off playing back and downloading the audio. We told people that at the start. So the transcript is the record. I'd rather have this conversation with you than with a resident who heard their own voice played back in committee.

Hm. That's a trade-off. It is. For a lower-stakes topic I might not do it. For this one, people talked about which of their kids they can't afford to bring, and about their neighbours, and I didn't want that kept as audio.

Has the model been told what answer we want? Fair question. This is the project context, it's what the model is given about the project. Read it. "This is a consultation on the future of the Harlow Bay pool. Three options are on the table. The council has not decided. Do not recommend an option. Report what participants said, including disagreement and views held by a few. Do not mention names." Okay. That's actually okay.

And it doesn't write the recommendation. Officers write the recommendation, in the officers' report, the normal way, and you can disagree with it there. This document is only the record of what people said. If you want to argue with the recommendation, argue with me, not with the model. I will. I know.

So what you're telling me is, it's not that the machine is right. No. I'm telling you it's checkable. Every point goes back to a conversation, and you can go and read that conversation. And I'm not going to tell committee this makes the outcome sound, or proves anything about the town. It's a record of what people said, and you can check it. If you find something in there that's wrong, tell me, I'll fix it, and I'll tell committee I fixed it.

Can I have a go myself? Not now. Before the October meeting. Yes. I'll add you to the workspace as a member on this project, and we'll sit together for half an hour so you know where things are. And I'd honestly love it if you tried to catch it out. You know I will. I know. That's why I asked you. Okay, committee in five. Stop the recording? Stop it. And send me that transcript.

name: Students interviewing care home residents for the town vision
summary: Synthetic sample. In the garden of a care home in an invented Italian town, teacher Chiara, activities coordinator Paolo and fifteen-year-old student Matteo debrief after the second of three visits. For the town's centenary vision, a civics class paired up with residents to ask what the town was, and what it should become. Consent came first: only residents who could agree for themselves were invited, the legal basis was set with the municipality's privacy officer, parents signed for the students, and anonymise was on. Practical lessons: move away from the television and the bingo next door, put the phone near the resident because older voices are quiet, and keep the screen from locking inside a sleeve. Reading the transcripts showed the students talking most of the time, so the class practised "ask, then wait". Verify text was too small for residents, so students read the outcome aloud, asked about anything "not exactly", pressed revise, and only approved when the resident agreed. A large-print read-back at the next visit led one resident to correct the record about the old mill. Tags for the visit and for the pair, and a chat question on where residents and students disagree (cars in the piazza), feed a report the class will present to the centenary committee, with quotes copied from the transcripts.

chunks.text: Is it recording? Matteo, you're the expert. It's recording, prof. The time is going up. Good. So, this is Chiara, Paolo and Matteo, in the garden at Villa Morandella, after the second visit. Paolo runs activities here, I teach the civics class, and Matteo is one of my students and, today, our technical support. We're recording this because the other civics teacher wants to do the same thing next year, and I will forget half of it by September.

For her, the short version. The town is a hundred years old next spring and the council wants a vision for the next hundred. Very nice, very official. And we said: the people who remember the first half of those hundred years are sitting in this building, and the people who'll live in the next half are in my classroom. So we put them together. Pairs, one student and one resident, half an hour, two questions. What was the town like when you were fifteen? And what should it be when Matteo is your age?

Before anything else, consent, because that is the part that keeps Paolo up at night. It is. With the manager and the families we only invited residents who can agree for themselves. Some of our residents, with dementia, cannot, and we did not ask them, even when the family said "oh, she'd love to". That was hard. Then the municipality's privacy officer set the legal basis on the project with Chiara, and the students' parents signed a form, because the students' voices are recorded too.

And anonymise is on. Residents talk about their neighbours, their children, the nurse they like and the nurse they don't. That should not end up in a report with a name next to it. And we told the residents, slowly, in plain words: this phone writes down what you say, your name will not be in it, you can stop whenever you want. Matteo said it to his signora three times. She liked hearing it three times, I think.

Now the practical things, because the first visit was a bit of a disaster. Tell her. The first time we sat in the lounge. With the television on, because the television is always on. And next door they had bingo, and the bingo caller has a microphone. So one of my transcripts is half my signora talking about the market and half "thirty-seven, number thirty-seven". Today we used the library room upstairs and the small dining room. Quiet. Doors closed. Completely different.

And the phone goes near the resident, not near the student. Older voices are quieter, and the students are loud. On the first visit the phones were in front of the students, so you hear every word of the question and then something very far away. Also, two phones went dark because the students held them, or put them in a sleeve, and the screen locked. Today, phone flat on the table, screen on, closer to the signora than to you. It's on the sheet we printed for the students, with the QR code.

Can I tell the thing about the transcripts? It's a bit embarrassing. Go. After the first visit the prof made us read our own transcripts. And in mine, I talked like seventy per cent of the time. I asked a question, she started to answer, and I helped her. I finished her sentences. Every time. In the transcript it looks terrible. So in class we practised "ask, then wait". Count to five in your head. Today she told me a whole story about the flood without me saying anything.

That was the most useful thing we did, honestly. Not for the report, for the students. You can tell a fifteen-year-old a hundred times to listen. When he reads his own transcript and sees that he spoke three lines for every one of hers, he understands. Every teacher should do this, with or without the town vision.

Naming and tags, for my colleague. Every pair has a number. The students open the portal by scanning the code, and they choose two tags: the visit, first, second or third, and their pair number. And they write the pair number in the name. So "Visit 2, pair 6". When I look in the project I can see each pair's three conversations in a row, and I can follow one relationship over three visits. That's the thing I didn't expect: by the third visit, some of them really are friends.

Verify. We tried it today at the end, for five minutes. An outcome comes up on the phone, and the resident should approve it if it's right. But the text is small for most of our residents, and the buttons too. There's a read-aloud button, but the students read it themselves, slowly. When it's "not exactly", the student asks what she meant, and the phone is still listening, so her correction is there too, and then they press revise. Only when she says yes does the student tap approve.

And the read-back. That was Paolo's idea. After the first visit I made a short summary in the chat for each pair: what the resident told us, in bullets, in simple Italian. Paolo printed it very large. And today, before the new questions, the student read it out to the resident. Signor Aldo listened to his, and at the point about the mill he said, "no, no, I never said they should knock it down. I said they should never have closed it." Which is the opposite.

The summary had made it neat. He'd talked about the mill, and how it's empty, and dangerous now, and the chat turned it into "the old mill should be demolished". He was quite upset. And then quite pleased that we'd asked. So now his correction is in today's recording, and when we write the report, it's the correction we use. If we hadn't read it back, it would have gone to the council as Aldo's opinion. My rule now: nothing goes in the report that the person hasn't heard read back.

For the analysis I've only just started, but the most interesting question so far was a plain one. I asked the chat: where do the residents and the students want different things for the town? And the first answer was nice and general, everybody loves the piazza. So I asked again, more specific: where do they disagree, with a quote from each side. And then it was cars. Most residents want to park in the piazza, because they can't walk far. Most students want the piazza without cars.

And the funny part is that in some pairs they worked it out between them. Matteo, tell her. My signora said she wants cars in the piazza. I said I want no cars. And then she said, okay, but then I need a bench every fifty metres, because I can't walk from the car park to the church without sitting down. And I thought, that's actually a good idea. It's not cars or no cars. It's benches. I said that in class and now three other pairs are asking about benches.

That is exactly what I want to bring to the centenary committee. Not "the elderly want this, the young want that", but what came out when they talked to each other. In June the class will present a short report. What the town was, what they want, where they disagree, and what they found together, like the benches. Every quote copied from the transcripts and checked by the student who was there. And two residents have said they will come to the council meeting to hear it.

What I'd do differently. Do the first visit without recording at all. Just tea, and getting to know each other. The first recordings are stiff, on both sides. And ask the residents who didn't want to talk why. Some of them told Paolo it's not their town any more, it's for the young people now. That is also something the committee should hear, even without a recording. I'll write it down as a note and add it to the project as text, marked as mine.
Good. Matteo, anything to add? Charge the phone the night before. And don't let them put the bingo next door. Stop the recording.

name: Care team evaluation leads, coaching call
summary: Synthetic sample. Solveig, who leads a qualitative evaluation of community care teams in a Norwegian city, and her analyst Sanna coach Pieter, who starts a similar evaluation in a Flemish city in November. Solveig explains why they made one project per district, all sharing one project context template where only the last paragraph changes, plus the same four questions every month so districts can be compared. Teams record the last 25 minutes of their regular team meeting, never the case round; one team leader forgot and they deleted a recording full of case details, because anonymise transcripts removes names and addresses but not schools or diagnoses. The biggest issue was staff feeling surveilled: one district said no for two months, and its conditions (team reads its summary first, no managers in the project, pause any time, Verify at the end) became the rule. Sanna describes a district stuck on the wrong conversation language that could not be retranscribed, because retranscribe is off for anonymised conversations, and the workaround for comparing districts: the same saved Ask template in each project, then the seven answers pasted into a comparison project as text, always checked back against transcripts. Solveig and Sanna still disagree about projects versus tags. They are holding back on MCP until the privacy officer has looked at it.

chunks.text: Okay, it says recording, so I think we are on. Pieter, just so you know, I am recording this call with dembrane too. My phone is lying next to the laptop speaker, no headphones, that is the trick for online calls. Sanna will want to listen to it later, and honestly it is a habit now. Is that alright with you? Yes, of course, no problem. And it is a bit funny, recording a call about recording. So, we start in November.

Nine neighbourhood care teams: social workers, a community nurse, sometimes someone from the debt service. The city wants to know if the one-door approach actually works in practice. And my director said, use what Harsvik used. So here I am. Where do I begin? Begin with the structure, because that is the one decision you cannot easily undo later. We have seven districts and we made one project per district. Seven projects, all in one workspace just for the evaluation. The reason was simple.

Each district team leader is invited only to their own project, and they read their own conversations first. No other district sees them. That mattered a lot for trust. I will come back to that. And the downside? Because there is always a downside. The downside is Ask. The assistant works inside one project. So when the steering group says, compare District Two with District Five, you cannot type that in one place and get an answer with sources.

We found a workaround, and Sanna will explain it better than me, she is joining in a few minutes. If I did it again I would still do one project per district, I think. Sanna disagrees a little. She would have made one project with a tag for each district. Okay. Noted. Two camps already. Always. The second thing, and this is what I am most proud of, is that every project has the same project context. We wrote one template, about a page, and only the last paragraph changes per district.

The shared part says what the evaluation is for. It says we evaluate the way of working, not individual people. It lists the four questions we come back to every session. And it explains the words people use: the one-door approach, the case round, the family plan, our abbreviation for the debt service. Can you read me a district paragraph? I want to steal it. Of course.

For District Four it says, more or less: this team covers the harbour area and the two islands, six staff, they started with the new way of working in January, they meet on Thursdays, and many of their residents are older people living alone. Then the place names, the islands, the harbour, the health centre. Those also go in the key terms. Key terms are where spelling gets fixed. Before we added the island names, the transcript turned them into some kind of fish. Ha. A fish. And the four questions?

What did you try this month that was new? Where did the one-door approach help a resident? Where did it get stuck, and on what? And what do you need from the organisation? The same four, every month, every district. That is what makes comparison possible later. If every team talks about something different, the language model can still summarise each one, but you cannot compare them. Comparability you design before the first session, not after the last one. And how did you record? Separate evaluation sessions with each team?

No, and that was deliberate. Nobody had time for extra sessions. So we took the last twenty-five minutes of the regular team meeting, once a month. The team leader puts one phone in the middle of the table, scans the QR code on the printed host guide, and starts recording only when they reach the evaluation item on the agenda. Not before. And the conversation gets named by the team leader: district number, then month. District Four, March. Boring, but you can sort it. Why only at the evaluation item?

Because the first part of every team meeting is the case round. Client names, addresses, family situations, everything. That must never be in a recording. We wrote it on the host guide: start after the case round, stop before any other business. And still, in May, one team leader pressed record at the start of the meeting and forgot about it. Forty minutes of case round, in the recording. Oh no. What did you do? We had anonymise transcripts switched on, so the names were gone, and the addresses.

But the school, the diagnosis, how many children, all still there. Anonymise takes out personal details like names and addresses. It does not make a case unrecognisable. So we deleted the conversation that same afternoon, told the team, and told our privacy officer what happened. And we changed the host guide. That line is now the first thing on the page, in red, not the third line in grey. That is exactly my fear.

And the other fear, which my teams already said out loud in the first meeting: they will feel watched. A phone on the table during their own team meeting, and management listening in. Yes. That was the biggest issue of the whole evaluation. Bigger than any technical thing. District Six said no for the first two months. And we accepted that. Looking back, I think it was the most important decision we made. You just accepted it? My director would not like that. Mine did not like it either.

We said, fine, we will come back in March and you decide then. In the meantime the other districts started, and the people in Six heard from their colleagues how it actually was. When they joined in March, they came with conditions. And the conditions were good, so we made them the rule for everybody. What were they? First, the team reads its own summary before anybody else does. Second, the managers above the team are not in the project at all, not even to look. Third, nothing is about one person.

If someone says my colleague never picks up the phone, that is not evaluation data, and the team can ask us to remove it. Fourth, anyone can say pause, and the team leader pauses. And fifth, the last five minutes are for Verify. Verify, on the same phone? Yes. After twenty minutes of talking, the team leader opens Verify and the points from their conversation come up. Someone reads them out loud, and the team says yes, no, that is not what we meant. They edit them on the spot.

Those verified points are what goes into the comparison. Not the raw transcript and not my interpretation. That changed the feeling. Less like being observed, more like going on the record by choice. Hello, sorry, sorry, the other meeting ran over. Hi Pieter, I am Sanna. Has Solveig told you about District Three and the language yet? No, go ahead, that is your story. So when we made the seven projects, we copied the setup from the first one, and in District Three the conversation language stayed on English.

The team speaks Norwegian, obviously. The first two sessions came out as a strange half-English transcript, and the summaries were really poor. Like reading a bad translation of a bad translation. Can you not just change the language and transcribe again? Normally yes, you fix the language and retranscribe. But we had anonymise transcripts on, and for anonymised conversations retranscribe is switched off, together with audio playback and download. So there was no way to redo them. Those two sessions were basically lost.

The team was kind about it and did a short version again. So my advice: check the language in every project by hand, and make a thirty-second test recording in each project before the first real session. Then delete the test. Okay. Now the comparison, because that is what my director actually cares about. How did you compare districts if Ask only sees one project? Two steps. First, in each district project I used the same saved template in Ask.

We wrote a custom template with our four questions and some instructions: use the verified points and the transcripts, give a quote and the session for each point, and say clearly when a district did not talk about something at all. That last line is important. Same template, seven projects, every quarter. And then? Then I read each of the seven answers against its sources, corrected what was wrong, and pasted the corrected answers into one extra project through its portal's text option, one text conversation per district, named by district.

We call it the comparison project, and only the evaluation team is in it. There I can ask, where do districts differ on the debt service, which districts mention the waiting list for home care. It compares across the seven texts. So you compare summaries of summaries. Yes, and that is the weakness. A photocopy of a photocopy. So whenever something interesting comes up in the comparison project, I go back into the district project and find it in the actual transcript.

For example, the comparison said four districts had problems working with the GP practices. When I checked, it was really two districts. The other two had one sentence each. The language model had counted one sentence as a theme. That is why I would have done one project with tags. Then the sources are one click away, and you can ask, now just District Two, now just Five. And I still disagree.

With one project, every team leader can see every other district's conversations, unless we keep them out, and then we lose the part where teams read their own summary first. For us, trust was worth more than convenience. Fair. I would only say: decide it on purpose. We sort of slid into seven projects without really discussing it. That is useful, honestly. My director will want one big project, so now I have both arguments. And the MCP connection? Our data person read that you can connect your own tools now.

Yes, the MCP connections came in September, and our research unit asked about it the same week, because then their own model could read across all seven projects. We said not yet. Our privacy officer first wants to understand where the transcripts would end up. It is a nice possibility. But it is a new door, and with social care data you open new doors slowly. What did you show the steering group in the end?

A short report per district, which the district team read first and could correct, and then a four-page comparison with quotes. And I did not email it. We sat for an hour, Sanna and me and three team leaders, and went through it together. The team leaders explained what the quotes meant. Best meeting of the year, honestly. The steering group asked better questions than they ever did after a written report. One more thing, the Monitor.

Since August I keep it open on my laptop on Thursday afternoons, because four teams record at the same time. If a phone screen locks, it shows. Before that we lost a session in District One, the phone went to sleep after a few minutes and nobody noticed. Now I just send the team leader a message: your phone is asleep. So someone is watching after all. Watching the phones, not the people. We say that sentence a lot. And online? Two of my teams meet only online.

District Seven does that sometimes. It works, but it is awkward. One person puts the phone next to the laptop speaker, no headphones, and people have to speak one at a time. When they talk over each other, the transcript suffers. If you can, put the evaluation item on the days they meet in person. And Verify still happens on that one phone. Someone reads the points aloud on the call and the others react.

Okay. Last question. If you had one sentence for me. Write the template before you talk to anybody, then throw it away and write it again together with the team leaders. Mine is: let a team say no. That is two sentences. We are generous people. Shall I stop the recording? Yes. Thank you both, really. This helps a lot.

name: Nurses and researcher, burnout dialogues look-back
summary: Synthetic sample. Siobhán, a workforce researcher, looks back with three nurses (Aoife, Comfort and Raj) on eleven burnout dialogue sessions at an Irish hospital. They moved out of a staff room full of bleeps and fridge visits to a quiet library, and learned that if you can follow the talk yourself, the phone can too. Anonymise transcripts was switched on before collecting, with name and email off and the legal basis set with information governance; nurses came because nobody could play back their voice, though it meant misheard drug names could not be checked. Groups of five let one senior nurse dominate, so they switched to trios; Comfort found trios too intense, and they settled on trios for personal experience and groups of six for ward ideas. People spoke openly because the researcher left the room and the phone "doesn't nod". A face-down phone locked and lost twenty minutes until the Monitor was used. Explore helped one trio and sounded like a staff survey to another. Verify let nurses sharpen a vague point. The first report missed night staff until asked directly, and named a small ward. Results went back as one-page summaries with a QR code for reactions, but too slowly, and without saying what was turned down, so pages will get a "not taken forward, and why" box.

chunks.text: Right, the little dot is green, so we're recording. This is the look-back on the burnout dialogues, and it's going into the same project as everything else, so if anyone wants something taken out afterwards, tell me and it's gone. Aoife, Comfort, Raj, thanks for coming in on a day off, Raj I know you came straight from theatre. There are biscuits, the good ones. The good ones. She does listen. Go on, Siobhán, you start, it was your idea in the first place. Okay.

So, for the record, we ran eleven dialogue sessions between June and August, about fifty nurses across medical, surgical and nights. I'm the workforce researcher, the university side, and the question was what actually drains people and what keeps them going, in their own words. I want to talk about what we set up, what worked, and what I'd do differently. And I want you three to be honest, because you were in the rooms and I mostly wasn't. Can I start with the room?

Because that first session in the staff room was a disaster. It was. The ward phone rang every four minutes. And the bleep, and someone came in for their yoghurt from the fridge and stood there reading the rota. Nobody's going to tell a phone they're thinking of leaving nursing while a care assistant is getting a yoghurt. After that we moved to the old library on the second floor, the quiet room with the bad carpet.

Door shut, a sign on it, no bleeps, phones on Do Not Disturb except the recording one. That move mattered more than anything I did in the settings, honestly. The rule I use now is simple. If you can sit in the room and follow the conversation easily yourself, the phone can follow it too. In the staff room you couldn't follow anything. And in the library the transcripts went from patchy to almost clean.

Even the drug names, mostly, because I'd put the common ones and the ward names in the key terms. Tell them about anonymise, because people on my ward asked me about it before they'd come. Yes. Before the first session, I switched on anonymise transcripts in the project. That was decided before we collected anything, because it doesn't work backwards. It takes names out of the transcripts and it means nobody can play back or download the audio. I also turned off asking for a name and an email on the portal.

And I went through it with the hospital's information governance lead, and we set the legal basis on the project together before anyone was recorded. And that's what made people come, to be fair. I said to the girls on nights, nobody can listen to your voice afterwards. Not Siobhán, not the director of nursing, nobody. That was the sentence that did it. Not the data stuff, just that nobody can hear your voice saying it.

The trade-off, which I'll be honest about, is that I couldn't go back to the audio when something was misheard. There was one transcript where a medication came out as complete nonsense, and I just had to leave it, because with anonymise on you can't play the audio back or retranscribe, so there's nothing to check against. I'd still choose anonymise for this. But it's a real cost, and I'd tell any other researcher that up front. Okay, the groups. I know Comfort and I don't agree on this. We don't.

So the first two sessions we did groups of five, around one phone. And when I read the transcripts afterwards, in one group a single senior nurse did most of the talking. Lovely woman, but she ran it like a handover. Two people in that group said almost nothing for forty minutes. So from session three we switched to trios. Three people, one phone, twenty-five minutes, then everyone back together. And I liked the trios. You can't hide in a trio, but in a good way.

If one person goes on, the other two just turn to the third. I saw it happen. A very quiet newly qualified girl from surgical, and the two of us just kept turning to her. She talked about crying in the car park after her first death and nobody had ever asked her about it. And that's exactly why I didn't like them. It got very intense very quickly, and for some people that's too much. In the group of five you can sit back a bit, listen first, then come in.

Nurses are used to debriefs in a group. A trio felt like being interviewed, for me anyway. I'm not saying it's wrong, I'm saying it isn't for everybody. Which is fair.
