So where we ended up, for the last four sessions: trios for the first part, where it's about your own experience, and then two trios together, a group of six, for the second part, which was what would actually help on the ward. Two phones in the trio part, one in the group of six.

I think that combination is what I'd recommend. Can I ask the question I actually care about? Which is why people talked so openly to a phone. Because they did. I've been on wards twenty years and I've never heard nurses talk the way they did in some of those recordings. Raj, you were the sceptic on that. I was. I thought it would be weird. Talking to a phone lying on a table, like a voice note to nobody. And the first five minutes were weird, people were performing a bit.

But then it's just a phone. It doesn't nod. It doesn't make the face a manager makes when you say you're short-staffed again. You forget it's there. And Siobhán left the room after she pressed record, that was huge. That was deliberate. I'd start the recording, read out the three questions from the card, and leave. The card was printed, on the table, with the QR code and the questions. What takes it out of you on a shift? What keeps you coming back?

And what's one thing that would make next week a bit easier? And on the back, in big letters: keep the screen on, phone face up, don't press anything until the end. The face-up thing, tell them about the face-up thing. Ha. So in one of the June sessions, a trio turned the phone face down, which is a very natural thing to do if you want privacy. The screen locked about ten minutes in, and the recording paused. They talked for another twenty minutes into a sleeping phone.

I only found out the next day. From August I had the Monitor open on my laptop outside the room, and it shows when a screen is locked, so I could knock and say, sorry, your phone is asleep. And honestly, that was less disruptive than you'd think. A knock, a thumbs up, back to it. What about the ECHO button, the Explore thing? We had mixed results with that. Mixed is generous.

One trio pressed it after about ten minutes, and the question that came back was something like, what support structures could your organisation put in place? And they all laughed, because it sounded exactly like the staff survey. It broke the mood a bit. But the one in our trio was good. We'd been going round in circles about staying late, and the question was something like, you've each described staying after your shift ended, what made you stay? And that opened it right up.

Because the honest answer is guilt, and nobody had said guilt until then. So it depends. When the conversation was already alive, it helped. When it was flat, it felt like a form. And Verify at the end of each session, five minutes. That was the bit I was most nervous about and it was the bit people liked most. Because you could change it. Ours said staff feel unsupported by management. And we went, no, that's not what we said.

We said we feel unsupported on nights when the bed manager changes the plan at three in the morning and nobody tells the nurse in charge. And we edited it to that. It's much more specific. And it's ours. I'd stand behind that sentence anywhere, because I wrote it. Now the analysis, and where it went wrong. I did two things in parallel. I exported the anonymised transcripts as a zip and coded them myself, the old-fashioned way, because I'm a researcher and I need to know the data.

And I used Ask in the project. And the first report I generated was fine but it was missing nights almost completely. Of course it was. There's always fewer of us. Yes, and the report followed the volume. Eight of the eleven sessions were mostly day staff. So I asked directly: what did night staff say that isn't in this summary? Show me the quotes. And there was a whole set of things. The isolation, the meal breaks that don't happen, the bed manager point.

None of that was in the first version. Minority views don't surface unless you ask for them by name. And the ward names. Tell them about 4B. Right. The summary at one point said nurses on 4B describe a culture of blame. Anonymise had taken out all the people's names, but not the ward. And 4B has a small team. Everyone would know who was in that session. So I added a line to my report instructions: never name a ward or a unit, use medical, surgical or nights.

And I went through every quote by hand before anything left the project. Sharing back. This is where I'd give us maybe six out of ten. Six is fair. What we did: a one-page summary for each area, in plain language, what you told us, with five quotes taken from the transcripts, not from the chat answer, pinned in every staff room. And a QR code at the bottom that went to a small second project, where anyone could leave a voice note or type a reaction to the summary.

About thirty people did. Some of them hadn't been in any session. And the nursing practice council. We presented it, not Siobhán. Comfort read the nights quotes. I did. And I'll be honest, a couple of people on my ward said, we said all this in the staff survey three years ago and nothing changed, why would this be different. And I didn't have a good answer. The only thing that has changed so far is a trial of protected break cover on nights, on two wards. It's small.

But it came straight from the sessions, and we can point to the quotes it came from. That's the bit I'd underline for anyone else doing this. The tool made it possible to hear people clearly and to show where every point came from. It doesn't make anything change by itself. That's on us, and on the people who read the summary. Can I say what I'd change?

Can I go first, Siobhán? Because it's in the reactions. A lot of the reactions were the same question: what happened to the rest? The page said what we told you. It didn't say what had been looked at and turned down. The agency cover on nights, the parking, the rota system. People assumed it had been lost. It hadn't been lost, it had been turned down, and that's different. Fair. I'd rather be told no, with a reason, than hear nothing.

So next time every page gets a box at the bottom, not taken forward, and why, one line each. Yes. And mine: I'd do the sharing back faster. People in June heard nothing until September. That's too long. By September half of them had forgotten they'd even taken part. Agreed. Next round, a short what we heard within a week, and the full thing later. Okay. Anyone want anything taken out of this one? No? Then I'm stopping it. Thank you. Biscuits are yours.

name: School alliance dialogue evening, team retrospective
summary: Synthetic sample. Three weeks after a dialogue evening on the move from grade 8 to grade 9, the organising team of a Canadian regional school alliance looks back: Danielle (alliance coordinator), Marc (a secondary vice-principal who hosted tables) and Hana (parent council rep), with Gus from support staff joining. About 140 teachers, parents and support staff sat at 14 tables for three rounds: home tables by role, then mixed tables, then "what we try first". Table hosts named each conversation by round and table and picked a role tag. They used Verify at the end of each round; parents trusted it, Marc found it too much, and round three skipped it. The board report followed written instructions (two pages, five points, differences between groups, one quote per point, how many tables) and the first draft was too vague. Support staff, only two tables, were missing until Gus asked. What went wrong: an "everyone scan now" moment left about sixty empty rows, editing the portal changed the printed QR image, two phones locked, a table of nine was too big for one phone, a French-speaking table was transcribed badly in an English project, and the live chat on the projector fell flat for a tired room.

chunks.text: Okay, we're on. This is the retro for the transitions evening, so it'll sit in the project with the rest. Marc, Hana, thank you for staying late. Gus is coming at quarter to, he's finishing a bus duty. Let's do it the way we said: what we set up, what happened in the room, the report, and what we'd change. And Hana, you're allowed to be blunt, you're the only one of us who isn't on the payroll. I'm always blunt, Danielle. That's why you put me on the committee. Fair.

So, setup, quickly, for the record. One project for the whole evening. The question was, what would make the move from grade 8 to grade 9 go better for every kid in our schools. Fourteen tables in the library and the two classrooms next door, about a hundred and forty people. Three rounds of about thirty minutes. Round one at home tables by role, so teachers with teachers, parents with parents, support staff with support staff.

Round two mixed, and round three mixed again but on one question, what would we actually try first next September. Right. And I put a lot of effort into the project context, because I'd read that it steers everything afterwards. I wrote what the alliance is, which schools, the three rounds and the exact question for each round, and that this is not a decision meeting, the board decides in the fall. And I wrote out our jargon, because we have so much of it.

IEP, EA, Grade 8 Day, the transition binder, the names of all fourteen schools. Those went into the key terms as well. And it showed. I read a few transcripts and it spelled our school names right, which is more than the district newsletter manages. Ha. Okay, table labels. Each table host scanned the QR code on the table card and typed the name as round and table. R1 T07. That's it. And in round one they chose a tag for the group at the table: teachers, parents, support staff, or mixed.

In rounds two and three everyone was mixed, so the tag was just mixed. And that naming worked really well, actually. When I went into the conversation list afterwards, I could sort by round in two seconds. Compare that to the parents' night last year where we had notes called Table, table 2, tbl2, and Brenda. I'll stand up for Brenda, she took good notes. Okay. Verify. We built five minutes into the run sheet at the end of each round.

The table host opened Verify, read the points out loud, and the table fixed them. And for the parents, that was the moment. I'll be honest, a lot of parents came in suspicious. They thought this was the school board collecting quotes to justify something already decided. And then at the end of round one, the host reads out, parents want more homework in grade 8 to prepare. And Mrs Ferreira at my table goes, no, we said more practice with organising homework, not more of it.

And they changed it, right there, on the phone. You could see the table relax. I'm going to disagree a bit. Five minutes three times is fifteen minutes of a ninety-minute evening. In round two my table was just getting good when the timer went for Verify, and the energy dropped. And by round three people were looking at the clock, and we skipped it at most tables. We skipped it at all tables, Marc. I called it from the front. It was twenty to nine and parents had babysitters.

So what I'd say is, Verify after round one, because that's where trust gets built, and after round three, because that's the stuff that goes to the board. Skip it in the middle round. And make round three shorter so there's actually time. I can live with that. Hana? Yes, but keep the first one no matter what. That's the one parents remember. Okay. Now the things that went wrong in the room, and there were a few. The first one is completely my fault.

At the start I stood at the front and said, everyone get your phones out and scan the QR code so you know how it works. A hundred and forty people scanned. And we got about sixty conversations that were completely empty. Sixty empty rows. I remember opening the list the next morning and thinking we'd lost half the tables. So the lesson is, only the table host scans. Everyone else just talks. If people want to see how it works, show the host guide on the screen.

And deleting the empty rows afterwards is fine, but be careful with the bulk delete, there's no undo. I checked the count three times before I pressed it. The second one. The QR code on the table cards. Ugh, yes. The afternoon before, I changed the finish text in the portal, just a nicer thank-you message. And then I noticed the QR image in the dashboard looked different from the one on the printed table cards. I panicked, I thought all fourteen cards were dead, and I reprinted everything at four o'clock.

It turned out the old ones still worked. But you don't want to find that out at seven in the evening. So, any edit to the portal, scan the printed card again with your own phone. And the screen locks. Two phones in round one, both parents' phones, both locked after a couple of minutes, and nothing more got recorded. The host guide says keep the screen on, but nobody reads the host guide when they've just sat down.

Next time I'd do a twenty-minute briefing for table hosts before the doors open. Screen timeout off, Do Not Disturb on, phone charged, and the screen stays lit or it isn't recording. Then there was my table of nine in round one. The parents' table by the window. Too many people for one phone, and the two at the far end barely show up in the transcript. Plus the library has that echo. Second phone, or split it into two tables.

If you can't follow the far end of the table yourself, the phone can't either. And the French table. Right. We had one table of francophone parents in round one, which was great, we wanted them there. But the conversation language of the project was English, and the French transcript came out pretty poor. The summary was almost useless. Next time a French table gets its own project with French as the conversation language, and its own QR code on that table.

Then we read the two side by side in the analysis. Hi, sorry, sorry. The bus was late. Did I miss the part where we talk about support staff? Not yet, Gus, perfect timing. We're onto the report. So the board wanted something they could read in ten minutes. I generated a report with my own instructions, and I'll read them out because I think they're the most reusable thing we made. Two pages. Plain language for trustees who weren't there. Start with the five things we heard most.

Then where teachers, parents and support staff saw it differently. Then things only one group raised. One quote per point, taken word for word from a transcript. No names. And say how many tables the point came from. And the first draft was mush. It was. Communication between schools is important. Students benefit from early relationships. Nobody on the board would argue with that, and nobody would do anything with it either. So I went back and asked for concrete examples, what exactly people said should happen, and in which round.

The second version was much better. Things like the grade 9 teachers visiting grade 8 classes in May, not in August. And support staff disappeared. That's the honest bit. We had two support staff tables out of fourteen. The report followed the volume, so the EAs barely showed up. Gus, you saw the draft. I saw it and I said, where's lunch? Because at our table the whole conversation was about lunch hour.

That's when grade 9 kids with an IEP fall apart, no structure, no adult they know, and the EAs are on supervision covering four hundred kids. It's the thing we see and nobody else does. And it wasn't in the report at all. So I went to the chat and asked: what did support staff tables say that isn't in this report? Show me the quotes. And there it was, lunch hour, the bus, the first week. A whole section.

It's in the final version now with a line saying support staff were two of fourteen tables, so read this section with that in mind. Two tables doesn't mean less important. It means fewer people in the room. I like that line. And I liked the comparison. Tell them about the table thing. In the chat I asked for a table: the three groups in columns, the main themes in rows, and an X wherever a group talked about it.

That one picture showed what everyone talked about and what only one group raised. The board loved it. I checked every X against the transcripts, and two were wrong, which I fixed by hand. It's a draft. What we sign is ours. Last thing from me, the live bit. At the end I put the chat on the projector and asked a couple of questions live. What are the main themes from round three. And I'll say it, I thought it fell flat. It did fall flat.

Everyone was tired, it was nearly nine, and watching someone type is not exciting. A few people liked seeing their own words come up. Most were putting their coats on. I actually liked it. My table saw the bus point come up and they were proud of it. I think both are true. So, next time, no live analysis at the end. People get a short what we heard email within a week, and the report goes out to everyone who left their email when it's done.

And with the board, I walked them through it in person instead of just sending the PDF. I'd do that again. How did the board meeting actually go, last Tuesday? Twelve minutes on the agenda, and they asked about lunch hour first. So that tells you something. Okay. Anything else for the record? No? Then I'm stopping it. Thank you all. Gus, there's pizza left in the staff room, probably cold.

name: Tenant committee kitchen table, renovation planning
summary: Synthetic sample. At Bernie's kitchen table, a housing association's tenant participation officer (Shona) plans a renovation consultation on a three-block estate in England with two tenant committee members: Bernie, the 74-year-old chair, and Delroy, who is sceptical. They argue and settle on several practices. Tenants never need their own phone: committee members act as table hosts with one charged phone per table, screen on, and anyone can type instead or use a paper table, with paper cards typed in afterwards through the portal's text option. Shona will edit the printed host guide in large type, starting with "you do not have to be recorded". Delroy insists the project context and the opening say what is fixed (fire rules) and what is open (colours, timing, moving out during the works). Bernie wants names on so long-standing damp complaints are on record; they keep anonymise on and put a repairs desk at the door instead. Delroy calls Explore patronising, Bernie wants to see it handle the bins, and they trial it at two tables. They decide against Popcorn on a hall screen. Results go back on paper through every door, at a feedback evening, and by email to those who leave one, worded as "what happens next and when", not "we did".

chunks.text: Is it on? Shona, is that thing on? The light's going. It's on, Bernie. It's recording, we said we'd record it so I don't have to take notes and we can check later what we actually agreed. Delroy, you okay with that? Fine by me. Saves us arguing about what we argued about. Is that the cat on the table? That's Duchess, she's on the committee as well. Right. Tea's poured.

Go on then, Shona, tell us how this phone business is going to work on the day, because I've told you already, half of my lot in Ash House haven't got a smartphone, and the other half won't let you touch theirs. And that's fine, because nobody needs their own phone. That's the first thing. On the Saturday in the community hall we'll have tables, roughly by block, and each table has one phone in the middle, and the person who holds it is a table host.

That's you two and the other committee members. You scan the QR code, press record, and leave the phone in the middle with the screen on. Everyone else just talks. And Doris? Doris won't come to the hall. She hasn't left the fourth floor since the lift went in March. But she'll talk your ear off in her front room. Then we go to Doris. Home visits, with her say-so, one phone on the coffee table, same as the hall. I'll tag those as home visit so we can see them separately.

And for anyone who'd rather write, there's a type instead option on the phone. And there's a paper table with comment cards, and I'll type those in myself afterwards through the same type instead option, one text conversation per block, named by block. Paper counts the same. Does it, though? Count the same? It goes into the same project, and when I ask questions of it, the cards come up next to the conversations. I'll make sure of that. And I'll check it, because I want to see Ash House's cards in there. Okay, my question.

I've been on this committee four years. I've been to three consultations. Every time they'd already chosen the windows. So before I sit at a table holding a phone, tell me straight. What's actually open? Because if it's all decided, recording us is just theatre with better equipment. That's fair, Delroy, and I'll give you the straight answer. The window specification is mostly fixed, because of fire safety rules and the building regs. That's not up for debate and I won't pretend it is.

What's open: the colour and finish, the order the blocks get done, the timing around school holidays, how people get moved out during the works, and the communal gardens. That's genuinely open, and the board decides in January. Then that has to be the first thing anybody hears. Not on page four. On the table, at the start. Agreed. It goes in the project context too.

That's the bit of the setup where I describe the consultation for the system, so when it summarises later it knows what's fixed and what's open, and it doesn't present people's window complaints as if they're a choice we're making. I'll write which parts are fixed, which are open, and when the board decides. Plus the names of the blocks, the estate, the drying room, decant, Juliet balconies. All of that goes in the key terms as well, so the spelling comes out right. Decant. They'll love that word.

Makes us sound like wine. It's the official word for moving out during the works, Bernie, I can't help it. Now, the printed bit. Each table gets a printed host guide. It's a sheet that comes out of the system, but I can edit it. I want your help with the wording, because it's in my language, and it needs to be in yours. Big letters. Proper big. Half of Birch House can't read the gas bill. Big letters. What goes at the top?

At the top: you do not have to be recorded. There's a paper table, and nobody minds. Then what it's for. Then what to do with the phone. And what about where it goes? People will ask where their voice ends up. My neighbour works in IT, he'll ask. So I went through this with our data protection officer. We set the legal basis on the project together, and the first screens after you scan the code explain it.

The host reads that out to the table, and nothing records until the table has agreed. What I won't do is make promises on the day that I'm not sure about. If someone asks something I can't answer, I write it down and I ask dembrane, and I come back to them. I'd rather say I'll find out than make it up. Fine. That's honest, at least. Now, names. Bernie, I know you've got views. I have.

Mr Okafor in Cedar House has been complaining about the damp in his back bedroom for nine years. Nine years. He wants his name on it. He wants it on the record that it's him and it's his flat. If you take his name off, it's just somebody somewhere has damp. I get that. But here's my worry. If we leave names in, then the summary will say Mr Okafor said this, Doris said that, and that report goes to the board and to the whole estate.

Some people will say things about neighbours, about the caretaker, about who's been subletting. So I want to switch on anonymise transcripts before we start. It takes names, addresses and phone numbers out of the transcripts. And it has to be decided before we collect, it doesn't work backwards. I'm with Shona on this one. Sorry, Bernie. I don't want my name in a report next to what I said about the last contractor. So what happens to Mr Okafor's nine years? This is the bit that matters.

dembrane isn't the repairs line. It's for what the estate thinks about the renovation. So at the door of the hall we have a repairs desk, someone from the repairs team, with the proper forms. Mr Okafor's damp goes there with his name and flat number, and it gets a job number. And if he wants to talk about damp at the table as well, that's fine, it'll be in the consultation as damp in Cedar House, which is true. Hm. All right.

As long as somebody from repairs actually turns up and doesn't leave at eleven. I'll make sure. Next one, Delroy, and I know you don't like this. The Explore thing. It's a button the table host can press, it says ECHO on the screen, and after the table has been talking a while, it comes back with one question based on what's been said. The host reads it out. The table can answer it or ignore it. That's the bit I think is patronising.

A machine asking pensioners how they feel about their windows. These people have lived here forty years. They don't need a robot to prompt them. I'd quite like to see it try. Honestly. I'd like to see it get Vera off the bins. Every meeting, forty minutes on the bins. If a machine can move her on, I'll buy it a drink. So here's a middle way. We try it at two tables only. Bernie's, and one other.

The hosts press it once, maybe twenty minutes in, when it's either going round in circles or has gone quiet. And they note down whether it helped or whether it was rubbish. If it's rubbish, we don't use it next time. Two tables. Fine. And if it asks anything stupid, the host just doesn't read it out. Exactly. Then there's Verify at the end. That's where the phone shows the points it's picked out of your table's conversation, and the table can say yes, no, change that.

I'd like five minutes for that at the end of each table session. They'll be gone for the eleven-twenty bus, Shona. Five minutes is a lot when the bus is coming. Then the hosts do it with whoever's left, and if it's just the host, the host does it. Better than nothing. And Delroy, you've seen the screen thing, the live slides one, Popcorn. I was wondering about putting it up on the wall in the hall. No. Absolutely not.

A big screen with words floating about in a hall full of people who are worried about losing their homes for six weeks? It's early beta anyway, you said so yourself. They'd think it was the bingo. Okay. No screen. I'll have the Monitor up on my laptop at the side, though, that's just for me, so I can see if a table's phone has gone to sleep and nip over. You'll see me wandering. Fine. Last thing. How do people find out what was said?

Because that's where it always falls down. They have the meeting, then nothing for six months, then the scaffolding goes up. Right. The system can email the report to everyone who leaves an email address on the phone. But I reckon that's maybe a third of the estate. Less. Put it through the doors. Paper. Big letters again. Every flat in all three blocks. Paper through every door, in the newsletter, and a copy on the noticeboard by the lifts.

And a feedback evening about a month later, where the committee reads out what we heard, and people can say, that's not what we said. And I'll record that too, in the same project, so the corrections go in. And don't call it you said, we did. You haven't done anything yet. The board hasn't decided. Call it what you told us, and what happens next and when. That's better. I'll use that. What you told us, what happens next, and when the board decides.

One version for tenants, in plain English, by block. And a separate one for the board, which you two can read before it goes. And it's the board deciding. The system just helps us show what people actually said. It doesn't pick the windows. Nobody picks the windows. The fire regs pick the windows. You said so. Ha. Fair. Shall I stop it there? Stop it. Duchess wants her tea.

name: Youth council handover to next year's council
summary: Synthetic sample. Four members of a Scottish youth council (Ailsa, Josh, Mariam and Leo), with their youth worker Fraser mostly listening, record a handover for next year's council about "getting home after dark", a consultation they ran themselves with about 140 young people. Before using dembrane at all, the council held a debate and a vote, with a slide on what they would gain, what they would lose without it, and the privacy and environment worries Mariam raised. They passed it 11 to 3, and every session then voted again on phone or paper; two groups chose paper, which was typed into the portal as text. They rewrote the adult-written project context in their own words and filled key terms with bus numbers and local nicknames. The first session ran with anonymise off and the summary named the facilitator, so they switched it on for every later session and deleted that one. Trios held the phone like a microphone. Explore felt "cringe" until it rescued a flat conversation. The report missed rural young people until they asked who they had not heard from. What adults got wrong: jargon, sessions in exam season, a teacher staying in the room, softening quotes, asking for transcripts, and quoting a percentage that no one had ever counted.

chunks.text: Okay it's recording. Hi, next year's youth council. This is your handover, from us, the old lot. It's going in the same project as all the after dark sessions, so if you're reading this as a transcript, or asking the chat about it, hello. I'm Ailsa, I chaired this year. With me are Josh, Mariam, who's off to uni in two weeks, and Leo, who's new and staying on. And Fraser, our youth worker, who has promised not to talk much. I've promised. I'm just here to hold the biscuits. So.

This year the council asked us to find out what it's like for young people getting home after dark. Buses, lighting, feeling safe, lifts. It goes into the transport plan. And we ran it ourselves. Nine sessions, in three schools, the college, the youth club, and the football club. About a hundred and forty people. And we used dembrane to record the conversations. But the first thing you need to know is, we nearly didn't. Because of me. Because of Mariam. Mariam, tell them.

So the adults, the council officer and Fraser, sorry Fraser, came to us and said, there's this tool, it records your sessions and a language model helps you make sense of them, it's great. And I was like, no. Why are we giving our words to a company? What happens to the data? And all the data centres, the environment, all of that. If we're the youth council, we should be the ones who decide if young people's voices go into an AI. Not adults deciding for us.

And she was right, to be fair. So we had a proper debate at the March meeting. And we made one slide, with three columns. What we get if we use it. What we lose if we don't. And what worries us. Josh did the slide. What we get: we can talk to way more people, because nobody has to write everything down. Our report uses people's actual words, not our notes of their words. And you can check where everything came from.

What we lose without it: probably half the sessions, because we'd need a note-taker at every table and we don't have that many people. What worries us: privacy, the environment, and the AI making stuff up. For privacy we asked dembrane our questions directly and read the privacy page, and Fraser got the council's data person to set the legal basis on the project. We put the answers on the slide in our own words. On the environment we didn't have a great answer, honestly. We wrote that on the slide too.

Then we voted. Eleven for, three against. I voted against. And I'd still vote against, a bit. But the bit that changed my mind was the next decision. Which was that every session also votes. At the start of every session, the facilitator explains it in about one minute, and the group decides. Phone, or paper. Two groups chose paper, one at the college and one at the football club. And for those, we wrote notes on big sheets and afterwards typed them into the portal with the text option, one text conversation per group, named by group.

So they're in the project too. Same as the others. Next year's council: vote again. Don't just inherit our vote. Seriously. Okay, setup. This is where the adults got the first thing wrong. The council officer wrote the project context, which is the bit where you describe your project so the language model knows what it's about. And it was full of stuff like youth voice outcomes and stakeholder engagement priorities. Nobody talks like that. So we rewrote it.

We're the youth council, we're asking young people aged twelve to twenty-one about getting home after dark. Then the questions, and the places. And in key terms we put all the local stuff. The bus numbers. The underpass. The Brae. The chippy everyone meets at. What people actually call places. Before that, the transcript turned the Brae into the bray, like a donkey. Leo, tell them about the phone thing. So in trios we hold the phone upside down, like a microphone. Pointing at whoever's talking.

The adults thought that was weird, but it works so much better than leaving it flat on the table. And trios were the right size. Three of us, one phone. At the youth club we tried five and it turned into two conversations at once. Now, the big mistake. Our very first session, at the high school, we didn't switch on anonymise transcripts. We didn't really know what it did. And the summary said things like, Josh says the forty-seven never comes after nine. Which is true. But I was facilitating.

I didn't want to be in it. So after that we turned on anonymise for every session. It takes names out. But you have to turn it on before you record, it doesn't go back and fix old ones. So we deleted that first session and went back to the school and did it again. Switch it on before your first session. Not after. Explore. You'll see a button on the phone screen that says ECHO, and it gives you a question about what you've been talking about.

The adults were so excited about this. They thought young people would love it. It was cringe. The first time, at the college, it sounded exactly like a teacher. Like, how might your community work together to address these concerns. Everyone laughed. Someone did the voice. But then at the football club. The conversation was dead. Fourteen-year-old boys, they'd said the buses are rubbish and then nothing. And Leo pressed it, and it said something like, you said the underpass is fine in summer, what changes in winter?

And they talked for ten more minutes. About the lights being broken, about walking round the long way, about one of them getting chased. So it's good when the conversation is stuck or already going. It's cringe when it's going fine and you interrupt it. Okay, what we found. Mariam, you did the most with the chat. So we asked the chat loads of things. First, what are the main themes. Then, show me the quotes about the underpass. Then, what's different between what girls and boys said.

That was a big one. Girls talked about planning routes, sharing locations, keys between fingers. Most boys didn't notice any of that was going on. And we found the last bus from the college is at twenty to ten, and most evening classes finish at half nine. But here's the thing. The first report we made said young people feel unsafe after dark and want improved public transport. Which is so vague. You could write that without asking anybody. So we asked for specific stuff.

What exactly do people say should change, and where. And then Ailsa asked the best question of the whole year. I asked, who haven't we heard from? And then, what did the young people outside town say that isn't in this report? And there was this whole thing about lifts. The kids from the villages don't care about the last bus because there isn't a bus. They depend on their parents, and if your parents work nights you just don't go to anything.

That wasn't in the first report at all, because there were only two sessions with rural kids. It doesn't come up unless you ask. Okay. What else did the adults get wrong. We made a list. Leo. One. They scheduled two sessions in exam season. Nobody came. Two. At one school a teacher stayed in the room, at the back, marking. And nobody said anything real. As soon as the next group came in without her, totally different. The phone wasn't the problem. Adults in the room were the problem. Three.

When we wrote the report, an adult wanted to change the quotes. Somebody said the buses are a joke, and the adult wanted it to say young people expressed dissatisfaction with bus services. We said no. The whole point is it's in their words. Fraser backed us up. I did. That's my one sentence. Four. The council officer asked if she could have all the transcripts. And we said no.

The deal with the groups was, the youth council sees the conversations, and what goes out is the report and quotes without names. She wasn't happy, but she got the report. Five, and this is the worst one. In a meeting, an adult said seventy per cent of young people feel unsafe after dark. And we were like, where did that come from? Nobody counted anything. It turned out she'd taken it from something the chat said, and it wasn't in any transcript. The chat isn't a survey.

If you want a number, you have to count it yourself. Always click the sources. So what happened in the end? We presented it to the transport committee ourselves, in June. We read out the quotes, the real ones. And the committee said they'd look at the underpass lighting by spring and talk to the bus company about the college times. Look at, not fix. Next year's council, please check.

And we put a one-page what you told us poster in every school and the youth club, and the report went to everyone who left an email. Most didn't leave one, so the posters matter more. Anything else? Mariam, last word, you're leaving us. Just, it's okay to be sceptical. I still am. Being sceptical is why we did it properly. Okay. Bye. Stop it, Ailsa.

name: Social work team, ground rules for reflection sessions
summary: Synthetic sample. A social work team at a public social welfare centre in Brussels (coordinator Nadia, Joris, Fatou and Mehdi) meets their data protection officer Elif after two trial reflection sessions to agree written ground rules, and records the agreement itself as the first conversation in the project. The sessions follow a case-consultation-style method about the workers' own practice, never client data. Never recorded: names, initials, addresses, ages with nationalities, schools, case numbers, diagnoses, anything from the file, colleagues from other services. Their test is "if you can picture who it is, it's too much". In the second trial, anonymise transcripts removed a client's name but not "the father with the bakery", so they deleted the conversation that day; anonymise is a safety net, not the rule. Elif set the legal basis on the project, and they discuss why consent between colleagues and a coordinator is tricky. Who sees what: a private project with only the five team members, the head of department kept out, no transcript export, no MCP, no case details in the assistant's memory (Nadia checks its project notes monthly), and only a quarterly learning note goes upward after the team edits it. Fatou warns against treating a pattern the model spots as a finding. Mixed French, Dutch and English talk remains unsolved.

chunks.text: So, it is recording. Nadia here. This is the first conversation that counts in the reflection project, and it is on purpose not a reflection session. It is us agreeing the rules, so the rules are in the project for everybody to see. Elif is here from data protection. Joris, Fatou, Mehdi. We did two trial sessions in July, and today we decide what stays and what never goes in. Okay? Okay. Can I say first, for the record, that I am still not completely convinced?

I will say yes to the rules, but I want it written that I asked the questions. It will be written, Fatou. That is the point of recording it. So, first what we are doing, in one minute, for anyone who reads this later. Once a month, forty-five minutes, the team does a reflection session. One colleague brings a situation from their own practice. Not a case file, a situation.

The others ask questions to understand, then everyone reflects: what did it do to you, what did you try, what would you try next time. And the purpose is learning about our work. How we deal with aggression at the counter. How we hold boundaries when clients message us at night. Over a year, we want to see what we keep coming back to. It is not supervision, not evaluation, and absolutely not a case file. Good. So, what must never be recorded. Elif, you made the list. Yes.

I will read it, and you tell me if it is complete. Never: names of clients, also not first names, also not initials. No addresses or streets. No age together with nationality together with family size, because that combination identifies someone in a neighbourhood like ours very quickly. No schools, no case numbers, no diagnoses, nothing copied from the file. And no names of colleagues from other services, because they did not agree to be in this. I would add one thing. A test you can do in your head.

If, listening to it, you can picture who it is, then it is too much. Say a client. A family. A young man in his twenties. Like a story in a training manual. That is good, Fatou. I will put that test at the top. And Joris, I am sorry, but we have to talk about the second trial. No, it is fine. It is good to say it. I brought the situation with the father who shouts at the counter every week.

And I said his first name once, without thinking, and that he has the bakery by the market. Anonymise transcripts was switched on, and it took out the name. But the bakery by the market was still there. Anyone from this neighbourhood would know who it is. And we deleted the whole conversation the same afternoon, and I informed Elif. Which was the right thing. So what we learned: anonymise is a safety net. It is not the rule. It takes out names, addresses, phone numbers.

It does not take out the bakery, the school, the father who shouts every week. The rule is what Fatou just said. Describe the situation so nobody can picture the person. And the pause. Anyone can say pause, at any moment, and whoever is holding the phone pauses. No discussion, no explanation needed. If you realise afterwards that something slipped, you tell Nadia the same day and the conversation is deleted. Deleting has no undo, which in this case is exactly what we want.

Can I ask why we can't record the real case consultations? The ones on Thursday. Because honestly, that's where the learning is. When we discuss a real family and someone says, have you tried this. That's where I learn the most. I understand, Mehdi, but no. Real case consultation is about the client, and that belongs in the case file system, with all the rules around that. This project is about us, about our practice. If client data is never in it, then most of my questions disappear.

The moment client data goes in, it becomes a completely different processing, with a different purpose, and I would have to say no to the whole thing. It's a clean line. I like a clean line. Thursday is about them. The reflection session is about us. Okay. Then legal basis. Elif, can you explain what you did, because the team asked me and I could not explain it well. So in the project settings there is a legal basis, and I set it for this project after I did the screening.

It changes what people see on the screen before the recording starts, so it matches what we actually do. I will put my reasoning in our processing register, and anyone in the team can read it. The difficult point, and I want to be honest, is consent between colleagues. Because Nadia is our coordinator. Exactly. If your coordinator asks, do you agree to be recorded, it is not completely free to say no. So whatever the basis, there is one rule that does not depend on it.

Anyone can skip a session, or join it and not speak, or ask for the conversation to be removed. And it will not be held against them, and it will not be mentioned. Nadia, you agreed to this. I agree, and I will say it again at the start of every session. Okay, who sees what. Fatou, this was your big question. My big question. Because the head of department was very enthusiastic, and when someone above us is enthusiastic about recording us, I get nervous. Fair.

So, this is what we set up. The project is private, inside our team's workspace. In the project there are five people: the four of you and me. I am admin, you are members. The head of department is not in the project, and does not get added. Not to look, not once, not for a demo. If she wants a demo, I make a separate demo project with invented material. And what goes upward? Once a quarter, we write a short learning note.

I start it in Ask, asking something like, across the last three sessions, what did we keep coming back to, with the quotes. Then the five of us read it, change it, cut what we don't want to share. Only that edited note goes to the department. No transcripts, no export of the conversations, no individual feedback. Nobody is evaluated with this. And the other tools? I heard there is now a way to connect other AI tools to it. The MCP connection. We are not using it. Elif and I agreed.

Also the assistant has a memory, where it can keep notes about the project. Nothing about any situation goes into those notes. Only practical things, like which method we use and that sessions are monthly. And once a month I open the project's notes in the settings and remove anything that shouldn't be there. You can't edit them, but you can delete them. Okay. Then I want to raise the thing that worries me more than the data.

After the two trials, Nadia asked Ask what patterns there were across the two sessions. And it said, we often say I didn't want to make it worse. And then it called that an avoidance pattern in the team. And Mehdi, you said in the corridor, wow, it's right. I did say that. It felt right. But that is a language model noticing a phrase that came up four times in two sessions. It's not a finding.

Maybe it is a pattern, maybe we just all say that sentence because it's a normal sentence. We decide if it's a pattern. Not the summary. I agree completely. So the rule for the learning note is that we always check the quotes ourselves, in the transcripts, not in the answer. And if the answer gives an interpretation, like avoidance, we treat it as a question for the next session, not a conclusion. Actually, that is a nice reflection question. Do we avoid? Let's bring it in October. Ha. Okay.

That I can accept. And at the end of each session, five minutes for Verify. The points from the conversation come up on the phone, and we approve them, change them or throw them out. The verified points are what we use for the learning note, more than the raw transcript. Two practical things from the trials. The phone stays in the middle of the table in the small meeting room. Never in the open office, because you hear the counter and the phones and other colleagues' calls. And the language.

Yes, the language. We are a team of French, Dutch and English. The project is set to English, because most of the sessions are in English. The first trial was fine. But when Joris brought his situation, half of it was in French, because that's the language it happened in, and the transcript of that part was not good. I don't think there is a perfect answer.

Either the person who brings the situation chooses the language and we make a separate project for French sessions, or we agree that the session is in English, and you tell the situation in English even if it happened in French. I prefer the second, it is simpler. But it costs something, telling it in a different language than you lived it. Let's try English for three months and talk about it again in November. And key terms: the counter, the duty roster, emergency aid, our names for the services.

I already put them in. So, summary of the rules. Nadia, you read them, and then everybody says yes or no. Okay. One, nothing about clients that lets you picture the person. Two, anyone can say pause, and slips are deleted the same day. Three, anyone can skip, stay silent, or ask for removal, without consequence. Four, only the five of us in the project. Five, only an edited learning note goes up, no transcripts.

Six, no external connections, no case details in the assistant's notes. Seven, we check quotes in the transcripts, and interpretations become questions. Joris? Yes. Yes. Yes. And with my questions written down. They are now. Yes from me too. Yes from data protection. I will send you the register entry this week. Good. Then I stop the recording. Thank you, everybody. Coffee?

name: Voice memo from a parked car: support workers' weekly notes
summary: Synthetic sample. Jo, who coordinates home support workers for older people across a large rural region in Australia, records a voice memo in her parked car for Brodie, who starts the same project in a neighbouring region. For six weeks, 22 support workers were invited to record a two-to-five-minute reflection in their cars between visits, answering one question a week. Rules: parked with the engine off, never while driving, never outside a client's house, no client names, describe the task, not the person. Jo kept the dembrane Go beta, which records without signal, for herself, since it needs a dembrane account that can open the project's recordings; workers used the portal through a weekly link that fills in the week's tag, which meant waiting for signal and keeping the screen on. Car Bluetooth took over the microphone, the radio got in the way, and early notes were often under thirty seconds. Uptake fell in week four until Jo sent back a short voice note reading workers' own words, copied from transcripts. Ask's first answers were too polite until she asked for complaints raised more than twice with quotes. A manager quoted a line in a board paper that appeared in no transcript. Results so far: a fixed key-safe list and a recalculated travel run; travel pay is still unresolved.

chunks.text: Morning Brodie, it's Jo. I'm parked outside the bakery in town, engine off, which you'll understand in a minute is the whole point. You asked me to tell you how the car notes went before you start yours in November, and I figured the most honest way was to do it the same way the workers did. So I'm recording it on dembrane Go, into the same project as theirs, and I'll send you the transcript. Grab a coffee, it's a long one. So, the idea.

We've got twenty-two support workers across the region, mostly doing personal care and domestic help for older people living at home. And they spend half their working life in the car. Ninety minutes between some clients out west. And the office never hears what the job is actually like, except when something goes wrong. The car is the only private room they've got. So, I thought, let's use the car. Every Monday I sent one question to the team group chat.

Week one was, what's one thing from today the office never sees? Week two, what took longer than the roster says? Week three, a moment this week you felt you did good work. Then week four, what nearly made you quit this week, which I was nervous about. Then week five, after the roster change, what's different? And week six, what would you tell a new worker on their first day? And people recorded two to five minutes, whenever it suited them, between visits. That's it. No meetings, no forms.

And it worked, mostly. But let me give you the rules first, because the rules are the bit you can't skip. Rule one. Parked, engine off. Never while driving. Not even at the lights. I said that in the first message, the second message, and every Monday after. Rule two came after week one. Never outside the client's house. Drive around the corner first. Because one of our girls recorded in a client's driveway, and the client's daughter came out and leaned in the window and started talking about her mum's medication.

Lovely woman, completely the wrong place. I deleted that one the same day, and I told the worker why, so she wasn't embarrassed. Rule three. No client names, ever. Not first names, not my nine o'clock Mrs whatever. Describe the task, not the person. I had anonymise transcripts on from the start, so names get taken out anyway. But in a town of eight hundred people, the only client with a farm dog and a blue front door is not anonymous.

Anonymise takes out names and addresses, it doesn't take out the farm dog. So the rule is about what you say, not about what the system catches. Now the tech, because this is where you'll lose a week if I don't warn you. My first plan was dembrane Go for everyone with an iPhone. It's the iOS app, still a beta, through TestFlight, and out here it's brilliant, because it records on the phone with no signal and uploads when you're back in range. Half our runs have no reception at all.

But Go means signing in with your own dembrane account, as a member of the workspace, and members can open the project's recordings. I didn't want twenty-two people able to read each other's notes. So Go is just for me, like this memo. The workers all use the portal in the browser. Same as scanning a QR code, but I sent them a link. And each Monday the link was a new one that fills in the week's tag for them, week one, week two, and so on.

Saves them choosing, and I never sorted a thing by hand. The catch with the browser is it needs signal and the screen has to stay on. So people mostly recorded when they got back into range, on the edge of town, which is a shame, because the best thinking happens out west. Two problems I didn't see coming. The car Bluetooth. If the phone's connected to the car, sometimes the car takes over the microphone, and you get this distant, tinny recording with the engine fan.

So, disconnect the Bluetooth before recording, or pick the phone's own microphone in the mic check before you start. And the radio. One bloke recorded three weeks with the country station going in the background. You can hear every word of the song and about half of his. And the short ones. In the first two weeks, about a third of the recordings were under thirty seconds. Um, nothing really, all good. So in week three I said, even nothing is useful, but tell me why it was nothing.

Was it a good day, or are you too tired to talk? And that changed things. People started saying, honestly, I'm too stuffed to think. Which is data, Brodie. That's exactly what the office needs to hear. Uptake. Fourteen of the twenty-two recorded at least once. Nine recorded most weeks. And then week four it dropped right off, five recordings. And I worked out why. They were talking into a void. Nothing came back. So in week four I recorded a three-minute voice note for the group chat. Not a report.

Just, here's what you told me so far, and I read out six or seven of their own lines, no names. And week five went back up to eleven. People heard themselves, or heard a mate, and went, oh, it's going somewhere. Every second week after that I did the same. And here's the important bit. I copied every line I read out from the actual transcript, not from what Ask gave me. Because Ask paraphrases, and if you read out a paraphrase, someone goes, I never said that.

And they'd be right. Speaking of Ask. First time I asked it what the main themes were, it gave me this lovely polite list. Workers value their clients. Travel is a challenge. Teamwork is important. All true, and all useless. So I got specific. What complaints came up more than twice, with the quotes. What did people say about travel time between visits, and show me where. What changed between week four and week five, after the roster change. Now that was useful. The roster one especially.

I used the tags for that, only week four and only week five, and compared. And what came out was that the new roster fixed the mornings and broke the afternoons. Two workers on the west run were now doing a seventy-kilometre stretch between visits with fifteen minutes allowed. You'd never see that on the roster screen. You hear it in the car, at half past two, with somebody sighing. Now the cautionary tale, and you'll need this one.

My regional manager, lovely, means well, read the summary I shared and put a line in the board paper. Workers report feeling unsupported by head office. And I went looking for it. It isn't in any transcript. Nobody said head office once. It was the assistant's wording for a few comments about not being able to reach the on-call phone. That's a different problem, with a different fix. So now I tell everyone, if you quote it, click the source and copy it from the transcript. What I'd set up the same.

One project for the whole six weeks. Project context that explains who the workers are, that it's reflections between visits, that we're interested in the work, not in grading anyone. And the town names and the run names in key terms, so the spelling comes out right in the transcripts. Even if people shouldn't say them much, they do, and you want them spelled properly when they slip through. And the legal basis.

I sat down with our privacy person and the union delegate before I sent a single message, and we set the legal basis on the project together. The delegate saw the setup, saw that my manager isn't in the project at all, only me and our quality lead. And workers know they can ask me to take any recording out. Two did, and I just deleted them, no questions asked. That bit has to be real, not just in a policy somewhere. So, results, honestly. Small things fixed fast.

The list of key-safe codes was out of date, came up four times in week one, fixed in a week. The west run travel time got recalculated after the roster tags showed it. And the fifteen-minute visits, the ones where you can't even make a cup of tea properly, that's gone to the board. What hasn't changed: pay for travel between clients. That came up every single week and it's still sitting there. I won't pretend otherwise to the team. What I'd do differently.

Start the voice notes back from week one, not week four. Shorter questions. Week four's question, what nearly made you quit, was too much for some people. A couple of them told me that later, when I asked. Something like, what was the hardest bit of this week, gets you most of the same stuff and doesn't feel like a trap. And I'd test the weekly link on everyone's phone at a team meeting before week one, not one by one over the phone on a Saturday. Oh, and one more.

If your workers have older phones, test them first. One worker's phone was so old the recordings were really muffled, and she thought it was her fault. It wasn't. We swapped her onto the work phone for those six weeks and it was fine. Right. There's a kookaburra on the bonnet having a good laugh at me, so I'll take that as my cue. Call me when you've written your first question, I'll tell you if it's a trap. Cheers, Brodie.

name: Leadership offsite, organiser and facilitator on the train home
summary: Synthetic sample. Hanne, who runs the strategy office at a furniture manufacturer in Denmark, and Tomasz, the external facilitator, debrief on the train the day after a two-day leadership offsite with sixty leaders at ten tables. They explain why they kept one project with day tags, and how a long project context said plainly that the four strategy pillars were the board's proposal, so leaders repeating the pillar names did not count as agreement. They talk about key terms for internal acronyms, table numbers in the name field so the Monitor showed where to walk, and recording the CEO's opening as its own conversation. The low point came on the first evening, when a board member read an "overall verdict" answer as broad support. Tomasz asked a matrix question instead (tables against pillars: supported, contested, not discussed) and then asked where tables disagreed, opening the sources each time. A summary had named a manager because anonymise was off, so they added a no-names rule to the context and prompts. The next morning tables corrected a one-page paper summary while recording. They disagree about using Verify and agree the language model does not write the strategy.

chunks.text: Okay, it's recording. Hanne, I put the phone between the coffee cups, I hope the train isn't too loud. So this is our debrief, the day after, while we still remember things. And I want to do it properly, because the board meeting is in two weeks and I think we need to agree what we say about how this was recorded. Not only what came out of it. Yes. And honestly, because I was nervous on Wednesday evening, you saw that. Okay, from the start.

Sixty leaders, ten tables of six, two days at a hotel by the fjord. We had one project for the whole offsite, which I almost didn't do. I wanted one project per day. You talked me out of it. Because you would report on it as one thing. One strategy, one offsite. The days are tags. Day one, day two, and the tags were picked when people scanned, so I never had to sort anything afterwards. If the two days had completely different questions for different readers, then yes, two projects.

But it was really one question: does this draft strategy make sense to the people who have to deliver it? And the context. I want to tell the board about the context, because I think that's what made the difference. My first version was two lines. Strategy offsite, leaders discuss the draft strategy. And you read it and said... I said a curious friend reading that would know nothing. Who you are, what the draft says, what the tables are asked. Nothing. Right. So in the end it was maybe fifteen lines.

Who the company is, furniture, three factories, about nine hundred people. The four pillars with their working names. The questions for each round. And then the sentence you insisted on: the four pillars are the board's proposal, they are not the participants' views, and when participants repeat the pillar names that is not agreement. That sentence did a lot of work on Wednesday night. People say the pillar names all the time, they're on the wall, they're on the table cards.

Without that line, the first answer reads like, everyone talks about made-to-order growth, so everyone wants made-to-order growth. Which is not the same thing at all. And key terms. Our acronyms, we have so many. The made-to-order programme, the three business unit names, the CEO's surname because nobody spells it right, even the hotel's name because people kept saying it. After that the transcripts were really clean. The test I did on Monday, before key terms, was full of strange words. The room, then.

One phone per table, the table host's phone, in the middle on a little stand. I printed the host guide and put it next to every QR, and on top a yellow sticky note: in the name field, type your table number and the round. So "Table 4 round 1". Most did it right. Most. We had one "Mikkel", one "test" and one that just said "table". I fixed those in the evening. But on the Monitor it was so useful that the rest were table numbers.

When "Table 7" showed Screen locked, I knew where to walk. If it says Mikkel, I have to remember where Mikkel was sitting, and I don't. How many times did you walk over? Three, on day one. Twice Screen locked, the same table both times, the host had battery saver on. And once Audio stopped?, which was just a long silence, they were reading the handout. I learned to wait a minute before walking. Day two, nothing.

Because in the morning the CEO said it from the stage: screen on, battery saver off, phone in the middle, Do Not Disturb. And we recorded her opening. I want to say that to the board too. The opening talk and the questions after it are their own conversation in the project. So when a table says "we heard the board say margins first", we can check whether the board actually said that. And it did, more or less. Okay. Now the hard part. Wednesday evening. The bar. The bar.

So about nine, Lars from the board comes over with his laptop open. He had asked the assistant something like, what is the overall verdict on the strategy. And it gave him four tidy paragraphs, and the first one said, more or less, there is broad support for the four pillars with some concern about pace. And he was so happy. He said, great, broad support, we can tell the employees on Friday. And I felt my stomach go.

Because I had walked past those tables all afternoon and I did not hear broad support. I heard people being polite about two pillars and quite upset about the third one. To be fair to the language model, it answered what it was asked. "Overall verdict" asks for one verdict. And the first answer is always a bit, how did someone put it to me, nice and political. It doesn't volunteer the disagreement, you have to ask for it.

So we sat down, the three of us, and I said, Lars, let's ask it differently, and you watch. First I asked for what I call the matrix. Tables in columns, pillars in rows, and in each cell one of three words, supported, contested, or not discussed, plus one short quote. And that table told a different story. Pillar three was contested at six of ten tables. Pillar four was hardly discussed anywhere. Which is also information. That was the moment for Lars, I think.

Not discussed is not the same as agreed. And then you asked the second one. Where did tables disagree with each other, and what would the person who disagreed most strongly say, in their own words, with sources. And then I clicked into the sources. Because the quote in the answer is close to what was said, but the transcript said it much sharper. Much sharper. "We are asked to grow made-to-order with the same people who already do the overtime." That was table two.

Lars read it in the transcript and went quiet. I think reading the actual sentence someone said is very different from reading the assistant's sentence about it. We should also be honest about names. We kept anonymise transcripts off. Internal offsite, people know each other, and we wanted the audio so we could check things. But I had warned you the summaries might name people. And one did. A table summary said "Jesper argued that the regions..." about one of the regional managers. Not terrible, but not what we promised either.

So two fixes. We added a line to the project context: do not mention participants by name in any output, refer to the table. And I added "don't mention names" to my saved prompt template. We regenerated that summary and it came back as "one participant". And on day two the CEO said in the opening: we don't need names, we need what you think. Then the morning. This is the part I'm proudest of. We had promised a summary back at breakfast. And Tomasz, you stayed up.

Till half past one, yes. But mostly checking, not writing. I used a Specific Details chat on only the day one conversations, so I knew exactly what was in scope. And I asked for three short lists. What most tables shared, where tables split, and the questions the room has for the board. Then for every line I opened at least one source. Two lines I deleted, because I couldn't find them in the transcripts with the meaning the answer gave them. One was a "broad support" line again, actually.

It was built from people repeating the pillar names, even with the context. So the context helps, it doesn't replace reading. And then we printed it. One page, A4, three columns. Not on a screen, on paper on the tables, so people could write on it. And the title was not "conclusions". The title was: what we think you said yesterday, tell us where we are wrong. And the first fifteen minutes of day two were tables correcting it, with the phones recording. So the corrections are in the record.

That's my favourite thing. Table five said, you made pillar three sound like a capacity problem, and it's not only capacity, the sales bonus pushes people towards the wrong work. That wasn't in my sheet. Now it's in the data. And Lars heard that. In his closing words he said something like, I came in thinking there was broad support, and I'm leaving thinking we have two pillars and two open questions. Which, for a board member, is quite a lot. What would we do differently. I'll start. Verify.

We didn't use it, we did the paper version. I think paper was right for this group, leaders like a pen. But maybe table hosts could do a five-minute Verify at the end of round two, so each table already approves or corrects its own points on Wednesday. I'm not sure. Five more minutes with sixty leaders after a long afternoon? Half of them would have gone to the bar. My one: I would decide earlier which template to use.

I tried the Strategic Planning template on Wednesday night and it went straight to an action plan. That's not its job at this stage. The leaders write the action plan. Agreed. The model doesn't write the strategy. The room works on it and the board decides. Compare & Contrast fitted us better. And for the board report I want four sections. Where tables agreed, where they split, what nobody discussed, and the questions for the board. Each with quotes copied from the transcript, not from the chat answer.

And one line at the top saying what went into it. Ten tables, two rounds, the opening, the morning corrections. Because the first thing a board member asks is "is this everyone?". I'll check the count in the conversation list before I send anything. Good. I think we're going into the tunnel. Shall we stop? Stop. Thank you, Tomasz.

name: Festival crew retro, 52 tables in the tram depot
summary: Synthetic sample. Four days after a three-day ideas festival in Belgium, crew lead Lotte, Monitor desk lead Sofie, floor runner lead Yannick and producer Bart hold a retrospective over a café table. On Saturday the festival ran 52 kitchen-table conversations at once across two halls of a former tram depot. They explain the Monitor desk (laptop plus a big screen, the Scanned to Recording states, what Audio stopped?, Screen locked and catch up ~N min meant in practice), per-table QR cards that filled in the table number and hall, a group chat for runners, and the A4 sheet every floor helper carried. They cover the rehearsal that showed neighbouring tables bleeding into each other and led to wider spacing and a side room, the crate of numbered power banks, and old volunteer phones. The honest failure was Friday's "everyone scan now" moment on the main stage: about 230 rows in fifteen minutes, many empty or a few seconds long, in the same project as the tables, plus overloaded venue wifi. Yannick defends the energy and the one-liners; Lotte wants any mass moment in its own project, closed afterwards. They list what they will repeat next year.

chunks.text: Okay, Bart's phone is recording, it's on the sugar bowl. This is the crew retro for the depot weekend. I'm Lotte, I'll keep us moving. Sofie, Yannick, Bart. We have an hour, and then Bart has to go and explain the invoice to the city. Let's start with Saturday, because Saturday is the thing everyone will ask us about. Fifty-two tables at the same time. Fifty-two in the end. We planned sixty, and eight never filled, so we closed them before the doors opened.

Thirty-four in the big hall, eighteen in the old workshop. And actually, the reason there were eighteen in the workshop is the rehearsal on Thursday. Yannick, you tell it. So Thursday afternoon we put the crew at two tables, side by side, like the floor plan said, about one and a half metres apart. Both tables talking, both phones recording. And then we read the transcripts. Table A had full sentences from table B in it. Not a lot, but enough that you go, hm, whose idea is that.

The depot is all concrete and glass. It echoes like a church. So we used the rule the dembrane people gave us: if you can still follow the conversation at your own table yourself, the phone can too. And sit closer to your own phone than to the next table. At one and a half metres you could not. At two and a half, more or less yes. So we lost space, and we moved eighteen tables into the workshop, which has a wooden ceiling and is much softer.

Fewer tables per square metre, but I'd rather have fifty-two good recordings than sixty mixed ones. Bart was not happy about the extra chairs. I was fine about the chairs. I was not happy about the extra crew. But okay, go on. The Monitor. Yes, the Monitor desk. So I had a laptop on the crew desk by the bar, and we plugged it into a big screen next to it so two people could watch. On the Monitor every conversation goes through Scanned, then Setting up, then Recording.

And then there are the warnings. Audio stopped? and Screen locked. Those two are basically our whole job. And the names helped so much. We printed a card for every table with its own QR, and the link already filled in the name and the tag. So the name was "T23" and the tag was "Workshop" or "Big hall". Nobody at the table had to type anything. On the Monitor I could see "T23 Screen locked" and I knew exactly where T23 is, because the floor map was taped to the desk.

How did it get from you to the runners? A group chat on our phones. I typed "T23 screen locked" and whoever was closest put a thumb up and went. We had six runners, about one per nine tables. Yannick's people. And they each had the A4. I want to talk about the A4, because I think it was the best thing we made. Front side, the floor map with table numbers and their own section in a colour. Back side, five things.

What the three stages and the two warnings on the Monitor mean. What to do for each. What to say to the table. What never to do. And who to call. Read us the "what never to do". Never take the phone off the table. Never interrupt someone who is talking, wait for a pause. Never read the screen out loud. And never say "it's broken", say "let me just wake it up". Because people get nervous when you say broken, they think their words are gone.

And what you say is: "Sorry, just checking your phone is still awake. Carry on." That's it. Most of the time it was Screen locked. Somebody's phone had auto-lock at thirty seconds. You tap it awake, check it says Recording again, you leave. Ten seconds. The Setting up ones were different. If a table sat in Setting up for more than two minutes, it was nearly always the microphone permission. If you click the dot on the Monitor, it shows you whether the mic check was blocked.

People tapped "don't allow" without thinking. Then the runner helps them allow it, and the mic check shows the level moving, and then it says Recording. What about the catch up thing? I saw that number on the screen and I panicked a bit. Catch up, yes. At the peak, around half past three, the Monitor said catch up about eight minutes. That means transcription is behind, not that something is lost. The recordings are fine, the text just arrives later.

I told the runners in the chat, ignore the catch up number, only act on Screen locked and Audio stopped?. By five it was back to normal. Power. Let's do power, because that was my crate. The famous crate. Thirty power banks, each with a sticker with a table number, charged on Friday night in the office, with both kinds of cable rubber-banded to them. On every table the card said: battery below thirty percent, take the power bank under the card. And the runners checked battery when they passed.

We used maybe twenty of them. Without the crate we would have lost at least ten tables in the second hour. And the phones themselves. Because a lot of table hosts were volunteers with their own phones. Two had very old phones and the mic check level was tiny. We swapped them for crew phones. Next year I want to ask on the volunteer form how old the phone is. That sounds rude but it matters. Okay. Now Friday. The main stage. Here we go. So Friday night, the opening.

Four hundred people in the big hall, before the tables were even set up. And the presenter, this was Bart's idea... It was a shared idea. It was Bart's idea. The presenter says: everyone take out your phone, scan the QR on the screen, and tell us in one sentence what you wish for this city. And there is this beautiful moment where four hundred phones come out. It looked amazing. It looked amazing. And then I looked at the Monitor and it was a waterfall.

About two hundred and thirty rows in fifteen minutes. And a lot of them never got past Setting up. People scanned, saw the consent screen, got distracted by the band starting, and put the phone away. And the wifi in the hall basically gave up with four hundred phones on it. So on Sunday morning, when Bart wanted a first look, we opened the conversations list and it was full of rows with nothing in them. Some had a few seconds. Some had one lovely sentence.

And they were in the same project as Saturday's tables, because we only made one project. And then I asked the assistant, what are the main themes from the festival, and the answer was half Saturday and half one-liners from Friday. All mixed. It treated "more trees please" as if it was a forty-minute table conversation. Can I defend Friday a little? Go. The energy was real. People talked about it all weekend.

And the good ones, the sixty or so that actually have a sentence, those are the most quotable things we have. "I want my kids to be bored in this city and still be safe." That's from Friday. That's on the poster now. I agree with that. I'm not saying never. I'm saying not in the same project, and not like that. If we do it again: its own project, its own QR. The presenter shows on stage how to press record and how to press finish.

A timer on the screen, ninety seconds. Tell people to use mobile data, not the venue wifi. And afterwards we close it with the conversation toggle, so the QR stops creating new rows when people find it on their phone at midnight. And cleaning. I spent Monday morning cleaning. Filtered the Friday ones, opened them, and deleted the empty ones in bulk. But slowly, because bulk delete has no undo. I checked the count three times before I pressed it.

And I didn't trust the duration column, I opened them, because a few that looked empty had a sentence. And the Thursday rehearsal tables were also still in there. "Crew test A", "Crew test B". They showed up in Ask too. Delete your test recordings. That's on next year's list in capital letters. Okay, so the list for next year. I'll say them and Bart's phone hears it. One. Rehearsal on Thursday in its own project, not the live one. Two. Per-table QR cards with the name and tag filled in, again.

Three. Monitor desk with two people and a big screen, runners in a group chat, one runner per eight or nine tables. Four. The A4 sheet, same as this year, plus the line about mic permission. Five. Two and a half metres between tables in an echoey hall, or a softer room. Six. The power bank crate, and ask volunteers about their phones. Seven. Any "everyone scan now" moment gets its own project and gets closed after. And eight.

Brief the crew an hour before doors open, with the sheet in their hands. Half of what went well on Saturday is because Yannick walked every runner through the sheet with a coffee. Fine, eight. And Bart, the city wants the report when? End of the month. And I want it per hall first, so we can see whether the workshop tables went deeper. My guess is yes, it was quieter in there. That's a good question to actually check, not guess. Okay. We're done. Thanks, everyone.
