name: Member network general assembly to roadmap, peer phone call
summary: Synthetic sample. Rafael, who directs a network of food cooperatives in Portugal and is planning his own general assembly in November, phones Birgit, general secretary of a German federation of about 140 community energy cooperatives. He records the call on speaker to keep notes. Birgit explains how her annual general assembly became a member roadmap: the formal votes were not recorded, then three rounds at fourteen tables, with a new recording per round and names like "R2 T09" so round and table are readable everywhere. Round three tables drafted roadmap items themselves and read them aloud. She pasted the board's strategy paper from last year in through the portal's text option, one text conversation per chapter, named with a DOC prefix, and said in the project context that these were board documents, not member voices. Her first report draft still presented an idea from the strategy paper as a member wish, which a board member caught; she fixed it with report instructions and by checking every item against a member source. Small rural cooperatives only showed up when she asked for them directly. The report went by email to members who left an address at the finish screen. They disagree on whether documents belong in a separate project.

chunks.text: Okay, I'm recording this on my side, Birgit, if that's alright. It's only for my notes, I won't share it. I have the phone on the desk next to the speaker. That's fine, Rafael. It's what I would do. So, you have your assembly in November? The twenty-first, yes. Ninety cooperatives, maybe a hundred and fifty people. And the board wants to come out of it with a roadmap for the next two years.

Last year we did the usual thing, flip charts, someone typed them up, and in March the board still hadn't seen it. So I want to know how you did yours, because I heard it went well. It went well and it went wrong in one interesting place. Let me start with the structure, because I think that's most of it. The formal part, the votes on the accounts and the board seats, we did not record. That's governance, it has its own minutes.

We recorded only the table part, two hours in the afternoon. Fourteen tables, about seven people each, one phone per table. Seven is quite a lot for one phone, no? In a quiet room, it was fine. We had a hall with carpet, and the tables far apart. One long table needed two phones, and I named those "T12 a" and "T12 b" so I knew they were one group. If your room echoes, make the groups smaller.

Some people swear by groups of three, but for a member assembly I want different kinds of cooperatives at one table, so seven. And the rounds? Three rounds. Round one: what has changed for your cooperative since last year's strategy paper. Round two: what should the federation do for you in the next two years. Round three: as a table, write two or three roadmap items on cards, and then read them aloud, so they are in the recording. That last part matters.

If it's only on a card, it's not in the data. So each round is one conversation? Each round is a new recording. At the end of each round the moderator says, finish on your phone, then scan again for the next round. And the name is the label. "R1 T09", "R2 T09", "R3 T09". Round and table. I printed that on the table card, exactly how to type it, with an example. Because if you don't, you get "Table nine", "tisch 9", "9", and someone's first name. Did everyone do it?

Twelve of fourteen. Two tables forgot to finish after round one, so one recording ran through round one and round two. I renamed it "R1+R2 T05" so at least it's honest. And I added portal tags for the rounds, so you can pick "Round 2" in the filter and get only those. The names are for humans reading the list, the tags are for filtering, in the list and when you choose which conversations a chat should look at. Now the strategy paper. That's the part I'm most curious about. Okay.

So after last year's assembly the board wrote a strategy paper, about forty pages. And this year's round one was literally, what has changed since that paper. So I wanted the paper in the project, so I could ask, where do members confirm it, where do they contradict it, where do they go further. And you uploaded it? Not uploaded, upload is only for audio. I opened our own portal link, chose the text option and pasted it in. But first I pasted the whole forty pages as one text.

Then every source in an answer just pointed at that one huge document, and you can't check anything that way. So I split it. One text conversation per chapter, five chapters. And I named every one with "DOC" at the start. "DOC Strategy, chapter 2, grid access". So in every list and every source you see immediately: this is a document, not a member talking. And in the project context I wrote it out. Something like: conversations whose name starts with DOC are chapters of last year's strategy paper, written by the board.

They are not member voices. When you describe what members said, never use DOC conversations as evidence. Clever. Clever, and still not enough. This is the part that went wrong. I generated the first report, and in the roadmap section there was this item: members ask for regional advice hubs. Sounds nice. And Jens from the board, who wrote chapter four of the paper, he reads it and says, Birgit, that's my chapter. Nobody at the tables said regional hubs. Oh no. And he was right.

I clicked the sources and it was the DOC conversation. So the language model had mixed the board's idea into the members' wishes. Which is exactly the thing you don't want in a member roadmap. It's the board talking to itself and calling it the members. So what did you do? Two things. In the report I added my own instructions: the roadmap section only contains items that appear in round three conversations, and for every item name the table. And then I checked every single item myself. Twenty-two items.

For each, I opened the source and found the table reading it aloud. That took maybe an hour and a half. Three items I removed, one I rewrote because the table said it more carefully than the report did. An hour and a half is fine. It's nothing, compared to typing up flip charts. And honestly, next year I think I would put the documents in a separate project. Keep the member conversations clean, and ask about the paper in its own place. Hm.

But then you can't ask the comparison question in one go, no? Where do members contradict the paper? That's the trade-off. In one project, you can ask it directly, but you have to watch for leaking. In two projects, it's clean, but you do the comparison yourself, side by side. I go back and forth. Maybe one project, but I select only member conversations for anything about what members want, and add the DOC ones only for the comparison question. Okay. What about the smaller voices?

We have tiny cooperatives, ten families with a vegetable plot, next to big ones with shops. Same for us. Rural cooperatives with forty members next to city ones with three thousand. And this is the second lesson. In the first report, the small ones were almost invisible. The big ones talk more, they have staff, they have positions. So the summary is mostly them. I asked the moderators to have everyone say their cooperative and its size when they introduced themselves, so it's in the transcript.

Then I asked, what did people from cooperatives under a hundred members raise that larger ones did not. And there it was. Insurance costs, volunteers burning out, the paperwork for grid connection taking a year. Completely different list. That became its own section in the report. You have to ask for it. You have to ask for it. It doesn't come on its own. Same with disagreement. I asked directly, where did tables disagree with each other about what the federation should do.

And there was a real split about lobbying, whether the federation should go to the ministry or stay out of politics. I kept that split in the report. I didn't let it become "members want more advocacy". And the report, who got it? The members. That was the whole point. In the portal I had name off, and at the end, on the finish screen, people could leave an email to get the report. About sixty did. I had participant updates switched on, so when I published, it went to them automatically.

Then the published link went into our newsletter for everyone, including the cooperatives who couldn't come. How did you shape it? For members, not for the board. First page: how many tables, how many rounds, what's in it and what's not, and that the votes are in the minutes, not here. Then, what you told us has changed since the strategy paper. Then the roadmap items, each with the table and a quote. Then where you disagree. Then what the board does next and by when.

I edited a lot before I published. The draft sounds like a press release; I want it to sound like us. And did the board accept the roadmap? The board took the twenty-two items to their October meeting, and they will answer each one: yes, not now, or no, with a reason. That answer goes back to members too. Because that's the part members always miss: you gave input, and then silence. The report doesn't decide anything, the board does, in public. Okay. Last thing. Language.

My members speak Portuguese, but we have two Spanish cooperatives near the border. Set the conversation language to what people actually speak, so Portuguese. And test it before the day, with a mixed table, a Spanish speaker in it. Record twenty minutes and read the transcript. Don't find out on the twenty-first. And put your words in the key terms: cooperative names, the ministry programmes, your acronyms.

That was the biggest difference in our transcripts. Okay. I think I have it. DOC prefix, round and table in the name, a new recording each round, read the cards aloud, ask for the small ones, check every roadmap item against a source. And send it back to the members. Don't let it go quiet.

name: HR walk-and-talk on the east loop, after the site walks
summary: Synthetic sample. Mireille, who leads people and culture at a food distribution company with nine sites in Canada, and HR business partner Theo walk the loop at the east site that employee trios walked during a listening programme on a new shift pattern. They record on the move to remember what it was like. They describe printed question cards for three stops on the route, one phone per trio, and the first site, where three of twelve recordings stopped because screens locked in pockets. After that, auto-lock went off before every walk, and HR phones ran dembrane Go, the iOS beta, which records in the background. They cover portal tags for site and shift, names like "S4 walk 2 trio C", anonymise transcripts switched on before collecting after talking to the privacy officer and employee representatives, and the limit that team names still appear. They argue about trios. Mireille saw newer staff and night shift speak more than in an earlier pilot with groups of six; Theo thinks some trios of friends just agreed with each other. They describe a runaway recording through a break room, moved out to a holding project, Compare & Contrast by site, asking directly for views raised by only one or two trios, and printed site reports with a QR for corrections.

chunks.text: Okay, it's on. Theo, I'm holding it like we told the trios, chest height, mic towards us, not in the pocket. And I'm recording with Go, so if I lock it by accident it keeps going. We're at the start of the east loop, by the trailer yard. I want to walk it once more and talk while we walk, because I think we learned more on these walks than in the whole engagement survey. Can I say first, it's windy. If this transcript is bad, that's the first lesson.

That is the first lesson. Site two was like this and two trios came back half wind. So, okay, from the beginning, for the record. Nine sites, a new shift pattern since the spring, and we wanted to know how it actually lands. Not the survey score. The stories. So trios of employees, twenty-five minutes, walking a loop around their own site. And three stops. Here at the yard, card one: what's one moment in the last month when the new pattern worked for you, and one when it didn't.

At the bench by the fence, card two: what does it do to your life outside work. At the gate, card three: if you could change one thing, what. Printed on cards on a lanyard, so whoever held the phone could also read out the question. And we asked them to actually do that, out loud, every time. Then the question is in the transcript, so later you can see exactly where card two starts. That one habit saved a lot of scrolling. The phones. Let's be honest about site one.

Site one. Twelve trios, and three recordings just stopped after a few minutes. The screen locked in a pocket, or someone checked a message. Which is normal. You walk, you put your phone away. With the portal in the browser, the screen has to stay on. If it locks, the recording pauses until someone wakes it, and in a pocket nobody does. We only saw it afterwards, because nobody was watching a Monitor at the site, we were walking with a trio ourselves. So from site two on, two changes.

One, before every walk the person holding the phone sets auto-lock to never, and we check it at the start, like a little ritual. "Show me your screen settings." People laughed, but it worked. Two, we put dembrane Go on the three HR phones. It's the iOS app, still a beta, we got it through TestFlight. It records in the background and stores the audio in small pieces on the phone, then syncs to the project.

So for the trios where someone wasn't comfortable using their own phone, or had an old one, we handed them an HR phone with Go. And it doesn't care if the screen goes off. That was maybe a third of the trios in the end. On those phones we added the site and shift tags in the app straight after the walk. The others used the portal QR on their own phone. And the portal tags. When they scanned, they picked the site and the shift. Morning, afternoon, night.

So we never had to sort by hand. And in the name field the HR person typed "S4 walk 2 trio C". Site, walk round, trio letter. Why do we have walk rounds again? I forget. Walk one in the first week, walk two three weeks later. To see if things moved. Some sites had a supervisor change in between. Okay, we're at the bench. Card two. So, the privacy part. I think this is the bit other HR teams will ask about, because it's employees talking about their managers.

Before we collected anything, I sat with our privacy officer and with the employee representatives. We set the legal basis on the project, and we decided anonymise transcripts on, from the very first walk. From the first walk, because it doesn't work backwards. It applies while the conversation is processed. If you turn it on after, the old ones stay as they are. And it costs you something. With anonymise on, audio playback and download are switched off, and so is retranscribe. So you can't listen again to check a word.

We knew that, we chose it. For this topic, people saying "my supervisor does this", I wanted names gone. And we said so on every walk: names are removed, nothing goes to your manager with your name. But it removes people's names, not team names. "The frozen team at site six" stays in. "The forklift guys on nights" stays in. And at a small site that's almost a name. So in the site reports we wrote "a team" or "one group" when it was that small.

We did that by hand, editing the report. Key terms helped a lot too. Our words. Reach truck, pick face, cross-dock, the scheduling system's name, the nine site names. Without them the first test transcript had "beach truck". With them, clean. Now the trios. Because you and I don't agree here. We don't fully agree. Go. So, before this, we did a pilot in a meeting room with groups of six. Long table, coffee. And it was the team leads and the people with fifteen years who talked.

The new hires said nothing. Night shift said nothing, they were tired. On the walks in trios, completely different. The people with less than a year talked. Night shift talked. You're side by side, not face to face, and I think it's easier to say a hard thing to the path in front of you than to someone's face. And we told every trio at the start: if one person talks a lot, the other two can bring it back. Two against one.

I heard a trio actually use that line on someone. "Two against one, Marco, let her finish." It was lovely. Okay, and my part. Some trios were three friends. They signed up together, walked together, agreed with each other for twenty-five minutes. Very nice walk, very little new. In a group of six you get more friction, more different views in one conversation. So I'm not against trios. I'm against trios people choose themselves. Which is fair. So at the later sites, mixing.

The sign-up sheet asked shift and how long you've worked here, and we made trios from that. A night person, a day person, a newer one. And the one hard rule: no supervisor in a trio with their own staff. That one was not up for debate. The one trio at site three that broke that rule, by accident, is the flattest recording of all forty-odd. Everyone was very positive about everything. Okay, gate. Card three. Let's do the analysis part while we walk back. Before analysis: the runaway. Tell it.

At site five, a trio finished the loop and walked straight into the break room, still recording. On the portal. An hour and a half. So the end of it is lunch, microwave, a story about somebody's brother-in-law. Anonymise took out the names, but it's still not something we asked people to share. So I moved it out into a small holding project that only I can open. A tag wasn't enough for me, because when you ask the assistant without narrowing it down, it reads the whole project.

And the lesson is on the card now. Card three says at the bottom: when you reach the gate, press finish. Analysis. We chatted with the assistant a lot, but mostly comparing. Compare & Contrast template, by site tag. And then the question that actually helped most: what came up at only one or two sites. That's where we found the site four thing, the bus from town doesn't match the new start time. Nobody at the other sites has that problem, so in an overall summary it disappears.

And the minority stuff. I asked, which views were raised by only one or two trios. You have to ask that directly, otherwise you get the big themes and that's it. Two of those small ones are now in the recommendations. One is about night shift and childcare that only two trios mentioned, but they described it very precisely. And I always open the sources. Because the chat answer says "several employees reported". Several. And then you open it and it's one trio, said twice. The reports.

One per site, for the people at that site. Printed, on the noticeboard by the time clock, with a QR at the bottom: if this is wrong or missing something, tell us. That goes to a small separate project. And one overall report for the leadership team, with the per-site differences up front, not buried. And next time, for the trios on the portal, I'd do a short Verify.

The person with the phone at the gate, two minutes, "is this what we said". We skipped it because it was another step, and I think we were wrong. I'm not sure, at the gate people want their break. But maybe in the break room, sitting down. Fine, we try it at the last site. Okay, we're back at the yard. I'll stop it.

name: Organisers' learning circle, Popcorn on the conference wall
summary: Synthetic sample. At a monthly learning circle for event organisers, host Ruth invites Aylin, who ran a public health conference in Austria with about 380 people and 34 afternoon tables, to talk about putting Popcorn live slides on the main screen. Popcorn was in early beta, switched on with the project toggle for living canvas and Popcorn. Florian, a process designer, is openly sceptical. Aylin describes what the room saw (short phrases in participants' own words, not conclusions), the slow start while transcription caught up, a refresh every couple of minutes, and the moment when the moderator read three phrases aloud and asked who said them, with the plenary recorded so the answers landed in the data. Her cautions: preview on a laptop before switching to the wall, a slide label saying the phrases were unedited and early, a fallback slide, no Ask answers or reports shown live, a misheard phrase, and a German phrase she could have shown translated with Popcorn's language setting, found too late. Florian argues that half-formed phrases on a wall can misrepresent a group and that anything shown should serve the next step. They partly agree: Popcorn as recognition, not output. Aylin explains what she checked before the written report.

chunks.text: Okay, welcome back everyone, it's the October circle. I'm recording as usual, it goes into our circle project and nowhere else. Today Aylin is going to tell us about her conference last month, because she did something most of us haven't tried yet. She put Popcorn on the big screen, live. And Florian has already told me he has questions, so this will be fun. I have opinions, Ruth. Questions too. Okay. So, the setting.

A public health conference, about three hundred and eighty people, two days in the last week of September. On the afternoon of day one we had what we called table conversations. Thirty-four tables, one phone each, the table host's phone. Ninety minutes, two questions on the cards. And on the big screen in front, Popcorn. Explain Popcorn for the two people here who've never seen it. It's live slides for the room, made from the project's conversations.

It's an early beta, you switch it on in the project with a toggle, it says something like living canvas and Popcorn. And it warns you that it may change or be removed. What our room mostly saw were short phrases, pulled from what people at the tables actually said. It can show more, tensions between views for example, but the phrases were the heart of it. Their words, not a summary. They pop up one by one on the screen. So, not "the room thinks X". No.

That's the main thing I want to say. It's not conclusions. It's more like, "the clinic is the last place people trust" from table eleven, and then "prevention doesn't have a ribbon to cut" from table twenty-two. Little pieces. Some funny, some sharp. And what did the room do with it? The first ten minutes, nothing. The screen was empty, which I had warned the moderator about. Transcription needs to start, and with thirty-four tables at once there was a backlog.

On the Monitor it said catch up, I think five or six minutes. So the first phrases came maybe twelve minutes in. And then it updated every couple of minutes, in batches. It's not instant. How long between someone saying it and it appearing? Several minutes. Never seconds. People expect seconds, so tell them beforehand. Our moderator said at the start: the screen fills slowly, you might see your own words in a while. That turned the delay into a little game. People kept looking up.

And then the moment that made it worth it, for me. Around forty minutes in, one table started pointing at the screen. "That's us, that's what Maja said." And then the table next to them. It's this small feeling of, someone heard that. In the coffee break, people were standing in front of the screen reading, with their cups. That's when it was most alive, actually. During the tables most people don't look up. Okay, and the plenary? That's the part I'd copy if I were you.

When we came back into plenary, the moderator picked three phrases from the screen, read them aloud, and asked: who said this? Can you say more? And people stood up and explained. And the plenary was recorded too, as its own conversation. So the explanation is in the data, next to the phrase. The phrase on the wall was the start of a conversation, not the end of one. Okay, Florian. Yes. So, I'm happy for you, honestly. But let me say what bothers me.

A phrase on a wall is a selection. Somebody, or something, chose that phrase out of a forty-minute conversation. And three hundred people read it as, this is what's being said at this conference. Half-formed ideas from minute twelve, presented on a five-metre screen. That can misrepresent a group quite badly. I agree with half of that. And my second point. Everything I put in front of a room should serve the next step in the process. If it doesn't, it's noise. Decoration. So what was the next step that Popcorn served?

The next step was the plenary. And I think the honest answer is: it served recognition, not analysis. People felt their table was part of something bigger. And three phrases started the plenary conversation. If I had used it as the output, as "here's what we found", then yes, I would agree with you completely. Which is why I want to hear your rules. You must have had rules. I had rules. Some I had before, some I learned on the day.

One: I previewed it on my laptop for ten minutes before switching it to the wall. Our tech person had the main screen on a fallback slide with the two questions, and only when I said okay did he switch. Two: the slide had a label at the top. "Phrases from your tables, unedited, early." So nobody reads them as findings. Three: nothing else from the language model went on the wall live. No Ask answers, no summaries, no report. I know some people do live chat on a big screen.

I'm too nervous for that in a room of public health people. They will read one wrong number and you've lost them for the day. Popcorn is their own words. An answer from the assistant is someone else's sentence about their words. That's a different thing to show. Four: if Popcorn had broken, fine. The event was not designed around it. The fallback slide was always ready. I'd say that to anyone: don't build your programme on a beta. Did anything go wrong? Two things made me wince. One phrase was misheard.

Someone said something about herd immunity and the phrase came out as something about a "hurt community". Which, you know, is almost poetic, but it's not what they said. A few people laughed. And the table it came from was a bit annoyed. Ah. And the second. Our conference language was English, and the project language was English. But three tables were Austrian public health officers who switched to German among themselves. And one phrase from them appeared on the screen in German. Not wrong, just not translated.

Fine for most of the room, but our international guests didn't get it. And that one was my fault. Popcorn has a language setting: you can choose a language to translate the phrases into, and the original stays. I only found it afterwards. So what would you do differently there? Set the translation to English before the day. For the transcripts of the mixed tables, I'm still not sure. Maybe ask those tables to keep to one language, or accept it. For the mishearing, key terms.

I had put in our conference terms, the agency names, the programme names. But not ordinary public health words like herd immunity, because I thought, everyone knows those. The transcription mostly does, but in a noisy hall, adding them costs you nothing. And the context, did that matter for Popcorn? I think so. The context steers what it picks up. I wrote who the people are, what the two questions are, and that we're interested in barriers to prevention in local practice. The phrases mostly stayed on that.

One or two were about the lunch. What about names? Health officials talking about colleagues. Anonymise transcripts was on, from the start. I discussed it with our privacy officer before. So no names in phrases. One phrase mentioned a ministry department, which is not a person, but it was a bit pointed. That's still sitting with me. It was true to what was said, but it was on a big screen in front of people from that department. Afterwards I saw you can hide an item from the presentation.

Next time someone on my team watches the screen with exactly that in mind. That's my point, though. The selection is a kind of editing. On a wall, it's public in a way the table wasn't. Yes. I think that's fair. Next time I'd tell the tables at the start, in plain words: short phrases from your table may appear on the main screen without your names. Then it's their choice what they say. We told them about recording and the report. We didn't tell them clearly enough about the wall.

Okay, and the report afterwards? That was a week later, not live. I took the time. I used Ask over all thirty-four tables, first broad, then by the two questions. Then I asked directly for disagreements, and for what only one or two tables raised, because those never come by themselves. And for every quote in the report, I copied it from the transcript, not from the chat answer. And on page one: how many tables, which ones had problems, what's not in it. Did any Popcorn phrases go into the report?

Two. But only after I opened the transcript and checked the phrase meant what it seemed to mean in context. One didn't. In context it was sarcastic. On the wall it looked like a real proposal. That's the best argument for my side you could have given me. It's an argument for checking. Which is my side too. Okay, we have ten minutes. Who else wants to try it, and what's your first question?

name: High street dinner by courses, hosts at the sink
summary: Synthetic sample. Eilidh, from a small development trust in Scotland, and her co-host Callum record themselves washing up after a dinner for 32 guests about the future of their high street. Five tables, a trust volunteer hosting each, and each course was a round: memories over the starter, what is in the way over the main, one thing to start this year over dessert. They explain naming conversations by table and course ("T3 Starter"), with a tag per course, and a glass rung between courses meaning finish and start a new recording. Table four never stopped, so its courses are mixed. They describe noise (cutlery, the coffee machine, staff asking who had the fish), a phone under a napkin spotted through the Monitor on Callum's phone, and a project context that listed the questions per course, warned about background noise and staff talk, and said a short talk by a former shopkeeper, recorded as its own conversation, was not the guests' table talk. Callum used Ask during the main course to pull memories shared by more than one table, checked the sources, and Eilidh read three back at dessert as questions, not conclusions. They close with a one-word round and email sign-up for the report, and agree to move the big question away from dessert.

chunks.text: Is it recording? The little dot. Yes. Okay, Callum, put it on the windowsill, away from the tap. We said we'd do this tonight while it's fresh, so. Debrief at the sink. Thirty-two guests, five tables, three courses, and about four hundred plates. Not four hundred. But a lot. Okay. Where do you want to start? With the courses, because that was the whole idea. Each course is a round. Starter was memories: tell us one memory of the high street that you still carry.

Main was the hard one: what's in the way of it being what it could be. And dessert: one thing we could start this year, and who would do it. And I think the courses really work as a structure. People know a starter takes twenty minutes, they know when the main is coming. Nobody needs a timer. The kitchen is the timer. The kitchen was a bit of a slow timer at the main. The lamb was worth it. Okay, the naming.

On each table there was a card with the QR and the name to type. "T3 Starter", then "T3 Main", then "T3 Dessert". And a tag for the course, picked when they scanned. So when I look at the list later I can go straight to all the starters, or everything from table three. Except table five typed "Pudding". Table five typed "Pudding" because it's table five. And table two typed "T2 Main course". So we have three spellings of dessert and two of main.

The tags are right though, so the filter still works. I'll tidy the names tomorrow. Next time the card says exactly what to type, in a box, with an example. No room for creativity. And the glass. I think the glass was the best bit. Yes. Between courses I stood up and rang my glass. That was the signal. Table hosts press finish, then scan again, then a new recording with the next name. Most tables had it by the second time. It's also a nice moment, everyone stops for a second.

Except table four. Except table four. Table four never pressed finish. So table four is one recording of two hours and ten minutes, starter, main and dessert all mixed together, and somewhere in the middle Jean's speech about the old cinema. I'm not deleting it, it's good, but it can't go under just one course. I'll rename it "T4 all courses" and give it all three tags. Then at least nobody thinks it's only the starter. Fine. Now the noise. I was so worried about noise. It was loud.

Cutlery, the coffee machine in the second half, the kitchen door every two minutes. And Kirsty doing the service, asking "who had the fish?" at every table. That's going to be in every transcript. Which is why I wrote it in the context. I'll tell you what I wrote, because I think it helped. First, who we are, the trust, and what the dinner is for.

Then who is at the tables: shopkeepers, two councillors, young people from the youth club, the bus driver, the receptionist from the surgery, a few people who just moved here. Then the three questions, one per course, written out word for word. So the assistant can tell which question a bit of conversation is answering. Then a line saying, this is a dinner, expect background noise, and staff talking about the food. That is not the guests' view, please ignore it. And Ina's talk. And Ina's talk.

Because between the starter and the main, Ina stood up, she ran the hardware shop on the corner for forty years, and she talked for five minutes about the street when it was full. And I recorded that separately, as its own conversation called "Ina's talk". And in the context I said: Ina's talk is a short talk to the whole room. It is not the table conversations. Good, because half the tables quoted her back during the main. "Like Ina said, the bakery with the garden behind."

Which is lovely, but I don't want a report saying the community wants a bakery with a garden because one woman remembered one from 1975. Okay. Key terms. I put in the street names, Harbour Wynd, the Cross, the old cinema's name, the bus number, the trust's name, and the councillors' names. And dembrane, because someone always says it. Did the Monitor help? You kept looking at your phone during service, I saw you. I had the Monitor open on my phone in the kitchen. Not perfect, small screen, but enough.

In the main course table two went to Audio stopped?. I went out with the bread and the phone was under a napkin. Somebody had put the napkin over it to keep the crumbs off. Very thoughtful. I moved it next to the candle, said nothing, and it went back to Recording. And the phones were on those little stands? The little stands, yes, between the salt and the candle. Not under the bread basket. Not near the wine bottles, because people move bottles.

And the stand tilts the phone up a bit, so the mic faces the people, not the tablecloth. Then you did the clever thing during the main. The slightly risky thing. While everyone was eating the main, I sat in the corner of the kitchen with my phone and asked the assistant, only on the starter conversations: which memories came up at more than one table, with quotes. And it gave me five.

Then I opened the sources for each, because I didn't want to read out something that someone didn't actually say. How many survived? Three. One was really from only one table, said twice. And one was Kirsty asking about the fish, I'm not even joking, it had made a memory out of "the fish shop" in her sentence. So, three. And those three I read at dessert. But as questions. "At three tables, people remembered the Saturday market under the Cross. Is that right? Is that still something?"

Not "the community wants the market back". And people corrected me. Table one said, it's not the market, it's that you met everyone there. That's a different thing. And that correction is in the dessert recordings. I liked that. It felt like the evening was talking to itself. Dessert was the messiest, though. Two glasses of wine in, everybody talking at once, louder, more overlapping. I listened to a bit of table three on the way home and you can hear four conversations at once. The transcript will be rougher.

And dessert was the question where we wanted the most precise answers. Who will actually do something. So next time we swap. The concrete question goes with the main, when people are awake and sober. Dessert gets the easy, warm one. Yes. And the closing. I think the closing worked. Tell it for the recording. After dessert I stood up with my coffee. Said thank you, very short. Read the three things and said thank you for correcting me.

Then said what happens next: a short report in about two weeks, and a public evening in the hall in October where everyone can see it and argue with it. And that if you want the report by email, leave your email on the last screen when you finish. And then the one-word round. The one-word round. Every table, each person, one word they take home, into the phone. "Hopeful", "buses", "tired", "Saturday". Someone said "finally". It took four minutes and it's all recorded. I think it's my favourite four minutes.

Did anyone try the Verify thing? Table one, with the coffee. The table host had read the host guide. They got five points from their conversation on the phone, approved two, edited one, threw one out. The others didn't bother. Nobody wants homework with their pudding. Fair. Okay, what do we do tomorrow? Tomorrow. Delete my test from this afternoon, the one where I said "testing testing, the soup is hot".

Rename table four. Fix the dessert spellings. Then start with the main course conversations, because that's the hard question. And ask for what only one table said, because the young people were all at table five, and I don't want them averaged away. And no report until we've both read it. No report until we've both read it. Pass me that tray.

name: Ferry crossings as a meeting place, voice memo from the upper deck
summary: Synthetic sample. Signe, community liaison at a small ferry company in Norway, starts a voice memo on the upper deck for her colleague Helga, who will run the next round, and the purser Arvid joins her. For two weeks the company held conversations at saloon tables during the forty-minute crossing about a new timetable and the move to an electric ferry, because the crossing is where islanders already sit together. They describe a test sailing that found a dead zone mid-crossing, the Monitor at the office showing Audio stopped? at every table at the same minute, gaps in transcripts, and their fix: start straight after leaving the quay, hold the big question for the coastal stretches, and use dembrane Go, the iOS beta, on two crew phones because it records locally and syncs later. They cover engine noise and loudspeaker announcements, tags passengers picked at scan time (islander, mainland commuter, visitor, crew), names by sailing, a two-minute docking warning, type instead for a passenger who wanted to write, and a project context that said the timetable was the company's proposal. The board wanted a yes or no count; Signe explains why the report shows reasons by group instead, and what only night-shift commuters raised.

chunks.text: Okay, Helga, this is a voice memo for you, I'm recording it into the project so you have it before you take over next week. I'm on the upper deck of the four o'clock to the mainland. It's windy, so I'm behind the funnel. Arvid is here too, he's on his break. I want to tell you everything we learned in two weeks of crossings before I forget, because some of it is not obvious. Hello Helga. She's going to make me sound clever. He doesn't need help.

So, the idea, for the record. We need to talk with people about the new timetable and the electric ferry next year. And every time we hold a meeting in the community hall, the same twelve people come. But the crossing is forty minutes, and every islander sits in the saloon anyway, often with people they half know. It's the only meeting room on this island that meets eight times a day. So for two weeks, four tables in the saloon, each with a card. "Talk with us about the new timetable.

Scan here, it takes as long as the crossing." One phone per table, sometimes a crew phone, sometimes a passenger's own. Twenty-eight sailings in the end. Now the important thing. Signal. Before we started, Arvid and I did a test sailing with three phones recording on the portal. And in the middle of the crossing, past the lighthouse, there's about twelve minutes with almost no mobile signal. We knew that, everybody here knows it. We didn't think about what it means for recording.

The first day, Helga, our colleague at the office had the Monitor open. And she messages me: all four tables say Audio stopped?. All four at the same minute. She thought everyone had gone quiet at once. It was the lighthouse. And afterwards the transcripts had gaps in the middle. Not everything, but holes. So the Monitor was actually telling the truth, the recordings were struggling, we just didn't understand it the first day. Now we look at it like a map.

If all tables stop at the same moment, it's the signal. If one table stops, it's a phone. The ship's wifi is no help. It goes by satellite and it's slow, and with sixty passengers watching videos it's nothing. Don't tell people to use it. So we changed three things. One, tables start right after we leave the quay. The crew says it: if you want to talk, scan now, not in ten minutes. Two, the big question is on the coastal stretches, where there's signal.

On the card, question one is for the start, and the main question, about the timetable, says "after the lighthouse". People found that funny but they did it. Three, the two crew iPhones have dembrane Go. It's the iOS app, still a beta, you get it through TestFlight, I'll send you the invite. It records on the phone itself, in small pieces, and sends it to the project when there's signal again. So the dead zone doesn't matter.

For the table closest to the kiosk, where a crew member is anyway, we use Go. The crew member adds the tag in the app afterwards, because nobody scans anything with Go. The other tables use the portal with passengers' phones. Noise. This is my part. Arvid's part. The engine. The two tables at the back are above the engine room, and on the first days the transcripts from there were bad. Lots of missing words. We moved those tables forward to the windows. Also, and Helga, this is important, the announcements.

"Car deck passengers please return to your vehicles." It's in every transcript, every sailing, twice. So in the project context I wrote it down. That this is a ferry, that there will be engine noise and loudspeaker announcements from the crew, and that announcements are not passengers' views. And I wrote that the new timetable, the one on the poster, is the company's proposal. So when people read out the times from the poster, that's not them wanting those times.

And key terms: the island names, both quays, the ferry's name, the route number, the bus company, the school. The tags. Explain the tags, because I think that was the best idea. That was your idea. When people scan, they pick one tag. Islander, mainland commuter, visitor, or crew. The crew one Arvid insisted on. Because nobody asks us. We do this crossing eight times a day. We know which departure has the school kids and which one has the night-shift workers going to the fish plant.

So in the evenings, three or four of us sat at a table after the last crossing and talked into the phone with the crew tag. I think it's the most practical stuff in the whole project. And the name field is the sailing. "Mon 0640 to mainland", "Tue 1600 to island". So you can see which departure a conversation was on. The morning ones are commuters, the afternoon ones in summer are more visitors. That matters a lot for a timetable. What about docking? The docking deadline.

Every conversation has a hard end, because the ferry arrives. So two minutes before, I make an announcement. "If you're talking at the tables, please finish your conversation on the phone now, we're docking." Before I did that, people just put the phone in the pocket and ran for the car. And the recordings kept going on the car deck. Engine, car doors, someone's dog. And the finish screen says: thank you, the report comes in October, leave your email if you want it. About a third did.

Consent was easier than I thought. People are curious. The crew asks, would you like to, and most say yes. One fisherman said no, he doesn't talk into phones, and that's fine. He talked to me instead and I wrote notes, which I added later as text with the tag. And one woman who is hard of hearing used type instead and wrote the longest answer of all of them, about the evening ferry and the hospital. Now the hard part. The board. The board wanted a number.

How many are for the new timetable, how many against. And I had to say, that's not what this is. These are conversations, not a vote. The people at a table don't all say yes or no, they say "it works if the bus connects" or "it's fine for me but not for my mother". So I asked the assistant to compare by tag. Islanders against mainland commuters against visitors, on the new timetable. And that gave the board something better than a number. The visitors mostly don't care.

The islanders care about the last ferry back. And the commuters, especially the early ones, are worried about the first departure moving. And then I asked, what did only a few people say that the others didn't. You have to ask that, Helga, or it doesn't come. And that's where the night-shift people came out. Only five conversations, all on the late sailings. With the new timetable, the night shift at the fish plant finishes after the last ferry. Nobody at the office had seen that. It's five conversations.

It's the most important finding. And for every quote in the report, open the source. The answer says "several commuters". Check if it's several. I'll add one thing. Don't keep the tables going too long. Two weeks was right. In the second week we started getting the same people again, the regulars, and they were telling us the same thing they told us on Monday. The tag doesn't tell you if it's the same person. The names of the sailings help a bit.

And the electric ferry questions, we'll do those in the next round, you'll have them, Helga. Keep them separate. A new project. The timetable is one thing to report on, the new ferry is another, different questions, different people who care. That's the horn. We're coming in. I have to go. Go. Okay, Helga, that's it. Start after the quay, big question after the lighthouse, Go on the crew phones, tag the crew, warn before docking, and ask for the small groups. I'll stop it now before the car deck.

name: Process agency partners, year-two retrospective
summary: Synthetic sample. Lone and Rasmus, the two partners of a small Danish process agency, record their year-two retrospective after running more than a hundred client projects in dembrane. They explain why they moved from one shared internal workspace and login to one external-client workspace per client after a client glimpsed another client's project, and why the data-owner email is now confirmed out loud with the actual person. They disagree about when to upgrade a client from observer to external, and settle on observer during collection and external from the joint sense-making session, with publishing as a shared step. They describe a naming convention for projects and tables, prefilled recording links per table, freezing the portal the day before printing QR codes (after a scare over a QR code that only looked different), a context skeleton kept in their own drive (including what is already decided), five custom Ask templates, and always asking what only one table said. On money, they moved from hourly billing to pricing per phase, with the platform cost as its own line on the quote. They admit depending on one colleague who knows everything and a handover that was only an email, and now hand over in a thirty-minute walkthrough after a clean-up.

chunks.text: Okay, it's recording. Rasmus, is the little level bar moving on your side? Good. So this is our year-two retro, and yes, we are recording it in dembrane, because we spend the whole year telling clients to record their sessions and then we hold our own retro on the back of a napkin. Ida said she'll join at four. Let's start with the boring one, which is actually the one that hurt most last year. Workspaces.

The boring one, yes. So for whoever listens to this later, which will be Ida, in year one we ran everything in our own internal workspace. Every client, every project, one long list. And one login the three of us shared, which I'm not proud of. Then in March I'm sharing my screen with the project lead from one of the harbour municipalities, and there, two lines up, is another municipality's project. With its name on it.

She was very gracious about it, Rasmus. But she saw it. And we had spent weeks telling her that her residents' words belong to her and nobody else. So that same week we asked dembrane to mark us as a partner, which you can't do yourself, you have to ask them. And from then on it's one external-client workspace per client. The client organisation is the data owner, we tick the partner agreement, and that happens before anyone writes a single line of context.

And the data-owner email. Tell that one, Lone. Ugh. Okay. So the data-owner email decides who gets invited as observer. For the regional health network I copied the address from an email signature and it was a shared inbox that nobody reads. For three weeks their lead thought we had forgotten to give her access. Now the rule is I read the address out loud on the phone, letter by letter, and the actual person says yes, that's me. Sounds silly. It works.

Can we talk about observer versus external, because this is where you and I still disagree. Go on. So an observer is free, they can watch everything come in, open the conversations, see the report when it's published. If they want to ask their own questions in Ask or generate reports themselves, we upgrade them to external, and that's a paid seat. And my view is, Lone, we upgrade too early. The moment a client can ask questions alone, they go shopping for the quote that supports what they already wanted to do.

And my view is that's their right, Rasmus, it's their data. And honestly, the ones who go quote shopping would do it with a printed transcript too. What I've seen is the opposite more often. The planning officer in the river town asked her own questions for two evenings and then rang me and said, I didn't realise how many people talked about the bus. She owned that finding. We could never have told her that in a slide.

Fine. Then a middle position. Observer during collection, so they see it arriving and nobody gets ahead of the room. External from the sense-making session onwards, when we sit together and ask the first questions side by side. And external people can generate a report but can't publish it, which I actually like, because publishing stays a conscious step that we take together. Deal? Deal. Write that down. It's recorded, Lone. That's the point.

Okay, naming. I went through all hundred and four projects last week, and the first forty are a mess. Bord 3, table three, T3, group three, and my favourite, 'Anders', who is a facilitator and not a table. Now we name projects the same way every time: year and month, client short name, programme, then the session. So 2026-05, harbour, waterfront plan, resident evening one. When you sort the list, it reads like a diary.

And the conversations? Table number, then who sits there, if the design has groups. T3 shop owners, T4 young families. And since August the recording links can prefill the title and a tag, so we print a separate QR per table with the label already in it. Nobody types anything. That alone fixed half the mess, because the mess was always people typing their own name into the name field at seven in the evening with a coffee in the other hand.

Careful, though. Tell them about the printed codes. Right. Sports hall evening. I edited the finish text the afternoon before, and then the QR code on my screen looked different from the laminated table cards in my car. I nearly cried. It turns out editing the text doesn't change the link at all, the pattern just looks different depending on where you download it, and the old cards worked. I didn't know that at five o'clock. So now: portal frozen the day before we print. If I want to change the wording after that, I don't.

Context templates. This is the thing I'd actually tell other agencies about. We keep one skeleton in our own shared drive, nothing fancy, a document. Who is in the room. The question, in one sentence. What is already decided and what is genuinely open. The rounds and the exact questions per round. Words people will use, street names, scheme names, abbreviations. What will happen with the output and who reads it. And warnings: noisy hall, two languages, the alderman is at table one.

And the 'what is decided' line matters more than anything else in there. If you don't say the parking garage is already approved, the summaries treat every complaint about the garage as a fresh proposal. When we put it in, the reports started saying things like, residents accept the garage but question the entrance on the dyke road. Which is what they actually said. Same with statements we put on the table ourselves. We tell the context those came from us, so they don't come back as if a resident thought of them.

The key terms list too. We paste the whole glossary from the client's own plan documents and then cut it down to the names people will actually say. And add dembrane, because otherwise the intro gets transcribed as 'them brain'. And for Ask we have five custom templates we save into every new client workspace. The matrix one, groups as columns, themes as rows. Tensions with quotes. What's fixed versus open. Who was mentioned but not in the room. And one that just says, now list what only one table said.

That last one is the one I use most, Lone. Because the first answer is always the polite middle. If you don't ask for the single table that said something odd, it never turns up. Okay, money. Which is awkward to record, but fine. In year one we priced by the hour, like everyone. And synthesis went from three days of typing up sticky notes to an afternoon of reading and checking. So we were, in effect, charging clients less for a better job.

Which felt noble for about two months. Then we changed it. Now we price per phase. Design, the session itself, the sense-making session with the client, and the handover. The sense-making session is where our time actually goes now: reading transcripts, checking what the report says against the sources, arguing about what's missing. We price that time properly. And the platform cost goes on the quote as its own line, at what it costs us. We don't hide it inside a day rate.

Has anyone pushed back on the separate line? One client asked why they should pay for it when their meeting software already transcribes. And I said, sure, try it with twelve tables and two rounds and then find me the one table that disagreed with the other eleven. She laughed. She signed. Ha. Okay, and the Ida problem, before she arrives. Every project ends up with Ida. She's the one who knows it all, and every project manager says, can Ida set it up?

And Ida is brilliant and also going on holiday in October. So the rule from now on is every project has a second pair of hands who does the setup with her, the portal, the context, the test on your own phone. Two people know every project. We train in pairs, never one person alone. And whoever set it up deletes the test recordings before the client ever opens the workspace. Because 'test test, is this on' in a client project is not a great first impression.

Handover. This is the bit I think we're good at now, and it took a disaster to get there. The ferry company. We emailed them a lovely PDF and a transcript zip, and asked dembrane staff to hand the workspace over to them. And then nothing. Four months later their new manager calls and asks what all these projects are. Nobody had ever walked them through it. They had the data and no idea what it was.

So now handover is a meeting, not an email. Thirty minutes with the person who will own it, workspace open on the screen. Here are your projects, here's how they're named, here's the report, here's how you check a line in the report against what a resident actually said: click the source, read the transcript. Then the PDF and the zip of transcripts as a backup on their side. Then the handoff. And a one-page note of what's in there, in plain language.

And we clean up before that meeting, not after. Retranscribe anything rough once the key terms are fixed, which makes a fresh copy, so delete the rough one. Tidy what's been reviewed, close the portal with the conversation toggle so nobody adds something by accident in December. Then hand it over. Okay, one thing each for next year. Mine: stop upgrading observers by default, ask each client what they want to do with access first. Mine: the context skeleton gets a line called 'what would make this a waste of everyone's time'. Ooh. Nice. Ida's here.

name: University research group, methods seminar on transcripts and coding
summary: Synthetic sample. A university research group in Portugal (a principal investigator, a postdoc, a PhD candidate and a sceptical methodologist) records a methods seminar about using dembrane in a qualitative study of neighbourhood food cooperatives: forty-one interviews and nine focus groups. They separate platform consent (onboarding cards, the legal basis set on the project, a link to their own privacy notice) from their own written consent for quotation, and describe review with the university's data protection officer. They debate the anonymisation trade-off: it only covers recordings made after it is switched on, it removes personal but not organisational names, and it switches off audio playback, download and retranscription, so a disputed word can no longer be checked. They keep participant data and researcher field notes in separate projects, export the transcript zip and metadata into their own coding software, and report an experiment comparing the assistant with hand coding against their codebook: good on obvious codes, weak on quiet ones, overcounting jokes, and finding minority views only when asked directly. The PhD candidate admits a week of reading summaries instead of transcripts. They agree what they would cite (checked verbatim quotes and a plain method description) and what they would not (model theme lists, counts and summary sentences).

chunks.text: Right, we're recording, and I've told everyone this goes into our own methods project, not the study project, so nobody needs to watch their words about participants. Rui has agreed to be the sceptic today, which, Rui, is not a big stretch. The question for this seminar is simple. We used dembrane for the food cooperatives study, forty-one interviews and nine focus groups. What would we stand behind in a methods chapter, and what would we quietly not mention?

Can I start with consent, because the ethics committee started with consent and nearly ended there too. Go ahead, Ama. So, two layers. Inside dembrane, the onboarding cards take consent before anything records, and we set the legal basis on the project, with a link to our own privacy notice. That setting arrived at the end of August, so the second wave has it properly. But that consent is for recording and processing. It says nothing about quoting someone in a journal article.

So we kept our own written research consent as well. Paper, signed, separate options. You may quote me. You may quote me but change details. Use my words for analysis only. And we ran the whole setup past the university's data protection officer before the first interview, which took two meetings and was worth it, because she asked questions we hadn't thought of. Like who else in the department could open the project. Answer: nobody, it's a private project with four people in it.

And anonymisation. This is where I have the most to say. Go on, Rui. We switched on anonymise transcripts for the focus groups. Sensible, the ethics plan says so, and it only covers what you record after you switch it on. But what nobody told the committee, because we didn't know it, is that it also switches off audio playback and download for those conversations, and you can't retranscribe them. So for nine focus groups we have a transcript and no way to listen back.

Which, for a thesis, is a real cost. Is it, Ama? Yes. I had a passage where a woman says the cooperative 'returned' something to the neighbourhood, or maybe 'retained'. It matters for my argument. And I can't check. I can ask the moderator what she remembers. That's it. So for the third wave I want anonymise off, in a private project only the four of us can open, and we pseudonymise in our own coding afterwards, the way we always did with human transcription.

And I'm not sure the committee will accept that, Ama. They liked the idea that names never exist in the system at all. I think it's a genuine trade-off and we should write it up as one. Less data held, versus being able to check your own transcript. And there's another catch: it removes people's names, but not organisational ones. The cooperative names, the market, the parish. Personally anonymised, not organisationally. We still had to strip those ourselves after the export.

Okay. Collection. For the interviews I recorded myself in the browser, small table microphone, one interview per conversation, named with the participant code and the date. P17, the twelfth of April. Never the name. Focus groups on one phone in the middle of the table through the portal. The portal screens don't come in Portuguese, so the moderator read the consent aloud. The transcripts follow what people speak, and I checked the first one before trusting that. Then key terms: all twelve cooperative names and the produce words. Without those, 'cabaz' came out as six different words.

And the pilot interviews from last year, the ones on the old recorder, I uploaded as audio afterwards. My field notes went in as text, but into a separate project. I didn't want my own impressions mixed into the same pile as what participants said, because then when you ask a question you can't tell whose voice the answer is built on. Participant data in one project, researcher notes in another. That's the one practice I'd tell every new PhD student.

Agreed. Export. Tomasz, you did this part. Yes. We exported the transcript zip, which is one Markdown file per conversation, and the spreadsheet of conversation metadata, and imported both into our coding software. All the coding happened there, by us. dembrane is not our coding tool and we shouldn't pretend it is. Where it was useful is the step before and the step after.

And the step after is the experiment we said we'd report today. So, I coded twelve transcripts by hand with the codebook, blind, before asking anything. Then I gave the assistant in Ask our code definitions, pasted in, and asked it to point me to every passage in those twelve that fits each code, with quotes. Then I compared. Not to score it. Just to see what kind of reader it is.

And? For the obvious codes, quite good. 'Price as a reason to join', 'distance to the pickup point', it found nearly everything I found, plus two passages I'd missed in a long interview. Fine. Where it struggled was what I'd call quiet codes. We have one called 'quiet withdrawal', people who stopped collecting their box without ever saying they were unhappy. It lives in the gaps, in how people talk around it. It found one case. I had five.

And it overcounted 'distrust of the council', because it took jokes as claims. A man says, oh, the council, they'll fix it next century, everyone laughs. That's not a policy position, that's a Tuesday. And it merged two of our codes, 'solidarity' and 'mutual aid', into one, which is honestly a debate we've been having ourselves for a year, so maybe it has a point. Don't say that in the chapter, Tomasz. I won't.

Did asking differently change anything? Yes, and this is the useful part. When I asked which participants describe leaving or reducing their involvement without giving a reason, it found three of the five quiet withdrawals. When I asked who disagrees with the majority view in each group, it found two minority positions that never appeared in the summaries. So the minority views are in there, but you have to ask for them directly. The first answer is the middle.

So what's the honest description of what it did? I'd say it's a second reader who never gets tired and has no theory. It flags passages for us to reread. We then read them in the transcript, not in the answer, and decide. That's what I'd write. And I would never compute an agreement score between me and a language model. Rui would leave the room. I would leave the building, Tomasz.

Then let me say the uncomfortable thing. In May, for about a week, I stopped reading transcripts and read the conversation summaries instead. It was marking season, I was tired. I started writing a memo, and when Inês asked me where a claim came from, I couldn't point to a participant, only to a summary. It was a photocopy of a photocopy. I had never touched the original. That week of memos went in the bin.

Thank you for saying that, Ama. That's the real risk, and it isn't the tool's fault. Okay, the question I promised. What would we cite? Me first. I would cite verbatim quotes from transcripts we have checked, against the audio where we have it. And I'd describe the method plainly: automated transcription, corrected by the team where we could check it; a language model assistant used to retrieve candidate passages; all coding and interpretation by the researchers.

And what would you not cite, Rui? Any theme list the assistant produced, as if it were a finding. Any number it gives, 'most participants', 'a third of the groups'. If we want counts, we count in our own software. And never the phrase 'the AI found'. Nothing found anything. We found things, sometimes after a machine pointed at a page. I'd add: we never quote a summary sentence. Even when it's nicely written. Especially when it's nicely written.

One more limit for the chapter. There are no speaker labels in the transcripts. For the focus groups we wanted to know which statements came from older members and which from younger ones, and the transcript doesn't tell you. We solved it the old way: the moderator kept a seating sheet and a few notes with timestamps. If your design depends on who said what, plan for that from the start. Don't discover it in month six like we did.

Last thing. Tomasz wants to connect his own assistant through the new MCP connection, so it can search the transcripts directly. I'm not against it, but it goes past the data protection officer first, same as everything else, and it only gets what Tomasz himself can already see. Fair. And I'll write a page on exactly what it read. Good. So, three things into the methods chapter draft: the consent layers, the anonymisation trade-off and the second-reader description. Ama, will you write the first one?

name: Dialogue programme co-leads, late debrief after the circles
summary: Synthetic sample. Yara and Daniel, co-leads of a dialogue programme between two feuding villages in an invented valley, record a late debrief for a new colleague. Safety came first: before collecting they asked who could be hurt if a transcript ended up on the wrong phone. They turned anonymise transcripts on in advance, switched off name and email, used programme-owned phones, and wrote a context rule that no output may name villages, shops or families, because anonymisation removes personal names only. They explain why circles became franker once trusted community members hosted instead of staff, why corridor confidences never go into dembrane, and how private projects and a report-only policy for the funder limit who sees what. The central story: asking the chat what people said the programme was not asking about surfaced one remark about the shared irrigation rota, missing from every summary. They read the source, found more passages from both sides in a Specific Details chat, and rewrote the next session themselves overnight. Verify at the end let a participant have a line revised before approval. They also cover a recording lost to a locked screen, a mixed-up project language in spring, and leaving out any line they could not check once the audio was gone.

chunks.text: It's recording. It's going into our learning log, Daniel, the private one, anonymise is on, so say what you like. I know. I'm just tired. Okay. Eight circles this week, four on each side of the valley, and one mixed circle on Thursday that we nearly cancelled. I want us to put down what we did and why, because the new programme officer starts in September and she will ask why we do it this way.

Start with the why, then. Before anyone recorded anything in March, we sat with the women's council and the two youth leaders and asked one question: if this transcript ended up on the wrong phone, who gets hurt? We did that for every setting. Not 'is it legal', our privacy adviser handles that. Who gets hurt. And the answers decided everything else. Anonymise on before the first circle, because it only covers what's recorded after you switch it on. Name off, email off. No exceptions.

And programme phones, Yara. That was your idea and it was right. Nobody records on their own phone. We have six cheap phones that live in the office, charged, Do Not Disturb on, nothing else installed. A facilitator signs one out in the morning and back in at night. Nobody's personal phone has a circle's portal on it. People asked about that, actually. The older men especially. Whose phone is it? The programme's. Okay.

Then the anonymisation problem we didn't expect. It takes out people's names. It does not take out village names, the name of a shop, the crossing everyone calls by a family's name, and not reliably a nickname. And in a valley this size, the shop is the person. So we wrote it into the project context in plain words: never name villages, shops, families or groups in any output; describe people as a participant from the hill side or the river side; if a place is mentioned, say 'a village'.

And the facilitators open every circle by saying the same thing: please don't say anyone's name, or the name of a house. By the second session people did it on their own. You hear them pause. The man from, you know, the one with the blue gate. And everyone laughs, because everyone knows. But the transcript doesn't. That pause is something we taught, and the record taught it back, because when people saw the first summaries they checked what it said about them.

Which brings me to who hosts, because the new officer will ask that first. Yes. In the first month a staff member hosted each circle. Lovely people. One of them is from the hill side and everyone knows whose cousin she is. And the circles were polite. Very polite. Then in April we changed one thing. Two trusted women from the community hosted, one from each side, and we sat at the edge of the room. No questions, no notebooks. The conversations were completely different.

Different how, for the record? Longer. Sharper. People said things about the other side, and about their own side, that they never said when somebody's cousin from the office was asking. And they knew exactly who would read the transcript, we said it at the start of every circle. So it wasn't about hiding anything, Daniel. It was who asked. A neighbour asking you about the school is a different question from an official asking it.

But not everything goes to the phone. That's the other half. After circles, in the corridor, women tell you things. About a husband, about a debt, about who voted which way when the school closed. They tell it to a person, not to a recording. And we decided early that none of that goes into dembrane. Not typed in, not summarised, nothing. If it matters for the programme, the two of us talk about it, and it stays with us. The record is for what people chose to say into it.

Access. Write this down for her, because it's the part the funder keeps poking at. The workspace is invite-only. Each circle series is its own private project. You and I are the only admins. Each facilitator is a member of the projects for their own circles and nothing else. So the hill facilitator cannot open a river circle and the other way round, and that matters, because they are neighbours. They meet each other at the shop.

And the funder asked for transcripts. Twice. And we said no, twice. They get the report, which we write and review with the facilitators, as a PDF. No observer account, no link into the workspace. And we don't export transcript zips onto anyone's laptop either. The only thing that leaves the workspace is a document we have both read line by line. The one time support needed access, for a stuck upload, we granted it for the day and wrote in the log why.

Okay. Now the Thursday story. Because that's what she'll hear about from everyone in the valley. Tell it properly. So. The plan for session three was a mixed circle at the community hall about the festival. The old harvest festival in the square. Both sides want it back and they want different things from it, and the funder loves it, it's symbolic, it's the big one. We'd planned it since February.

And on Monday night I was in the office going through the river-side circles in the chat, and the summaries were all about the festival, as you'd expect, because that's what the hosts asked about. Then I asked something different. I asked: what did participants say we are not asking about? And it came back with one line from the third circle, from an older woman. I opened the source and read the whole passage around it, three or four minutes of talk.

What did she say, exactly? I copied it from the transcript, not from the answer. She said: you want us to sit together and talk about the festival, we have not yet sat together and talked about the water. And then she talks about the irrigation rota. The channel that runs through both sides. Who opens the gate on which day, who skips their turn, the shouting at five in the morning. It's not in the summary at all. The summary was about the festival.

And I didn't believe one sentence was enough, Daniel, so I didn't call you yet. I made a Specific Details chat with all eight circles from both sides and asked only about water, the channel, the gate, the rota. Five more passages. Three from the hill side. A young man on your side says, the festival is one day a year, the gate is every morning. Both sides. Nobody had put it on an agenda because it's too ordinary. Everyone lives with it every day.

And then you rang me at ten past ten. I did. And we read the passages together on the phone, slowly. By one in the morning we had a new plan. Session three: mixed circle, at the pump house, not the hall, about the water rota. Same two hosts, one from each side. The festival moves to session five. We wrote that ourselves, by the way. I didn't ask the chat what to do. It found the sentence. We decided.

The funder was not happy on Tuesday. No. 'Off plan.' But we showed them the quotes, unattributed, from both sides, and said, this is what people told us. And Thursday was the first mixed circle where people laughed. Real laughing. They argued about the Wednesday turn for forty minutes and agreed on a swap that two families had refused for years. Small. Very small. But it's the first thing the two sides of this valley have agreed on in a room since the programme began.

And at the end they did the verify step on the phone, only ever at the end. It writes a short outcome and the host reads it aloud. One man stopped her because it said 'the hill side agreed', and he said, I agreed, I don't speak for the hill side. She pressed revise after he'd said that, and the line was gone before anyone approved it. Tell her that: people have authority over what the record says about them. If someone says that's not what I said, the record changes, not the person.

Mistakes. The first circle in March, a facilitator used her own phone because the programme ones weren't ready. The screen locked after twenty minutes and we lost half of it. That's why the programme phones have the screen timeout switched off. And in spring, the circle that spoke the other language went into a project set to the hill-side language, and that transcript was a mess. The newer transcription follows what people speak, I'm told, but we keep each language group in its own project, so the summaries come back in the language its facilitator reads.

And one I still think about. Because the audio is gone when anonymise is on, we can't listen back. In April a transcript said a man's house was 'burned'. The facilitator was sure he said 'turned', as in sold, changed hands. Big difference in this valley. We couldn't check. So we left that line out of everything. When you can't check, you leave it out. That's a rule now. Okay. I think that's enough for her. Is the phone still green? Still green. Stop it.

name: Trainer and facilitator cohort, practice round and decoy exercise
summary: Synthetic sample. Rosa, a trainer, debriefs a cohort of community health facilitators from a Canadian health authority after a practice round in which trios recorded each other on one phone. The mistakes are the common ones: a locked screen spotted on the Monitor, a phone held under the chin, a recording left running through the coffee break, people typing their own names, a French portal link mistaken for a French project, and empty rows because everyone scanned. She explains that Explore needs about a minute of talk and that Verify asks whether the summary reflects what was said, not whether people agree. The core of the session is a decoy exercise: she planted one plausible recommendation among five that Ask produced, and four of six trios approved it. The trio that clicked the sources found it. She then reveals that a real recommendation was overstated ('most participants' meant two of twenty-four). The habits that follow: click sources, count before saying 'most', copy quotes from transcripts, ask who disagreed. A facilitator questions the point of checking, group size stays an open question, and Rosa closes with 'people know how', a rollout checklist and a caution not to design sessions around Popcorn yet.

chunks.text: Okay, everyone back? Phones face down on the table for a second. I've started a recording of this debrief too, into the training project, so it'll sit next to your practice conversations.
