Which, by the way, are now eight conversations of you lot talking about your worst ever meeting. Some of them are very good. So. You did the practice round in trios, one phone per trio, ten minutes each. Let's go round. What went wrong? I want the wrong things first.

Me, I'll start. Brendan. Ours stopped after about four minutes and we didn't notice. We kept talking for six more minutes into nothing. And Rosa, you came over and said look at the laptop. On the Monitor it said screen locked, next to our trio. My phone locks after a minute, I never changed it. So, a four-minute conversation about the worst meeting, which honestly was the boring half.

Good, thank you, Brendan, that's the most common one in real life too. That's why Ready Check Go on the host guide says keep the screen on, and why someone runs the Monitor on a laptop during the real sessions. If you see screen locked, or audio stopped, you walk over quietly, you don't shout across the room. Who's next? Hannah. Ours recorded fine, but the transcript is a bit thin on my parts. Yusuf says I held the phone under my chin like a walkie-talkie.

You did, Hannah. I have the photo. Okay, phone in the middle of the trio, flat on the table, microphone towards the people, not towards you. A good rule I got from someone: if a person on speakerphone could follow the conversation, so can the phone. If not, move closer or find a quieter corner. Marc, your trio's conversation is fifty-one minutes long. The exercise was ten. Yes. We went to get coffee and left it on. It's mostly the coffee machine.

That's a real problem in the field too, Marc, not just funny. Long runaway recordings dilute the summaries and use up recording hours. Stop at the end of the round, every time. Colette? Mine's the naming one. I typed my own name in the name field. And then Arjun's trio typed 'Trio 2' and the other one typed 'group two'. Exactly. For the rollout, the name field is not a person's name. It's the clinic and the group. We'll print it on the table card.

And Arjun. Ours came out in French. Well, the welcome screens did. Ah. I think you scanned the French code from the other table's pile? The portal has a link per language, and that only changes the welcome and consent screens. Your transcript is English, because it follows what people actually say. The project's language decides what language the summaries come back in. So for the two francophone clinics we'll set up their own projects, in French, with their own codes. Not one project trying to do both.

And Yusuf, I saw you frowning at the empty rows. Yes, there are three conversations in the list with nothing in them. That's because when you said scan the code, all three of us scanned, but only one of us recorded. Right. One phone per group means one phone. If everyone scans just to see, you get empty rows for whoever does the analysis later. In the real sessions, the group decides whose phone it is before anyone touches the QR.

Last thing on the practice round. Two of you pressed the ECHO button after twenty seconds and got annoyed it wouldn't do anything. Explore needs about a minute of conversation first, it has nothing to work with before that. And honestly, for your clinic sessions, I'd leave Explore off at the start. Get the basics boring first. Verify, though, I want you to try today. Five minutes at the end of a group: does this reflect what we said? Not, do we agree with it.

Okay. Now the exercise you've all been suspicious about since lunch. Before the break I asked Ask a question across all eight practice conversations: what recommendations for running better meetings came up, with quotes. It gave me five. I printed them on the handout you have. And I added one of my own. One of these six recommendations nobody said. You have ten minutes, with your trio, with your laptops, to find it. Go.

Rosa, are we allowed to use the sources? You're allowed to use anything. Click the sources, open the transcripts, search the conversation, ask the chat. Anything a careful person would do. Ten minutes. Okay, time. Show of hands, which one is the fake? Number two, the one about rotating the chair? Interesting. Number five, the clear agenda one? Number six? Okay. And number four, end every meeting with five minutes of silence for reflection? Hm. Four trios said four is genuine.

Hands down. Number four is the fake. I wrote it this morning. And four out of six trios approved it. Don't feel bad, that's about what happens in every cohort. It sounds right. It sounds like the kind of thing a wise person says at a training. It even sounds like this room. Which is exactly the problem. Colette, your trio found it. How? Honestly, I remembered. Nobody in our trio would ever sit in silence for five minutes. We'd fall asleep.

Ha. Memory counts, Colette, but you won't remember forty clinic conversations. Hannah, your trio found it another way. Yes, we clicked the sources for each one. Every other recommendation had quotes and a conversation underneath it. Number four had a quote, sort of, but when we opened the transcript, the person said they wished they had five minutes before a meeting to read the agenda. Not silence. It was close enough to look real.

That's the lesson, and it's a good one: close is the dangerous zone. Now the bit I didn't tell you. One of the five real ones is also wrong. Not invented. Overstated. Look at number one. Most participants said meetings should be shorter. Go and count. Brendan? Two people. Two out of twenty-four. So 'most participants' is the model rounding up. It does that. It likes a tidy story. The quote is real and the number is fiction.

So what do you do with that in your clinics? Three habits. One, click the source for anything you're going to repeat to someone else. Two, never repeat a word like 'most' or 'many' without counting. Ask how many conversations mention this, and to list them. Three, copy quotes from the transcript, never from the chat answer, because the answer can tidy the words. And a fourth for free: ask who disagreed. The first answer is always the middle of the room.

Rosa, can I push back a bit? Sure, Arjun. If we have to check everything, what's the point of asking it? Fair question. The point is it reads forty conversations in a minute and points. It points well, most of the time. You still look where it points. It's like a colleague who has read everything and has a slight tendency to exaggerate. Useful colleague. You don't put their sentences in the report to the board without reading the file.

And here's the bigger thing. People in those clinic waiting rooms know how. They know what's wrong with the bus to the clinic, they know why the young dads don't come. Your job is the question and the room. The phone listens, the model helps you find things again. Neither of them writes what the community wants. If you ever catch yourself asking it what the clinic should do, stop. Ask it what people said the clinic should do, and then go and read it.

Can we talk about group size, because in my clinic the waiting-room groups will be six or eight people, not three. Good, Arjun, and I won't pretend there's one answer. Trios are great for practice and for making sure quiet people speak. Some facilitators swear by four to six. Above that, add a second phone at the other end of the table and keep them as separate conversations. Try it in your first session and tell the group what you saw. I'd rather we learn it than I decree it.

Okay, rollout checklist, then you go home. Each clinic works in pairs, never alone the first time. Test the QR on your own phone the day before, all the way to the recording screen. Print the host guide and put it next to the QR. Name field is clinic and group. Delete your test recordings before the real ones come in. And after your first session, record a five-minute voice memo of what went wrong into the training project. We'll go through them together in three weeks.

What about Popcorn? I saw it in the menu. I'm not teaching it yet, Yusuf. It's early beta. Play with it in the training project if you're curious, it's fun on a screen at coffee time. But don't design a clinic session around it working perfectly. Basics first. Okay. Phones face up. Before you go, one Verify each on today's practice conversation, five minutes, and if the outcome isn't what you said, say so out loud and press revise, or edit it, before you approve. Practise saying no to it. That's the whole course, really.

name: IT lead's integration review with privacy and engagement
summary: Synthetic sample. Karin, the data and IT lead of a Swedish regional public transport authority, walks the privacy officer and the engagement lead through how dembrane is connected to their own tools, on the record. Of the four webhook events they listen only to conversation summarised and report generated, check the signature header on every call, and post only a pointer to their team chat, because the payload carries the full summary and transcript and a pilot pushed a summary naming a driver into a channel of forty people. A generated report opens a task for the route team. Summaries lag when volunteers forget to press finish. A named person exports the transcript zip and metadata monthly into the records archive, checking the conversation count first. Since September an MCP connection lets their internal assistant search across projects for one scoped account, with read access only and no write permission; the analyst always opens the source, and once corrected 'most depot conversations' to four of nineteen. They set the legal basis without saying it on tape. The heart of the review is what they chose not to automate: complaint cases from transcripts, auto-publishing reports, a sentiment traffic light per route, writing back into dembrane, and copying transcripts into the data warehouse.

chunks.text: Okay, recording. This is the integration review I promised, Johan, so you can ask me everything on the record and it lives in the IT project. Leila's here for the engagement side. Short version first. Since spring, Leila's team has run about sixty projects: depot visits, ferry terminals, the night-bus listening tour. And until June, getting anything out of dembrane into our own systems meant someone copying and pasting. Now three things are automated, and a longer list isn't, on purpose.

Start with the webhooks, Karin, because that's the part I don't understand. Sure. A webhook is just dembrane calling an address of ours when something happens. There are four events: a conversation started, a conversation transcribed, a conversation summarised, a report generated. We only listen to two. Summarised and report generated. Started is too noisy. Sixty volunteers scanning at a ferry terminal would mean sixty messages, half of them from people who never pressed record.

And how do you know the call really comes from dembrane? Every call comes with a signature header, made with a secret we set up. Our receiver checks the signature and throws away anything that doesn't match. No valid signature, no processing. I spent an afternoon sending it fake calls myself. It ignored all of them. Good. And what does the receiver do with a real one? This is the part I changed after the pilot, and Leila can tell you why.

Because of the bus driver. So in the pilot the receiver posted the whole summary into our team chat channel. Lovely, instant, everyone could see it. And in one pilot project anonymise was off, because it was an internal session with drivers, and the summary started: Mikael explains that the late shift on route 4 feels unsafe. Into a channel with forty people in it, including his manager. Mikael had said it in a room of six colleagues. Not to forty.

That was my mistake, Leila, not the tool's. It did exactly what I'd built. The summarised event carries the whole summary and the transcript, so now the receiver throws the content away and posts only a pointer. New summary in project 'Night buses, depot north', open it in dembrane. The content stays where the access rules are. Whoever can open the project can read it, and whoever can't, can't. And for anything internal with staff, anonymise is now on, decided before collection, because it only covers what's recorded afterwards.

Good. That's the right instinct. The webhook can carry the thing, but you only use it to say that something happened. Exactly. The second one, report generated, does a bit more. It opens a task in our planning tool for the route team that owns that area: a report is ready, read it before Friday's meeting. Still a pointer. A person opens it and reads it. Small detail Leila found: the summarised event only comes once the conversation is finished, and volunteers forget to press finish.

So the channel is quiet for hours and then fifty arrive at once when the conversations finally close. Now 'press finish' is in big letters on our host guide, and I say it twice in every briefing. It helped. Not completely. Okay, second thing. Export. We have a records obligation for public consultation input. Once a month, a named person on my team exports the transcript zip, that's one Markdown file per conversation, plus the spreadsheet of conversation metadata.

Both go into a restricted folder in our document archive under the consultation case number. We looked at pulling it automatically through the API, and we will eventually, but for now I want a human who knows what they're exporting and checks the conversation count against the project before it's filed. Last spring someone exported halfway through a session and filed half a consultation. A person checking the number would have caught it.

And the third thing is the one I'm nervous about, Karin. The MCP connection. Go. Since the September release, dembrane has MCP connections. In plain terms, our own internal assistant, the one the planning department already uses, can be connected to dembrane, and then it can find projects, search conversations, read transcripts, and look things up in dembrane's documentation. Reading is the default. There's a separate write permission for project settings, and we didn't grant it.

Whose eyes does it read with? Good question, Johan. It acts as the person who connected it, with their explicit consent, and it sees exactly what that person can see in dembrane. Nothing more. And the organisation has controls over whether connections are allowed at all. We turned it on for one account to start, Leila's analyst Sara, because her access is already limited to the transport projects. Nothing from HR, nothing from the internal staff sessions.

And why do the planners need it, Leila? Because of one thing Ask in dembrane doesn't do for us. In dembrane I ask questions inside one project. Which is right, most of the time. But the timetable planners come to me with questions like, what have people said about night buses anywhere, this whole year? That's eleven projects. Before, Sara opened eleven projects and asked eleven times. Now her assistant finds the eleven projects, searches each one and comes back with conversations and quotes.

And then? And then she opens the conversations in dembrane before anything goes into a memo. That's the rule. The assistant points at transcripts, Sara reads the transcripts. Last week it told her that night-bus safety came up in most depot conversations. She checked. Four out of nineteen. A real concern, strong quotes, but four. The memo says four. The planners would have heard 'most' and moved budget.

Okay. Legal basis, since I'm on the record. We set a default legal basis on the workspace and an override on the internal staff projects, and I reviewed both. I'm not going to say on a recording which is which, it's in the processing register where it belongs. Fine. And the privacy text participants see at the start links to our own policy. I checked the portal on my own phone, all the way to the record button. Twice. You did. I watched you.

Now the list I'm actually proud of, Johan. What we decided not to automate. One. Customer service wanted every complaint in a transcript to open a case in their complaints system automatically. A man says the 63 was late every morning in March, and straight away there's a case with his words in it. No. People came to a conversation, not to file a complaint, and the consent they gave was for a conversation. If someone wants to complain, the facilitator gives them the card for that.

Two. Communications wanted reports published on the public website automatically as soon as they're generated. No. Every report gets read against the sources by Leila's team first, and a person presses publish. The report is a language model draft until a human has checked it. Three. Someone wanted a sentiment score per bus route on the dashboard, red, amber, green. I said no to that one too, and Leila was relieved.

I was very relieved. Because there are no speakers in the transcripts, one angry man talking for twenty minutes about route 9 is one conversation, but in a sentiment score he's a red light over a whole route. And most of the people who use route 9 didn't come. A traffic light would look like knowledge and it isn't. So the dashboard shows numbers we can stand behind: how many conversations, where, when, which tags. Counts. Not moods.

Four. The assistant doesn't write anything back into dembrane. No tags, no summaries, no edits. If Sara thinks a tag is missing, she adds it herself in the project, by hand. And five, which surprised me: we don't copy transcripts into the data warehouse. Only the metadata. Transcripts stay in dembrane and in the monthly archive export, and that's it. Two places, both with access rules I can explain to you in one sentence.

That's a short sentence, which I like. My questions, then, Karin. What happens if the webhook secret leaks? We replace it, update the receiver, and anything signed with the old one is ignored. The steps are in the runbook, and I'll test it next month with you watching. And if a participant asks to have their contribution removed? Leila deletes it in dembrane, and my team removes it from the monthly export folder. That second step is manual, and it's on the checklist.

Good. Last one, and I want an honest answer. Is all this worth it for sixty projects? Honestly, Johan, the webhooks are worth it because the route teams now read reports the week they arrive instead of a month later. The MCP connection I'll tell you about in December. If Sara stops checking sources, I'll switch it off. And the list of things we didn't automate is the most valuable part. Write that in your notes. I will. Stop the recording.

name: Community archive volunteers, oral history across decades
summary: Synthetic sample. Rhona, Euan and Shabnam, volunteers at a community archive in an invented Scottish harbour town, talk at the kitchen table about recording oral history with dembrane. They uploaded digitised cassettes from 1979 and 1994, but only where release forms or families allowed reuse, one file per tape side, named by year, tape and subject, with decade tags. A long list of local nicknames in key terms, followed by retranscribing (and deleting the rough copies), made the hissy tapes usable; a three-hour file was too big to upload until they split it. New interviews were recorded with record yourself in the browser, and walking interviews with dembrane Go. Consent has two layers: dembrane's onboarding plus their own deposit agreement with separate ticks for exhibition, website, schools and researchers. Anonymise is deliberately off for named narrators, so the audio stays, and on in a separate project for those who chose anonymity. Asking the same question of different decades showed how memories of the works closing shifted, and asking who was missing revealed that the 1979 interviewer had recorded almost only men. They describe a misdated quote caught by checking the source, using the Narratives template and Specific Details chats, writing exhibition panels themselves, and returning transcripts to narrators.

chunks.text: Is it going? The wee bar is moving, Rhona, it's going. Right. Well. This is for the heritage group's Tuesday meeting, because Elspeth asked how we've been doing the interviews and I said I'd rather tell it than type it. So. Euan, Shabnam and me, at the kitchen table in the centre, with the good biscuits. We've done thirty-two new interviews since March, and we've put in the old tapes. Where do we start? Start with the tapes. Everyone always asks about the tapes.

The tapes, okay. So the archive has a hundred and forty cassettes from two earlier projects. The 1979 one, when the bottle works closed, a schoolteacher went round with a recorder. And the 1994 one for the harbour centenary. Euan digitised them over the winter, one file per side of tape, and uploaded the audio into dembrane. But not all of them. Only the ones where we were sure we were allowed. That took longer than the digitising.

Much longer, Shabnam. The 1994 tapes had release forms, a bit vague, but they said the recordings could be used for the history of the town. Fine. The 1979 ones, for about half there's nothing. A name on the box. So for those we found families where we could. Eleven families said yes. Two said no, and one of those was a lovely no, she said her dad would have hated a computer listening to him. Those stay on the shelf. Digitised, but not uploaded.

And how did you name them, Euan? This is important for anyone else doing it. Year, tape number, side, and one word for the main subject. 1979, tape 12, side A, harbour. No names in the title, even though the narrators are named in the archive catalogue. And then tags for the decade, '1979 tapes', '1994 tapes', '2026 interviews', so we can ask questions of one decade at a time. That turned out to be the most useful thing we did.

The first uploads were rough, mind. The 1979 tapes hiss, and the narrators are broad, broader than us. The Glassie, which is what everyone called the works, came out as 'the glassy', or once as 'Cassie'. Poor Cassie. So I put a long list into key terms. Every place and nickname we could think of. The Ropewalk, the Bothy, the Shore Road, the Sheds, the foremen's nicknames, the boats. Then I retranscribed them. That makes a fresh copy, so I deleted the rough ones after. Not perfect. Better.

And the three-hour tape that wouldn't go in. Oh, that one. A 1994 interview someone had dubbed onto one long file, both sides and a second visit. The upload refused it, too big. I split it back into the original sides and uploaded those, and they went through fine. So now, smaller files. One sitting, one file. And anything that's still rough after the key terms, I tag 'check against tape', so nobody quotes it without listening first.

The new interviews, then. Shabnam? Mostly me. Long one-to-ones, an hour, sometimes two, in people's kitchens. I use record yourself in the browser on the laptop with the little clip microphone, one interview per conversation. Euan does the walking ones on his phone with dembrane Go, which is a test version, not in the normal app shop yet. It keeps recording with the phone in his pocket, and it saves to the phone first and uploads when it can, so the bad signal at the harbour wall hasn't cost us anything yet. iPhone only, mind.

Walking Alec round the old works was the best interview I've ever done, Shabnam. He stood where the furnaces used to be and just talked for forty minutes. You wouldn't get that in a kitchen. No. Consent, then, because Elspeth will ask. Two layers. dembrane asks for consent before recording, on the screen. And then we have our own deposit agreement on paper, for reuse. Where can your words go? The exhibition. The website. School packs. Researchers. Each one a separate tick.

And how they want to be named: full name, first name only, or anonymous. And we decided something about anonymising that I want to explain, because it sounds backwards. For named narrators, anonymise is off. On purpose. In oral history the name is the point. Jean's words are Jean's, and she wants them to be. And we need the audio to listen back. The four narrators who asked to be anonymous are in a separate project with anonymise switched on from the start.

Which means no audio for those four, Rhona. Exactly. Their transcripts are what we have. We told them that, and they were content with it. No retranscribing either, so the key terms had to be right before the first one. Different project, different rules, and nobody has to remember which interview is which. Right. Now the fun part. Ask. Because that's what I was most suspicious of, and Euan will tell you I was rude about it in March. You were very rude. I was. I said a machine can't hear a town.

And can it? It can't hear, no, but it can find. The first thing we asked, with only the 1979 tapes selected, was how do people talk about the day the works closed? And it gave us a picture: shock, anger at the owners down south, men worried about the mortgage. With quotes. Then exactly the same question, with only the 2026 interviews. And the grandchildren talk about it completely differently. Not anger. Loss. That's when the town went quiet. Three different people used the word quiet.

That gave me goosebumps, Euan. Same event, forty-seven years apart. Then Shabnam asked the question that changed the exhibition. I asked: who is missing from the 1979 tapes? Because I had a feeling. And it came back, quite carefully, saying almost all the 1979 narrators were men from the factory floor, and that women's work is mentioned, the packing room, the canteen, the offices, but always by men, in passing. My wife was in the packing room. That's it.

And the 1994 tapes are full of women. Because the 1994 interviewer was a woman and she went to the bowling club. The 1979 teacher went to the pub. So the archive had told us, for forty years, that the Glassie was men's work, and it just wasn't true. It was who held the recorder. That's now the first panel in the exhibition: who asked, and who answered. And that's ours, mind. The machine found the gap when we asked. We knew what it meant.

I want to say the mistake too, Shabnam, because it matters. It does. Once, it gave me a lovely quote about the harbour flood and said it was from the 1979 tapes. I nearly put it on a panel. Euan checked the conversation name under the source and it was 1994. The narrator mentions 1979 in the sentence, so it got muddled. Now the rule is: you open the source, you read the conversation name, you listen to the audio. Every quote, every time.

And the new Narratives template was good for the school pack. It pulls out the stories people tell as stories, with a beginning and an end, instead of chopping everything into themes. The kids don't want themes. They want the one about the horse that walked into the canteen. And I use a Specific Details chat when I'm writing a panel, with just the six or seven interviews that panel is about, so the answer only comes from those.

But it doesn't write the panels, Rhona. No. I write the panels. With quotes copied from the transcript and checked against the tape. I tried once, asking it to write the panel text, just to see. It was smooth and it sounded like a council leaflet. Nobody in this town talks like a leaflet. Jean would never have spoken to me again. The words on the wall have to be theirs, and the joining-up words have to be ours.

Sharing back, then. Every narrator gets a copy of their own transcript, printed, big type, and the audio on a stick if they want it. Three of them corrected things on paper. Two of the corrections were the transcription, and one was Alec deciding his memory had been wrong about which year the boiler went. We wrote both versions in the catalogue. And in November we're doing a listening evening at the bowling club. Fitting. Very fitting.

What would you tell another archive starting this? Mine: sort out the consent for the old tapes before you digitise anything, because that's the slow part. Euan? Name and tag everything by year from the first upload, and put every local word in key terms before you start, not after. Shabnam? Ask it who's missing. Not just what's there. And then go and listen yourself. Right. Biscuits. Stop that thing. How do I stop it? The red square, Rhona.

name: Verbatim theatre company, rehearsal-room break after previews
summary: Synthetic sample. Hine, Kit, Tama and Pip, the director, dramaturg, actor and stage manager of a small New Zealand theatre company, talk during a rehearsal break about making a verbatim play from forty kitchen-table conversations recorded in an invented river town after a flood. Every line in the script carries a margin note with its conversation name and position. Consent for the stage was a paper release with three options, which the stage manager turned into tags (stage verbatim, adapt only, background only) so every question in Ask can be limited to permitted material. Anonymise was left off on purpose, in a private project, so actors can learn from the audio. They found stories with the Narratives template, but the angry households only appeared when they asked who disagreed; laughter is not in transcripts, so an actor listened for it. A test monologue written by the model was smooth and false, so the model never writes a line. A resident spotted a transcription error that had made his line more dramatic, and the audio proved him right. Audience talkbacks went into a separate project via QR cards on the seats, and Popcorn in the foyer worked as a mood, not a record.

chunks.text: Is that going? Pip, is the dot green? It's green. Okay. So we're recording this break because the funder wants a process reflection and I would rather talk than write one. Kit, Tama, Pip, me. Two previews done. The show opens Thursday. For whoever hears this: the play is made entirely of words people in Larch Bend said to us after the flood. Verbatim. Every line an actor speaks, someone in that town said, and we can show you where.

And 'show you where' is literally true, Hine. Every line in the script has a margin note: the conversation name and roughly how far in. Kitchen 14, Moa Street, about twenty-two minutes. If you can't write that note, the line doesn't go in. That was the rule from day one, and it's saved us three times. Tell them how we collected, Kit. Right. Forty kitchen-table conversations over five weeks, two or three neighbours at a time, one phone in the middle, through the portal.

Conversation names are the street and a number, never people's names. Kitchen 14, Moa Street. The project context said what we were making, that it's a play, that people's exact words might be spoken on stage, and it listed every street, the river, the stop banks, the marae, the names people use for the paddocks. Without that, 'stop bank' kept coming out as 'stop back'. Which Tama wants as the title of our next show. I do.

Consent is where we did something I'd tell any theatre company to copy. dembrane asks for consent to record at the start. But for a play you need more than that. So after each conversation, we sat with people and went through a paper release with three options. Your words can be spoken on stage exactly as you said them. Your words can be adapted, so we can combine or shorten. Or, your words are background only, for us to understand, never on stage.

And then, Pip, you turned that into tags. I did. Every conversation got one of three tags: stage verbatim, adapt only, background only. And it changes everything when you're searching. When Kit asks Ask for stories about the evacuation night, he narrows it to the stage verbatim tag first. So nothing comes back that we're not allowed to use. The background-only material still shapes how we understand the town. It just never comes out of an actor's mouth.

And anonymise is off. On purpose. Because the actors need the audio. Tama, tell them. Yeah. I don't learn lines from the transcript first. I listen. I've listened to Aroha's twenty minutes probably fifty times. Where she breathes. Where she stops and starts the sentence again. The transcript gives you the words, the audio gives you the person. If the audio had been switched off, I'd be doing an impression of a piece of paper.

Which is why we were so careful about that being explicit, Tama. Everyone knew there would be audio, that actors would hear it, that it's a private project only the five of us can open. And one woman, after the second preview, asked us to take her out. She'd changed her mind. Fair enough. We deleted her conversation in dembrane that night, and Pip went through the script using the margin notes and cut her four lines. That's the other thing the margin notes are for.

Okay, how we actually used Ask, because Kit has opinions. I do. Good for finding. Bad for writing. The Narratives template, once it arrived in September, was the best start for the second draft, because it brings back stories as stories, someone getting the dog into the ute at two in the morning, not themes. Then I'd ask very plain things. Who talks about the council's buyout offer? Who disagrees with the buyout? Show me the quotes. That second question matters. The first answer was all people who were grateful.

And the angry ones were there, Kit. They were there. Three households who think the buyout is the town being quietly closed down. They didn't show up until I asked for disagreement directly. If we'd stuck with the first answer, the play would have been a thank-you card to the regional council. Which is not what the town said. What it can't do: it doesn't hear laughter. The transcripts don't mark it. I asked it to find the moments people laughed while talking about the water, and it guessed.

It guessed wrong, too. It picked the jokes. But people in that town laugh at the worst bits, not at the jokes. You only know that from the audio. So that one's my job. I listened for laughs. Tama found nineteen. And that's half the second act now. And I have to confess the test. Go on. One evening, early, I asked it to write a monologue from the evacuation stories. Just to see what it would do. It wrote a beautiful, smooth speech that nobody in Larch Bend would ever say.

It had the word 'resilience' in it twice. Nobody in forty kitchens said resilience. They said, we just got on with it, didn't we. I deleted it and we made a rule out loud: the model never writes a line. It finds, we check, the town speaks. The play is the town's words or it's nothing. Pip has a name for the checking. The line audit. Every Friday I take ten lines from the script and check them against the transcript and the audio, start to end.

And the line audit nearly missed the buyout one, Pip. Tell it. So, at the first preview, Wiremu came. Sat in the third row. And after, in the foyer, he says to Hine, I never said bail-out. In the play, Tama says, as him, it's not a buyout, it's a bail-out for the council. And Wiremu says, I said buyout both times, I'm not that clever. And I thought, it's in the transcript, I checked it. But I'd checked the transcript. Not the audio.

So Monday morning I listened. And he's right. He says buyout twice. The transcription heard bail-out the second time, and frankly I liked it, because it's a better line. That's the danger, isn't it. The mistake was more dramatic than the truth, so nobody questioned it. We changed the line back. He came to the second preview and nodded at that bit. Lesson: for any line you put in a real person's mouth, listen to the audio. The transcript is a map, not the ground.

Now the foyer, because that was new this week. For the previews we put a QR code on a card on every seat. After the show, people could pair up in the foyer for five minutes and talk about what they'd seen. Different project, by the way, completely separate from the town conversations. You don't want audience chatter about the lighting mixed into the words of people whose houses flooded. Two kinds of material, two projects.

And at the second preview we tried Popcorn on the foyer screen, the live slides. It's early beta, and it showed. Lovely when it works. It puts up short phrases and quotes from what people have just said, and a woman saw 'I didn't know my own town' come up and put her hand over her mouth, because she'd said it two minutes before. But it also mangled two local words, and once put up something that was half one person's sentence and half another's. We're keeping it for opening week. As a mood, not a record.

What did the audience conversations actually tell us, though, Hine? That's the question for the funder. Two things. People from outside Larch Bend thought the angry households were exaggerating, until the scene with the river gauge. And people from the town wanted more of the time after the flood, the boring months. Insurance phone calls. Waiting. I asked Ask about the audience talks the next morning, only that evening's, and then read the twelve longest ones myself. The answer gave me the shape. Reading gave me the reasons.

So we're adding the phone-call scene. All verbatim. Three different kitchens, the same hold music, basically. Pip, what would you tell another company? Tags for consent from day one. Not a spreadsheet next to the project, tags on the conversations, so the permission travels with the words. And name conversations by place, never by person. Kit? Ask for the disagreement. Every time. Tama? Listen to the audio. Don't trust a line you've only read.

And mine. The town sees it before anyone else does. We're doing a free performance at the hall for Larch Bend only, the night before opening, and every person whose words are in it gets a seat with their name on. If someone says that's not how I said it, we check the audio there and then, and if they're right, the line changes before Thursday. Okay. Break's over. Pip, stop it. Stopped? Stopped.

name: Town centre day, the blunt retrospective
summary: Synthetic sample. Five organisers of a residents' day in a small English market town (about 160 people, 22 tables) hold a blunt retrospective. Five recordings stopped because hosts' phones auto-locked; the Monitor showed Screen locked but sat minimised. The comms officer edited the portal's welcome and finish text the night before, the QR code on the dashboard looked different from the 30 printed cards, and the team reprinted at dawn before learning that text edits never change the link. A merged table put nine people on one phone: two voices and a murmur. Two Polish-speaking tables sat in an English-language project: the Polish transcripts held up, but consent screens were English only and two summaries were confidently wrong (sarcasm read as a request); the community liaison pasted in her own notes as text, clearly labelled. Changes for next time: a dedicated Monitor laptop and watcher, Ready Check Go read aloud with auto-lock set to never, the portal frozen 48 hours ahead with one owner and every reprint tested on two phones, a team walk of the live preview, six per phone at most with spares, a separate project for the Polish tables on coloured cards with a Polish consent sheet and a Polish speaker checking summaries, and portal tags per table. The failures go in the report's method section.

chunks.text: Right, it's recording. This is the Thornwick town centre day retro, it's Thursday, and I said in the invite we'd be blunt, so let's be blunt. It's me, Marta, plus Neil, Sian, Gareth, and Ola has joined for the language part. I want four things on the table: the screens, the QR codes, table six, and the two Polish tables. Then what we change. Nobody's on trial here. Most of these were my calls anyway.

Can I start with the screens, because that's the one keeping me up. Sian here, for the recording. We had twenty-two tables. When I went through the conversations on Monday, five of them just stop. One at eleven minutes, one at, what was it, four minutes, the rest somewhere in the middle. And the table hosts swear they never pressed stop. They didn't. The phones went to sleep and took the recording with them.

So that's the screen lock thing. We knew about it, though, Gareth, didn't we? It's on the host guide. Yeah, it says keep the screen on. The problem is we printed the host guide and then put it face down under the QR stand because the table looked messy. And the phones that locked were the hosts' own phones, with auto-lock on thirty seconds, because whose isn't. Nobody changed the setting at the start.

And the Monitor would have told us. That's the part I find hard, honestly. The Monitor shows Screen locked on the row for that table, in so many words. It was open. On my laptop. Which was plugged into the projector showing the welcome slides, so it sat minimised the whole morning. I looked at it once, at lunch, and by then two of the tables had been dead for forty minutes.

To be fair, Marta, you were also running the room. You can't watch a dashboard and do the welcome. No, and that's the lesson, Neil. Next time the Monitor gets its own laptop and its own person, and that person does nothing else. Gareth, I'm looking at you. Your whole job is to watch for Screen locked and Audio stopped and walk over to the table. Not fix the tea urn. Watch the rows.

Fine by me, I'd rather do that than the urn. But I want a rule for the hosts too. At the start, before anyone presses record, the host reads the Ready Check Go out loud. Phone charged, good wifi, allow the microphone, screen on, do not disturb. Say it like a flight attendant. Everyone hears it, everyone looks at their own phone, it takes forty seconds and it would have saved five tables.

And auto-lock off, specifically. People hear keep the screen on and think it means don't switch it off. They don't realise the phone does it by itself. We put settings, display, auto-lock, never, on the card in big letters. And then put it back afterwards, obviously, or we'll get angry emails about flat batteries. Okay. Thanks, Sian. Neil. The QR codes. Go on.

Yeah. So, my fault, and I'll own it. The night before, I went into the portal editor and tidied the welcome text and the finish text, because Marta's draft said thank you for your participation and I wanted it warmer, and to say when people would hear back. Which I still think was right. But after I saved, the QR code on the dashboard looked different from the one on the thirty laminated cards we'd printed that afternoon.

And I didn't know whether that mattered. It was half nine at night. So I panicked and reprinted all thirty at the library at seven in the morning, and laminated them in Gareth's kitchen, and we were forty minutes late setting up. And then it turned out the old cards were fine. Editing the text doesn't change the link at all. The code just looks different depending on where you download it. A couple of hosts used the old ones, no problem.

Which we didn't know at the time, and that's the point. The lesson isn't Neil, don't edit things. It's that the portal freezes forty-eight hours before the event. Any change after that, we print one card and scan it with two different phones before anyone touches the stack. And one person owns the portal settings. Not three of us dipping in and out of it the week before, which is what happened.

Can I add something? We should have walked the live preview earlier. I only rewrote the finish text because I read it properly for the first time that night. If we'd all gone through it on our phones a week before, I'd have said it then. Agreed. A week before, everyone on the team scans the real printed card, records thirty seconds, finishes, and reads every screen. Then we delete those tests so they don't end up in the analysis.

Table six. Sian, you were there. I was. So, the host for table seven didn't turn up, and rather than leave four people sitting on their own, I merged them into six. Nine people around one phone. It felt like the kind thing to do in the moment. Listening back, it's two voices. The man from the traders' association and a woman who clearly knew him well. Everyone else is a murmur.

The summary for table six is basically the traders' position on parking. Which is a real view, it should be in there, but it's not what nine people said. I know there was a young mum at that table who had a lot to say about buggies and the cobbles on the market square, because she told me at the coffee break. She isn't in the transcript. Not one sentence I can find.

Could we have just put a second phone down? We could, Gareth, and that's the quick fix, but I'd go further. Nine people isn't a table, it's a meeting. I should have split them into a four and a five, with two phones, and sat in with one of them. Six is the most I'd put on one phone now. And we bring three spare phones, charged, already on the portal page, in a box with my name on it.

And in the report, I've written a line saying table six was nine people on one phone and the recording is mostly two speakers. I'd rather say that than have the council read the parking view as if it were the whole room. Okay. Ola, the language thing. This is the one I genuinely didn't see coming, so tell us what happened from your side.

So we had two tables from the Polish community centre, about eleven people. They chose to talk in Polish, which was the point, we invited them to. And the transcription held up, honestly. The transcripts came out in Polish and they're mostly right, apart from the centre's name and the street names, because we had no Polish words in the key terms. The problem started before anyone spoke. Polish isn't one of the languages the portal screens come in, so the welcome and consent were in English.

So I crouched at each table and translated the consent out loud, which nobody had planned, and I'm not sure everyone took it in. Then the summaries. They come in the project's language, so English, and mostly they're fine, but twice they're confident and wrong. A man says, oh wonderful, another car park, the whole table laughs, and the summary says the table wants more parking. That scares me more than the gaps, Ola. A gap you can see. A confident wrong summary you can't, unless someone who speaks the language reads it.

I read both transcripts on Monday evening and wrote up the main points in English, two pages per table. We pasted those into the project through the portal's text option, one text conversation per table, labelled as Ola's notes. But they're my notes. They're my summary of their words, not their words, and I said that to the centre when I told them what happened. They were kind about it. They said, next time, ask us what language before, not on the day.

Next time the Polish tables get their own project and QR code, on a different colour card so nobody grabs the wrong one. Polish names in the key terms. A consent sheet in Polish that the centre helps us write, read out before anyone scans. A Polish speaker checks every summary against the transcript before it goes near the report. And we ask at registration, which language will your table speak? Not do you need a translator, that's a different question. And test it: two minutes in Polish, on the Polish card, the week before.

Right. Let me read back what I've got. Monitor on its own laptop, Gareth watches it and nothing else. Ready Check Go out loud, auto-lock to never on the card. Portal frozen forty-eight hours before, one owner, any reprint tested on two phones. Whole team walks the live preview a week before, then delete the tests. Six per phone at most, spare phones in a box. Polish tables in their own project on coloured cards, a Polish consent sheet, a Polish speaker checks the summaries, language question at registration, test the week before.

One more. Portal tags per table. We had the table number in the conversation name, but some hosts typed Table 3, some typed 3, and one typed her own first name. If the table is a tag you pick from a list when you scan, Monday is so much easier. I spent an hour just working out which recording was which. Added. Anything that went well? We should say that too, or the council will think we're a disaster.

The fifteen tables that worked were really good. I read three transcripts in full and they're rich, proper conversations, people disagreeing nicely. The library staff said people stayed later than at any consultation they've hosted. And the Polish centre wants to do it again, which surprised me. Okay. I'm putting the parts that went wrong in the report's method section, plainly, not hidden at the back. Thanks, everyone. I'm stopping this now.

name: Two analysts rebuild a flood plain report
summary: Synthetic sample. Two analysts at a regional water board in Germany record themselves rebuilding a report on flood plain dialogues (two village evenings and a farmers' breakfast, nineteen tables). The first draft, generated the same night, drew almost entirely on one evening: the project held 71 rows, including 23 empty ones from an 'everyone scan now' moment, five test recordings, tables still transcribing and an audio upload still processing. A farmers' union member replied 'Where are the farmers?' They tidy first (delete tests and empties while checking the bulk selection count, regenerate missing summaries, tag by event and group, rename, count against the nineteen tables they expect). Then they ask the assistant explicitly for disagreements with reasons and quotes, points raised at only one or two tables, and groups talked about but absent, and scope by tag to the farmers' tables. Clicking every source reveals a facilitator's provocation counted as a resident view and a quote the chat answer had made more dramatic than the transcript. They write report instructions that keep dissent and one-off views visible, read the draft against sources, rewrite a paragraph by hand, and share the farmers' section back. Their list for next time is in their own words.

chunks.text: Okay, recording. Tomasz, I want this as a log, because in six months we'll do the next round and we will have forgotten all of it. It's the eighth of September, we're in the small meeting room, and we're going to rebuild the Wiesengrund report. Do you want to say what happened, or shall I? I'll say it, Jana. It's my report. Well. It was my report.

So we had the two village evenings and the farmers' breakfast. On Tuesday night, after the second evening, I generated the report straight away, because the steering group meets Thursday and I wanted to give them something. I read it, it looked good, it had themes, it had quotes. I sent it to you and to the steering group as a draft. And on Wednesday morning Jannik from the farmers' union replied to all: where are the farmers?

And he was right. When I opened it I clicked through to the sources, and almost every quote came from the first evening in Nebelried. The second evening in Haselwinkel, nothing. The breakfast, one quote. So we counted. The project had seventy-one conversations in the list. Seventy-one. We had nineteen tables in total across three events. That number alone should have told us something was off.

So what were the seventy-one? Twenty-three of them were from the start of the Nebelried evening, when the chair said everybody please scan the QR code now so we can see it works. And everybody did. Then most of them never pressed record, or pressed it for four seconds. So twenty-three rows of nothing, most of them called Resident, because that was the default name and nobody changed it.

Then five test recordings from the week before, which I made, called things like test, test two, and Tomasz kitchen. Then the Haselwinkel tables, which at ten o'clock on Tuesday were still transcribing, because they'd only finished at half past nine. And the breakfast, which was recorded on your phone and uploaded as audio, and the upload hadn't finished processing. So the report saw the first evening, and a lot of noise.

And it didn't tell you that. Well, it can't know what it's missing. The report is a language model draft of whatever is there when you press the button. It's not going to say, by the way, half the room isn't in here. So the first rule we write down: before you generate anything, tidy the conversations, and count. Count what you expect against what is actually there.

So, what I did yesterday, in order. One, I deleted my five tests. Two, I went through the empty ones. The conversation shows Empty, or there's one line of someone saying is it on. I deleted those too, but I checked the selection count every single time before the bulk delete, because there's no undo, and I was very nervous about deleting a real table by accident.

Three, I checked every real conversation had a summary. Two of the Haselwinkel ones had a full transcript but no summary, so I regenerated those. Four, tags. Every real conversation now has a tag for the event, Nebelried, Haselwinkel or breakfast, and a tag for who was there, residents, farmers or mixed. Five, I renamed them, so it's Haselwinkel table four, not Resident. Now we have nineteen. Nineteen tables, nineteen conversations.

Then we did the second thing, which is harder. Because even when you regenerated the report with all nineteen, I read it and thought, this is too nice. It says broad support for the retention basin, with concerns about compensation. Which is a sentence. It's not wrong exactly. But I was at the breakfast. Three farmers' tables were against it, strongly, not concerns. And one of them proposed a completely different site.

And a woman in Haselwinkel, she uses a wheelchair, talked for maybe five minutes about evacuation routes. If the basin road floods, she cannot get out of the village. That's not in the report at all. It's one person, so I understand why it disappears. If you summarise nineteen tables, the one person is the first thing you lose. But that's exactly what the engineers need to hear.

So minority views don't come up by themselves. You have to ask for them by name. Tomasz, read what you typed into Ask. Okay. First: where did people disagree with the retention basin proposal? For each disagreement, say which conversation, what the reason was, and give a quote. That gave us a list of seven disagreements. Much more useful than concerns about compensation.

Then: which points were raised in only one or two conversations and would be easy to miss in a summary? That found the evacuation route, and something about the old drainage ditches that only one farmer seemed to know about. And then: which groups of people were talked about but were not at the tables? It said tenants in the riverside flats, and the campsite owners. Nobody from either was there.

That last one I want in the report as its own section. Who we did not hear from. Otherwise the steering group reads it as complete. Yes. And because we had tags, I could scope it. Now just the farmers' tables, what do they want instead? And it came back with the alternative site, the ditches, and compensation as a share of yield, not one lump sum. Things that were completely flattened before.

Now, here's the part I really want on the record, because I think this is where people get caught out. Every answer in Ask has sources. You click them, you see the conversation it came from. I made you click every single one for the disagreement list. Tell the log what you found. Two problems. One of the disagreements was actually the facilitator, not a participant. She was reading the counter-argument from the information sheet, to provoke the table.

And the language model took it as a resident's view. Second one: the answer quoted a farmer as saying we will lose everything. Strong quote. I almost put it in the headline. But in the transcript he says, we could lose the lower fields, not everything, I'm not being dramatic. Completely different sentence. The chat answer had smoothed it into the dramatic version. Which is why we copy quotes from the transcript, never from the answer. The answer is a pointer. The transcript is the quote.

So for the report itself we did it differently this time. I didn't just press generate. I gave it instructions. Can you read them out? Write for the steering group, in plain German. Keep disagreements visible, each in its own paragraph, do not merge them into general concerns. Do not combine options that exclude each other. Include a section on views raised by only one or two tables. Include a section on who was not present.

And even then, we read it against the sources. You took the first half, I took the second. It took us about two hours, which is fine for nineteen tables. One paragraph still said farmers broadly accept the basin if compensated, and we rewrote it by hand, because two of the three tables did not accept it on any terms. What we send is ours. The draft is the language model's. The signature is ours.

I also wrote back to Jannik. I said, you were right, half the conversations weren't in the draft, here is why, here is the new version, and here is the farmers' section, please tell us if it's what you heard. He replied in about twenty minutes, which for Jannik is some kind of record, and said the ditch point was the most important thing in the whole report. Which we would have lost.

Okay, for the log, what changes next time. One: no everyone scan now. The table host scans, at the table, when they're ready to record. Two: no report on the same night. We wait until everything has finished processing, and we count. Three: portal tags set up before the event, so people pick their village when they scan, not me afterwards. Four: test recordings go in a separate test project, never in the real one.

Five, in Ask, always ask for disagreements, for one-off points and for who's missing. Explicitly, every time. I've saved those three as a template, so it's one click. Six, click every source before something goes into a report. Seven, copy quotes from the transcript. And eight, Tomasz: when someone like Jannik says where are we, that's not a complaint. That's the check working. Okay. Stop it there. I'm hungry.

name: Reading the draft back to the room
summary: Synthetic sample. At a lunchtime session in a small facilitation collective in Portugal, Leonor explains her 'read it back to the room' loop to three colleagues, using a school-street consultation (about sixty parents, residents, shopkeepers and teachers at eight tables) as the example (the portal screens are not available in Portuguese, so table hosts read consent aloud). She prepares a chat template the day before, drafts short bullets in participants' words during the break, checks the strongest sources, reads the draft aloud as a draft, and records the room's critique on a front-table phone as its own conversation. The first draft said parents broadly supported closing the street; a father and a mother whose son uses a wheelchair corrected it to 'only if the disabled drop-off stays', other tables joined in, someone joked that the machine had been in a different room, and a teenager pointed out that nobody had said 'mobility hub', a phrase the model took from a council sheet pasted into the context. Version two, built from the round-one tables plus the read-back recording, carried the conditions. Colleagues push back on over-trust, timing and consent. Leonor describes an announced 'find the line nobody said' exercise, keeping official wording out of participants' mouths, and skipping the read-back when the draft is not ready.

chunks.text: Okay, so it's recording. Rafael, you asked me last week to explain the read-back thing properly, so here's the lunchtime version. Beatriz and Joaquim are here too, so interrupt me. It's not complicated. It's mostly about timing. You do round one, you draft a summary in the break, you read it out loud, the room tells you what's wrong with it, and that telling becomes part of the record.

Read it out loud. Not project it? I've done both, Rafael. Out loud is better, for me. When it's on the wall people read silently, at different speeds, and they nod politely. When you read it, the room hears it at the same pace, and when you reach the sentence that's wrong, you can feel it. Someone makes a noise. Literally a little hm. That noise is what you're waiting for.

Let me give you the real example, the school-street session in Vila Serrada in June. Around sixty people: parents, residents of the street, two shopkeepers, the bakery owner, a few teachers. The question was whether to close the street outside the primary school to cars at drop-off and pick-up times. A trial, proposed by the parish council. Eight tables, one phone per table, five or six people at each. The portal screens don't come in Portuguese, so each table host read the consent out loud first.

And the project setup? Because I think that's where mine go wrong. The context was about six sentences, Beatriz. What the question is, that it's a trial, the times, the names of the streets. And one sentence that I think matters a lot: recordings named read-back are the room's critique of a draft summary, treat them as corrections. So the language model knows those aren't just another table with opinions.

Key terms: the street names, the school, the bakery, and kiss and go, because that's what the parents call the drop-off zone, and it came out as something very strange when I tested it. Okay. So, round one, forty minutes. Then a twenty-minute coffee break. In the break, I sit with my laptop and a coffee I never drink, and I open a new chat in dembrane, and I select the eight round-one conversations.

What do you type? That's what I actually want to know. I prepared it as a template the day before, Joaquim, so I'm not composing while people eat pastries. It says something like: summarise what was said across these conversations as short bullets, in the words participants used. Keep the language simple. Show where tables disagreed. Do not add recommendations. Then I ask for quotes for each bullet, and I check three or four of the sources.

Only three or four? In twenty minutes, yes. I check the ones that sound strongest, because those are the ones that cause trouble if they're wrong. Then I edit it a little. Not to make it nicer. Mostly to cut. It always gives you more than you need, and you can't read two pages to a room, people's eyes glaze over. Eight to ten bullets. Two minutes to read, maximum.

Then after the break, before round two, I stand up and say: this is a draft. A language model put it together from your recordings in the last fifteen minutes. It is not what you decided, you haven't decided anything yet. I'm going to read it, and I want you to tell me what's wrong with it. What's missing, what's exaggerated, what you never said. The phone at the front is recording, so whatever you say goes into the next version.

So there's a separate recording for that part? Yes. A phone on the front table, scanned into the same project, named Read-back 1. So it's its own conversation. Okay, here's where it went wrong, which is the best part. Bullet three said, and I remember it because I read it with such confidence: parents broadly support closing the street to cars at school times.

And a father at the back, he'd been at table five, he said, quite loud: no, we said we support it if the drop-off for disabled children stays. There was a mother next to him whose son uses a wheelchair, and she said, that was the whole conversation at our table, the whole thing. Then from another table someone said, ours too. And the room, I don't know how to describe it, it sort of woke up.

Embarrassing? For about four seconds, Joaquim. Then someone said, the machine was in a different room, and everybody laughed, and after that people were almost competing to correct it. The bakery owner said bullet six made it sound like he was against the scheme, and he wasn't, he was against the loading bay moving. And a teenager who'd come with her dad said: we never said mobility hub. Nobody here says hub.

Mobility hub. Where did that come from? From the parish council's information sheet, I think, which I'd pasted part of into the context. That's my mistake. The language model picked up the sheet's vocabulary and put it in residents' mouths. Since then I keep official documents out of the context, or I write clearly, this is the council's wording, not participants' wording. The girl was right, and she was very pleased with herself.

So, round two. Same tables, a new question, and I say at the start, keep in mind what you just corrected. Then at the end, before the closing, I go back to the chat, I add Read-back 1 to the selection with the round-one conversations, and I ask: revise the summary using the corrections in Read-back 1, and show what changed and why. And then I read version two.

And was it better? Much better, Beatriz. The disabled drop-off was the second bullet, as a condition, not a footnote. The bakery owner's loading bay was there as its own point. Mobility hub was gone. And there was one line that said some participants felt the first summary did not reflect their table, which I liked, because it's true and now it's in the record. People clapped a little, actually. That has never happened to me for a summary.

But isn't that the risk? Version two is still the model. They clap, and now they trust it more than they should. Yes, Joaquim. That is exactly the risk, and I think about it a lot. Version two is better because they corrected version one. If I'd only ever shown them a perfect version, they would trust the machine. Showing them a wrong one, and letting them fix it, teaches them it can be wrong. That's half the point.

And I did something in the next session, in September, that you might hate. In the second read-back I told them: there is one line in here that nobody said. I wrote it myself. Find it. They found it in about thirty seconds, and then they found two more that the model had got slightly wrong, which I hadn't noticed. It makes people listen like editors instead of like an audience.

That's sneaky. It's announced, Rafael. I tell them before I start reading. I'd never slip something in without saying so. And the fake line goes straight away, I delete it, it never goes near the report. Okay, what else. The report afterwards includes both read-back recordings, and the method section says draft summaries were read aloud twice and corrected by participants. So the council can see the corrections, not only the final words.

And timing, honestly. Twenty minutes in a break is very tight. What if it's not ready? Then I don't read it, Beatriz. I've done that once. I said, the draft isn't good enough to read yet, I'll read it at the end, and nobody minded. Better that than reading something I haven't checked. If you have a co-facilitator, give them the laptop and you take the room. Don't do both. You'll be bad at both.

And people who don't like being recorded while they correct it? Same consent as the tables, Joaquim, it's the same portal, they've already been through the cards. But I say again before the read-back: the phone at the front is recording this part. Usually nobody minds. Once a woman waited and told me her point privately afterwards. That's fine. I wrote it in my notes and told her it would go in as my note, not her words.

So, the short version for Rafael. Template ready the day before. A chat on the round-one conversations in the break. Bullets in their words, simple language, disagreements, no recommendations. Check the strongest sources. Read it, don't project it. Call it a draft, out loud. Record the critique as its own conversation. Feed it back in for version two. Keep the official wording out of their mouths. And don't be afraid of it being wrong in front of people.

The wrong part is the part I'm afraid of. I know, Rafael. But the room was never more alive than when it was wrong. They weren't correcting the machine for me. They were making sure their table counted. And the second version belongs to them a bit more because of it. Okay, I need to eat something before the afternoon. I'm going to stop it.

name: Live or overnight, trios or fives: a friendly disagreement
summary: Synthetic sample. A recorded session at a practitioners' network day in Belgium. A moderator puts two hosts on stage: Wouter, who runs assemblies and neighbourhood labs and synthesises live, and Helen, who runs tenant and health consultations and synthesises overnight. Wouter argues for the moment people see their words come back the same day; Helen for calm checking, morning recaps on multi-day processes (tables sort a page of unsorted quotes themselves before she offers back what no table kept; she admits handing out six themes once made the room go quiet), and care with rooms that have been misheard before. Both concede points: typing live while sixty people wait is a mistake, prompts should be saved as templates and someone else should run the laptop, and a one-line steer between rounds is acceptable to both. They split on Popcorn (ambience in a coffee area versus half-formed ideas misrepresenting a group). On group size Wouter defends trios (no one shut out, no facilitator needed, rotations meet six people) and Helen fives (fewer phones, fewer failures, less tidying, older residents wanting to hear the room). Helen admits quiet people vanish in fives and now opens with a go-round; Wouter admits twenty-five rows on the Monitor need a dedicated watcher. Both refuse nine on a phone, and both say online sessions are awkward.

chunks.text: Good, it's recording, the light is on. Welcome back from lunch, everyone. This is the session the programme calls friendly disagreement. I've got Wouter, who runs assemblies and neighbourhood labs and does almost everything live, and Helen, who's run tenant and health consultations for, how long, Helen? Too long. Eleven years. And who records now and synthesises overnight. Two questions: live or overnight, and trios or groups of five. Wouter, you start.

Okay. My case for live is simple. When people say something and an hour later see it come back shaped, they feel received. Not just recorded, received. At our last assembly day I ran Ask over the morning tables at lunch, picked four points with quotes, and read them out before the afternoon. Three people came up to me and said, that's what I said. You can't get that the next morning. By then they've gone home.

But they don't go home in a multi-day process, Wouter. In a three-day assembly they come back. Day one, I record everything, nothing live. That night I sit with it properly. I ask the assistant for the strongest quotes from each table, I click every source, and I copy about forty onto one page, in no order. Day two, the tables sort that page themselves. Then I say, here's what I held on to that none of you kept, do you want it back? Nobody is typing at the front while sixty people wait.

You didn't always do it that way, Helen. Two years ago you put up six themes on a slide first thing. I was in the room. I did. And the room went quiet. They looked at my six headings, nodded, and that was the morning gone. When they sort the quotes themselves they argue about why two things belong together, and that argument is the useful bit. My six themes were just me, tidied up.

Point to Helen on the typing. I've done that. The worst moment of my year was standing at the front with a laptop while the answer was still coming in, and the room just watching me. Now I never ask anything live that I haven't prepared. The prompts are saved as templates the day before, and a colleague runs the laptop. I just read. That's the only way I'd do it now.

And when it's wrong? Live, it's wrong in front of everyone. Sometimes. And then they correct it, and that's good, it's in the record. It's good if the room can take it. I did a health consultation with patients who'd waited two years for an operation. You do not stand in front of them and read a half-right summary of their pain. They'd been misheard enough. I wanted to be sure before I said anything back to them.

So is it about the room, rather than live versus overnight? Partly. Trust in the room, and time to check. A summary at lunch has been checked by nobody. At two in the morning it's been checked by me, which isn't perfect, I'm tired, but it's someone. I'd say you can check three sources in ten minutes and say the word draft out loud. That's enough for here's what I'm hearing. It's not enough for a report.

And there's a middle thing I do now that maybe Helen would accept. Between rounds, I don't read a summary at all, I just say one line. In round two, keep in mind that three tables raised the bus route and nobody's talked about evenings yet. One sentence. It's light, it can't do much harm, and it steers a bit. I'd accept that. That's a facilitator's sentence, informed by the recording. That's not the model talking to the room.

Someone in the audience asked me at the break about Popcorn. Wouter, you've used it? Once, last month, on the screen in the coffee area. It's early beta, so I didn't build anything around it. People's own phrases on the screen, and they'd stand there and say, hey, that's ours. It kept the thing alive through the day. That's all I'd claim. I'll be honest, I'm not keen. Half-finished ideas on a wall can make a group look like it thinks something it doesn't.

For anything sensitive, I'd want it off. Fair. I wouldn't put it up at your waiting list consultation either. Okay, let's move on, because I know this one gets heated. Group size. Wouter, trios. Trios. Three people, one phone. At four, two conversations can start at once. At three they can't. And I've never seen a trio shut someone out. If one person dominates, the other two have the numbers. I tell them that at the start, literally. If someone talks too much, there are two of you.

And you don't need a facilitator at each table. That's huge. I can run sixty people in twenty trios with three facilitators walking around. And I rotate them. Three rounds of trios and each person has met six others. That's the same as a group of seven, except everyone actually talked. Everyone talked to two people at a time, Wouter. Which is when people actually talk, Helen.

My turn. Twenty trios is twenty phones. Twenty people who have to scan, allow the microphone, keep the screen on and press finish. At my one tenants' day with trios, I had four phones lock, two people who scanned and never pressed record, and one phone face down in a handbag. Twenty-one conversations, seven unusable. With fives I have twelve phones, twelve table hosts I've briefed, and twelve rows on the Monitor I can actually watch.

Point to Helen. The Monitor with twenty-five rows is a lot. I now have a colleague who only watches it, nothing else. And the tidying afterwards. Every trio is its own conversation. Twenty-one conversations with names like trio, Trio 4, me and Karin. I spent a whole morning on it. I use portal tags for the round now, and the name field for the table letter. It helps. It doesn't solve it.

The other thing. With tenants, people come with their neighbour. They want to hear the room. Trios felt like an interview to some of my older residents. One man said, I came to hear what the others think, not to be questioned by two strangers. In a five, you hear more views, you get a bit of the whole building. Diversity inside the group matters to people, not only across rotations.

That's real, I won't argue with it. For that kind of room I'd start with a plenary or a five, and maybe use trios for one round. But I'll give you this, Wouter. In my fives, the quiet ones drop off. I've listened back and you can hear it: a woman says one sentence in forty minutes. In a five it's very easy to disappear. So now every table starts with a go-round, one minute each, before the open part. It helps. It's not the same as a trio.

And above five? I saw a nine-person table on someone's slide this morning. No. No. Nine on one phone is two voices and a murmur. If you have to, two phones, and split them. Six is the most I'd ever put on one phone, and I mean six around a small round table, not six along a long one. Agreed. That might be the only number we agree on.

Let me try to sum up where you agree, and then questions. Live works if the prompts are ready, someone else runs the laptop, you check a few sources and you say draft. Overnight works when the room needs care, or when it's multi-day and the morning recap does the job of you were heard. A one-line steer between rounds is fine for both of you. Popcorn, ambience at most, and off for sensitive rooms.

Trios: everyone talks, no facilitator needed, but more phones, more failures, more tidying. Fives: you hear more of the room, fewer phones, but quiet people disappear, so go-round first. Nine: never. Can I add one? Whatever you do, decide it in the run sheet. The worst sessions I've seen are the ones where the host decides at lunch to try something live. Yes. That one I'd sign without reading.

Questions. Yes, at the front. Do you tell participants which one you're doing, live or overnight? Always. I say, tonight I'll read everything you said, and tomorrow morning I'll show you what I heard, and if I got it wrong, tell me. Same, but at lunch. And I add, it's a language model draft, so it'll be wrong somewhere, and finding where is your job. People like having a job.

One more, at the back. What about online, on video calls? Ah. Phone next to the laptop speaker, no headphones, two people per breakout recording in case one fails. And it's still awkward, I won't pretend. Online I do everything overnight. Wouter, even you? Even me. Live online is a stunt. Okay, on that rare moment of total agreement, thank you both. Coffee's at the back.

name: Library table hosts on Explore and Verify
summary: Synthetic sample. After the third of four evening conversations on the future of a public library system in a Canadian town, the coordinator and four volunteer table hosts (a retired teacher, a librarian, a seventeen-year-old youth council member and a volunteer in her seventies) debrief on Explore and Verify. Explore produced the best moment of the series when a question about who the opening hours exclude drew in a night-shift worker; it misfired when pressed in the first minute, when a table was stuck, and when a lively parents' table was interrupted, and pressing it again after the cooldown gave almost the same question, so the hosts settle on once per conversation. They conclude it lands only when a conversation is alive but could go deeper, and that briefing people first stops it feeling spooky. Verify ran as a five-minute moment in the run sheet with a timer on screen: tables had a half-joking point taken out, sharpened another, and added a widower's own sentence. Asking 'is this what we said?' instead of 'do you agree?' stopped tables debating, and a custom Verify topic gave shorter outcomes. For the final session on a branch closure they turn Explore off, keep Verify optional and read slowly, and switch anonymise transcripts on before anyone records, accepting the loss of audio playback.

chunks.text: Okay, everyone's got tea? It's recording. This is the hosts' debrief after session three, the nineteenth. Owen, Grace, Imran, Margaret and me, Nadia. I want to talk about the two buttons, Explore and Verify, because we've now used both three times, and I need to decide what we do for the last session, the one on the branch closure. Honest reactions, please. Imran, you go first, you've got the strongest opinions.

Okay. Explore. First session, I pressed it maybe ten minutes in, because the host card said to try it when the conversation's going.
