And it gave this question, like, you've talked a lot about opening hours, who isn't in the room because of the current hours? And my table just went quiet. Then this guy who works nights said, me, usually, I'm only here because I swapped a shift. That started like ten more minutes. Honestly the best bit of the whole series.

That's the one I want everyone to hear about. What did you do with the question, read it out? Read it out. The first time I did it in a robot voice, as a joke, and everyone laughed, which actually helped, because then they weren't nervous of it. Second session I just read it normally. Someone asked how does it know we talked about opening hours, and I said a language model reads the recording of our table and writes a question from it.

And she said, is it listening right now? And I said, it's recording, yes, that's what we all agreed to on the first screen. She was fine with it once I said it plainly. I think if I hadn't explained before, it would have felt creepy. So brief the table first. Say there's a button, say what it does, then use it. Don't just spring a question on them.

Mine didn't go so well. I pressed it at the very beginning, because I thought that's when you'd want help, when nobody's talking yet. And the button wasn't there yet, or it was grey, and then a minute later it worked, but the question was about nothing. We'd only done introductions. It asked us something about the value of community spaces, which, well, yes, dear, that's why we're all here.

I think that's the thing, Margaret. It needs something to work with. It only appears after about a minute of recording, and it's best when the conversation is already going. If the table is stuck, it's my job to unstick it, not the phone's. I tried it at a stuck moment in session two, and the question was fine, but nobody wanted to answer a phone. They wanted me to say something human.

My table was the opposite problem. They were flying. The young parents' table. I pressed Explore because I thought I should, and it asked something reasonable, about how the children's section could serve teenagers too, and one of the mothers said, very politely, can we finish what we were saying? She was right. It was an interruption. I put the phone back down and didn't touch it again that night.

So, Explore lands when the conversation is alive but could go deeper. Not when it's stuck, not when it's flying. That's a narrow window. And you can only press it so often, there's a cooldown, which is good, otherwise someone would press it every two minutes. I tried. It made me wait. Of course you did, Imran. And when it let me press again, the second question was basically the first one. Who isn't here because of the hours, in slightly different words.

Same table, same conversation. I suppose the language model reads the same talk, its own first question included, and still lands in the same place. My table noticed. Someone said, it's stuck on us. So that's a rule, then. Once per conversation, and if it lands, leave it. If you want a new question after that, it's your job, not a second press. Fine by me. Okay. Verify. For the record, the run sheet has it at seven forty. Five minutes, end of round two.

Before people get up for the final plenary. I put a timer on the big screen and say, table hosts, it's Verify time. The host taps the ECHO button on the recording screen, then Verify, picks the topic, and gets a short outcome written from their table's conversation. They read it out. The table says what's wrong with it, out loud, while it's still recording. Then the host presses revise so it rewrites from what they just said, or edits it by hand, and approves it when the table's happy.

That worked. Genuinely, better than I expected. My parents' table got an outcome that said the group supports reducing the adult fiction collection to make room for study space. And one of the dads said, that was one person, and it was me, and I was half joking. So that came out. Another line said quiet study space for teenagers, and they edited it to quiet study space for teenagers after school, until nine, because the times mattered to them.

Mine was lovely, actually, after the Explore disaster. We had a man who lost his wife last year and comes to the library every day, and the outcome said the library is important for people who live alone. And he said, put it's the only place I talk to anyone some days. I typed it in, and he watched me do it, and he said thank you. I think that was the most important five minutes of the evening for him.

The thing I'd change is the question we ask. The first time, I said to my table, do you agree with these? And they started voting, basically. Debating whether each point was right. That's not what it's for. Now I say, is this what we said? Not do we agree. Did we say it. Totally different conversation, and much faster. Write that on the host card, Grace. Literally. Is this what we said?

Five minutes is tight, though. Our outcome had six points in it and we spent four minutes on one. Should it be ten? Maybe seven. Or fewer points. We set a custom topic in the portal editor for session three, what we want the library board to hear, and that gave shorter outcomes, more focused. The general one gave too much. Okay, so we keep the custom topic. That's decided.

And the board will actually see these? The verified ones? Yes, Owen. They show up on each conversation as verified outcomes, and in the report I'll say which points were checked by the table and which only come from the transcript. I think the board should know the difference. A point a table said yes to, out loud, together, is worth more than a summary line nobody at that table ever read.

Okay. The real question. Session four is the Eastgate branch closure. People are upset. Some of them have used that branch for forty years. My instinct is to turn Explore off in the portal editor and keep Verify. What do you think? Off. Absolutely off. Imagine someone crying about the branch where they took their children, and a phone asks them about service delivery models. No, Nadia.

I'd keep it, honestly. It got my best conversation. For session four, though, Imran? Think of the Eastgate people. They're coming because they're angry. A question from a machine is going to feel like the library is trying to manage them. Okay. Yeah. Fair. Off for four. But back on for the next series, please. Agreed. Off for four, back on later.

And Verify stays, but differently. For Eastgate I'll ask the hosts to read the points slowly, and to say first, this is what the recording heard, you can change anything, tell us it's wrong, or say nothing at all. And if a table doesn't want to do it, they don't. Margaret, is that okay? That's okay. Give them the choice. Some of them will want their words checked very carefully, and some won't want to look.

One practical thing for session four. Can we turn on anonymise transcripts? People will say names, of staff at Eastgate, of each other. I don't want Linda at the desk in a report to the board. Good thinking, Grace. I'll do it tonight, before anyone records. It only applies to what comes in after you switch it on, so it has to be before. We lose audio playback, which is fine. And I'll reread the consent cards and the privacy link on the portal while I'm in there.

So, to sum up. Explore: lovely when the table is alive and could go deeper, useless when it's stuck, annoying when it's flying. Brief people first so it isn't spooky. Once per conversation. Off for Eastgate. Verify: five minutes in the run sheet, timer on screen, custom topic, ask is this what we said, maybe fewer points, optional for Eastgate. Anonymise on before session four. Anything I missed? The robot voice. We are not putting the robot voice on the host card. Thanks, everyone. Stopping.

name: Walk and talk: using it for a family care decision
summary: Synthetic sample. On a walk in the Netherlands, a facilitator tells a colleague how she used dembrane, very lightly, for three siblings deciding how to support their mother, who lives alone in Croatia with early memory problems. She used record yourself in the browser at a kitchen table, with her sister in Australia on video (the video call on a phone on speaker beside the laptop, no headphones), a private project, a short context, key terms for places, the day centre and medication, and a two-minute test first, because Croatian is not one of the languages a project can be set to (the transcript followed the Croatian anyway). What worked: her brother read the summary alone and finally heard what his sister had said twice; a chat question listing every practical offer and its conditions recovered forgotten offers; asking 'what did we not talk about?' showed that their mother was talked about constantly and almost never heard. A third conversation included their mother, who agreed to recording and an hour later said 'turn that thing off now', which they did at once. What felt like too much: consent screens, anonymisation (left off, names are fine at a kitchen table), a report with themed sections, and formal checking ('I'm not doing homework about our mother'). The family made the decision themselves.

chunks.text: Is it on? Okay. We're walking, so there'll be wind. Ana, you said I could record this because you're going to tell me the family thing, and I want to remember it for the training next month. People always ask whether it works for small stuff. It does and it doesn't, Femi. That's the honest answer. Can we go round the park, the long way? I think better when I'm walking.

So. My mum is in Croatia, in a small town on the coast. She's seventy-nine, and since last autumn she's been forgetting things. Not dramatic, but the stove, the post, once she got lost coming back from the market. My brother Marko lives twenty minutes from her. My sister Mirna is in Australia. I'm here. And for six months we'd been having the same phone call about what to do, and it went nowhere.

It always went the same way. Marko says he's doing everything, which is true. Mirna says she can't do anything from Perth, which is also true. I say we should look at options, and Marko hears you're not doing enough. Then someone hangs up. So in January I thought, I do this for a living. I sit in rooms where people can't hear each other. Why don't I do it for my own family?

And they agreed to be recorded? I asked. I explained it like I would to a client. It's so we have a record and stop arguing about who said what. Marko said, so now you're consulting us. Which, fair. But he agreed. Mirna loved the idea, she always feels she misses half of it on the phone. Mum wasn't part of the first two. That comes later, and it's the important part.

So I made a project in my own workspace. Private, just me. I didn't use the portal, the QR code, any of that. For three people it would have been silly. I just used record yourself in the browser on my laptop, on the kitchen table at Marko's when I flew down, and Mirna on video on my phone, on speaker, propped right next to the laptop, nobody on headphones, because otherwise her voice doesn't make it into the recording.

What did you put in the context? I'm curious what you write about your own mother. That's a good question, because it was strangely helpful to write. Something like: three adult siblings deciding how to support our mother, who lives alone and has early memory problems. We want to understand what each of us can realistically do, what the options are, and what we have not yet discussed. That last part, I wrote it out of habit. It turned out to matter.

Then key terms: her town, Marko's village, the name of the day centre, her doctor, two medications. And the words we use for her, because we switch. And when we argue, we argue in Croatian, even Mirna, and Croatian isn't a language you can pick for a project. So I tested two minutes first. It came out in Croatian, it follows what people say. Summaries came in English, my project's language, and the quotes stayed Croatian, which suited me fine.

First conversation, about an hour and a half. Second, two weeks later, an hour. Both times the transcript was good. Better than I expected, with three people talking over each other and Marko's dog barking at the postman. So what actually helped? Two things. The first was small. After the first conversation I sent them both the summary. Just the summary, a few paragraphs, nothing else.

And Marko called me, which he never does, and said, it says I'm the one who's there every day and I'm tired. Mirna said that? I didn't hear her say that. She had. Twice. He just couldn't hear it on the call because he was busy defending himself. Reading it on his own, in a quiet moment, he could take it in. That alone was worth the whole thing.

The second thing was the chat. I asked: list every practical offer that was made in these two conversations, and any conditions attached. Because offers get lost in arguments. And there were things in there I'd forgotten. Mirna offered to pay for a cleaner. Marko offered Sundays, but only if someone else covered one weekday. I'd offered to deal with the paperwork and then forgotten I'd offered.

And then I asked what I always ask at work: what did we not talk about? And it said, more or less, you discussed your own availability, money, the day centre and the stove at length. You did not discuss what your mother wants. She is mentioned all the time and almost never quoted. Oof. Yes. Oof. I sat at Marko's kitchen table and cried a little, honestly.

Because I do this for a living, and I'd forgotten the first rule. The person it's about wasn't in the room. So you brought her in? Third conversation, at her flat, with Marko and me there and Mirna on video. I asked her first, before anything, whether we could record, and why. She said, if it stops you three shouting, record what you like. Which is very her.

And for the first hour it was the best conversation we've ever had as a family. She told us she'd rather have someone come in than move anywhere. She'd thought about it much more than we knew. Then after about an hour she got tired, and she said, turn that thing off now. So I did. Immediately. Mid-sentence, actually, mine.

And we kept talking, and some of what she said after that was the most important. That she's scared. That she doesn't want Marko to stop his life for her. None of that is in the recording, and it shouldn't be. I wrote one line in my own notebook, that's all. Okay. So what felt like too much? Lots, Femi. Honestly, lots.

The first time I set up the project I went through all the settings like it was a client. Name on or off, email, anonymise. And I thought, what am I doing? Anonymise my own brother? I left it off, and the summaries use our names, which at a kitchen table is right. At work, names in a summary would worry me a lot. Here, it's just us, and it's our names.

I did read the privacy page properly, all of it, because I wanted to be able to tell mum honestly what happens to her words. That was worth ten minutes. But then I almost generated a report. A report! For three siblings! I clicked it, looked at the sections, and thought, nobody in my family is going to read theme two, availability constraints. I closed it. A summary and three chat questions was the right size.

And at one point I thought I should get each of us to go through the summary and correct it, like a proper check. Mirna did it, she likes that kind of thing. Marko said, Ana, I'm not doing homework about our mother. And he was right. In a family the check is the next phone call. You say, did I get that right, and they say no, idiot, and that's fine.

Did it change anything? The decision, I mean. We decided. Not the model, us, obviously. A carer comes in three mornings a week, Mirna pays for the cleaner, Marko does Sundays, and I fly down every six weeks and take the paperwork, because I'm the one who likes paperwork. Mum agreed to try the day centre once. It's not solved. But we stopped having the same phone call.

And what I keep thinking is, the record didn't make the decision better because it was clever. It made it better because Marko could read Mirna in peace, and because what did we not talk about had a very uncomfortable answer. The rest, the settings, the report, the checking, that's for rooms of sixty people. For three, you need a recording, a summary, and the nerve to ask the one question.

Can I use this in the training? Without names. And tell them the part about mum being talked about and not heard. That's the bit people need. That and turn that thing off now. When someone says that, you turn it off. Doesn't matter if it's your mother or a resident at a town hall. Okay. I'm turning this one off now. Good. Let's get a coffee.

name: We recorded ourselves first: an assumptions check
summary: Synthetic sample. A programme officer at a regional arts funder in Finland explains to a sceptical new board member why the team recorded its own planning meetings before consulting artists on new grant criteria. The planners' meetings went into a separate internal project; Explore, pressed during one of them, asked which they feared more, artists rejecting the criteria or nobody coming at all. The assistant then listed every assumption the team had made about artists, with quotes, and the team edited and signed off that list by hand. After six public sessions (anonymise on, artists told up front that the funder had recorded itself first), the list was pasted into the public project's portal as a text conversation, tagged and described in the context as the organisers' view, not participants'. Asking which assumptions artists contradicted showed they wanted smaller, faster grants rather than bigger ones, and that reporting, not the application form, was the burden; asking what the team had never considered surfaced care responsibilities and school-holiday deadlines. A report draft then presented an assumption as an artist's finding, so they moved the document back to the internal project and regenerated. They softened one 'contradicted' verdict by hand and published the assumptions and what happened to each.

chunks.text: Is that recording? Good. Mikko, you asked at the board meeting why we spent money recording our own staff, so I'm going to answer properly, and I'm recording it because I'll need to explain this again. It's the seventeenth. You're new, you weren't here in spring, and I think it looked strange from the outside. It is a bit strange. That's partly why it worked.

Okay, I'll be the sceptic, Aino, since that's apparently my role. We were consulting artists about new grant criteria. The artists are the point. Why record five people from our own office talking in a meeting room? Because we were going to decide what to ask the artists, and how, and I wanted to know what we already believed before we met a single one of them.

Every consultation I've run, the organisers walk in with a picture in their heads. Then they hear what fits the picture. Afterwards nobody can tell whether the picture came from the artists or from us. So this time we wrote it down first. Well, not wrote. Recorded. Three planning meetings, about ninety minutes each, in a separate project. Internal only, the five of us.

Separate why? Because I didn't want our voices mixed into the artists' data. If you ask the assistant about the public conversations, it should only see artists. The planning project had anonymise off, we're staff, we agreed, and the names don't matter. The public project had anonymise on from the first session, because artists here all know each other, and some of them depend on us for money.

And the planning meetings, did anything come out of them, or was it just a record? Something came out of the second one that I didn't expect. Halfway through, Petra pressed Explore, mostly as a joke, to see what it would do with us. And the question it gave was something like: which worries you more, that artists will reject the new criteria, or that nobody will come at all?

And there was this silence. Because the honest answer was, nobody coming. We'd spent forty minutes designing a beautiful session and zero minutes on whether a painter in a small town three hours north would ever travel to it. So that question changed the plan. We ended up with six sessions, four of them outside the city, two in the evening, and one online for people with small children.

Fine. One good question. Then what? Then after the third meeting I asked the assistant, in the planning project: list every assumption the team made about what artists need or want, stated as a claim, with the quote where we said it. It came back with nineteen. Some were obvious. Some were embarrassing. Artists in the north lack professional networks. Young artists want mentoring. The application form is the main barrier.

And you took that list as true? No. That's the important part. It's a language model's reading of our meetings, so the five of us sat down with it for an hour. We clicked every quote. Two of the nineteen were things Petra said ironically, so we took them out. One we'd actually said the opposite of. We merged a few. We ended up with fourteen, in our own words, and all five of us signed off on them.

So it's our list. Not the model's guess about us. That's the document that matters. Then the public sessions. And here's something I'd do again every time: at the start of each session, I told the artists, before we met you, we recorded ourselves, and we wrote down what we thought you'd say. At the end we'll show you which of our guesses were wrong. People laughed. Then they relaxed.

One woman in the second session said, so you're on trial today, not us. And I said, a bit, yes. Mikko, I think that did more for honesty in the room than any consent card. People were much more willing to say, no, that's not it, because we'd invited them to correct us. Six sessions, thirty-four conversations, groups of four or five, one phone each.

Okay. And how do you compare the list with what artists said, if they're in different projects? Ask works on one project at a time. So, after the last session, I pasted our fourteen assumptions into the public project's portal, using the text option, as one text conversation. Named it Organisers' assumptions, tagged it organisers, not participants, and added a line to the context saying exactly that: this document is the funder's own view, never treat it as something an artist said.

Then one question: for each of the organisers' assumptions in that document, did artists confirm it, contradict it, or not talk about it? Give quotes from the artists' conversations only. That was the most useful answer I've had from anything in years. Do you want the headlines? Go on. Assumption one, artists want bigger grants. Contradicted, nearly everywhere. They want smaller grants, faster, more often.

One sculptor said, I don't need forty thousand once every three years, I need four thousand next month. Assumption two, the application form is the barrier. Contradicted. The form is annoying, but the real burden is the reporting afterwards. Several people said they'd stopped applying because of the final report, not the application. We'd never even put reporting on the agenda.

And the northern networks thing? Mostly contradicted. They have networks, they're very well networked, actually. What they lack is studio space. And the mentoring one: young artists said, politely, that they want paid work, not advice. One said, everybody wants to mentor me and nobody wants to pay me. The summer deadline one was confirmed, by the way. Everybody hates the August deadline.

And then I asked a second question, which I'd recommend to anyone: what did artists talk about that the organisers' document does not mention at all? And the answer was care. Children, elderly parents. Deadlines in school holidays. Grants that assume you can go to a residency for six weeks. None of the fourteen assumptions touched it. Five people in an office, none of us with small children right now.

Okay, I'm less sceptical. But what went wrong? Because something did, you've got the face. Something did. I generated a first draft of the report from the public project, and the pasted document was still in there. And the draft said, artists in the north report a lack of professional networks. Which was our assumption. The one the artists had contradicted. It turned our guess into their finding.

I caught it because I clicked the source and it pointed to Organisers' assumptions. Tag and context line, and it still happened. So I moved the document back into the internal project, regenerated the report, and checked again. Lesson: you can bring a document in for one comparison, but take it out before anything that summarises the participants. And always click the source on the sentences you like most.

Was the model's comparison right, then? Mostly. One verdict I softened by hand. It said contradicted for the mentoring assumption, but when I read the transcripts, it was three young artists in one session. Strong, but three people. So in the report it says challenged by younger artists in one session, not contradicted. The verdicts are a starting point. What we publish, we read.

And you published the assumptions? With the five of us agreeing, yes. On the last page of the report: here's what we thought before we met you, and what happened to each guess. Fourteen lines. Confirmed, challenged, contradicted, or never came up. The artists' association shared that page more than the rest of the report put together. People like seeing the funder be wrong in writing.

So, for your board notes. Record the planning meetings in their own project. Ask for the assumptions with quotes, then edit and sign them off yourselves. Tell participants you did it. Bring the list in only to compare, tagged and named in the context, and take it out again before the report. Ask what you never considered. Soften verdicts that rest on a few voices. I'll put that in the minutes, Aino. Reluctantly impressed. That's all I wanted. Stopping.

name: Neighbourhood budget team, walking the timeline wall
summary: Synthetic sample. Four people from a district council in Spain walk a paper timeline taped along their office corridor, recording a retrospective of a year-long neighbourhood budget cycle for next year's team and two partner districts: Nuria, the participation officer, Óscar, a resident delegate, Maite from communications and Ramón from the budget office. About 340 residents in six neighbourhoods took part. They explain the scope paragraph in the project context and why it must also be read aloud (the first market session skipped it and residents proposed fixing the health centre), checking last year's and a 2024 project with the same question, word for word, before asking again, sessions at varied times with portal tags, type instead and typed-in paper cards, and one project per phase, closed to new conversations when the phase ended. A first ideas report was published unread and reached every subscriber with two proposals merged into one. Their "what happened to your proposal" report gave each of 31 proposals an outcome, residents' quotes and a reason, but went out months late. Ramón and Óscar argue about quoting proposals that lost; Maite and Nuria still disagree about how often to email everyone. A dog park split is shown as a split.

chunks.text: Is it recording? The red dot, yes. Okay. So, hello to next year's team, and hello to our friends in the two partner districts, that's why we do this in English, so forgive our accents. We are four. I'm Nuria, the participation officer. With me Óscar from the neighbours' association in Las Huertas, Maite from communications, and Ramón from the budget office. We taped the whole year on the corridor wall, February by the lift and September by the toilets. We walk it and say what we would keep.

And what we would never do again. Maite, don't look at me like that. I'm looking at the wall, Óscar. Okay, February. The first sheet is the scope paragraph, and I think it's the most important sheet here. We wrote it into the project context in February. Residents decide how a fixed sum from the district budget is spent on small works in public space in the six neighbourhoods. It can pay for benches, shade, lighting, play areas, small repairs to streets and squares.

It cannot pay for the health centre, the metro, the river path, anything that is regional, or staff. And then, the council funds the proposals that win the vote, inside the sum, if the technical check says they can be built. Five sentences. Ramón rewrote the last one three times. Because the first version said "will fund the winning proposals", full stop. And I've been in this job long enough to know there is always a winner with a gas pipe under it.

So the context had it, and the context steers what the chat and the reports say. But the context is for the language model. People need to hear it. And here's our first red sticker. The first market Saturday in March, I didn't read it aloud. I was setting up, Óscar was handing out cards, there was a queue for the churros. And at the Los Pinos table three people spent twenty minutes on the health centre. Their proposal was, fix the health centre.

Which is the only thing anybody in Los Pinos really wants, to be fair. I know. And in June they saw it wasn't on the ballot and they felt misled. One woman told Maite, you let us talk about it for twenty minutes, you recorded it, and then nothing. She was right. So from the second session, every session, I read the paragraph aloud at the start. Even at the home visits. Forty seconds. And then the second sentence. Óscar, you say it.

"You told us this last time. We are not asking again, we are asking what has changed." I stole it from my wife, she says it to the plumber. But it worked, because in Las Huertas we had been asked about the market square three times in four years. A survey, a walk with an architect, and something with post-its at the school. Nobody ever came back to us. So when Nuria's people came the fourth time, half my street said no, thank you.

That's the next sheet. Before any session, I checked what we already heard. The chat works inside one project, it doesn't look across projects, so I did it by hand. I opened last year's project, the small pilot, and the 2024 consultation project from urban planning, they gave me access. In each one I asked the same question, word for word, pasted from one note: what did residents already say about shade, lighting and the market square, with quotes, and from which neighbourhood.

Then I put the two answers side by side in a document and compared them myself, and opened the sources for anything I wanted to use. Heat and shade had moved up a lot. In 2024 shade was one point among many. Last year it came first almost everywhere. Parking went down. In 2024 it was parking, parking, parking. Because the summers are what they are now. Yes, Ramón, exactly. So we didn't ask "what do you want". We put the old quotes on a card and asked, is this still right?

Can I tell Las Huertas? It was the turning point for me. The association refused another session. So Nuria went to their Tuesday meeting with Óscar, with one printed page, eight quotes from 2024 about the square. The shade, the fountain that never works, the bins. And she said, this is what you told the city two years ago. Was this right, and what has changed? And they read it very slowly, and old Remedios said, that one's mine, I said that.

And then they talked for an hour, and we recorded it, with everyone's yes. One of the best conversations of the year. Okay, March and April, the idea sessions. Varied times, planned from the start. Market Saturday morning, the school gate at half past four, one evening in each civic centre, and home visits. One housebound man in San Roque, ninety-one, recorded with record yourself on my laptop at his kitchen table, his daughter next to him. He talked about the bench at the bus stop for forty minutes. It's funded now.

Every conversation got two portal tags when people scanned: the neighbourhood, and the type of session, so market, school gate, evening or home. Later I could filter on the school gate tag, select those conversations, and ask what the parents said about lighting. Type instead was on, a few people didn't want their voice recorded and typed on their phone. And many older people wanted paper cards. Those I typed in afterwards through the portal, switched to text, each table's cards as one typed conversation, with "idea cards, typed in, not a recording" as the name.

And two settings you should copy. Key terms: the six neighbourhood names, every square and street people mention, the civic centres, calle Tejares. Before that the square names came out wrong half the time. And anonymise transcripts on, all year. People name neighbours constantly. Paco's bar, the lady with the dogs on the third floor. That's how you talk about a street, but we didn't want it in summaries sent by email. You can't play back or download the audio then, we accepted that.

Structure. Why three projects, Ramón asked me in February. Ideas, deliberation, follow-up. Because each phase has its own report for a different reader. Ideas for the delegates, deliberation for the technical check and the ballot, follow-up for everyone. And at the end of each phase I closed the portal to new conversations, so when someone scanned an old QR from a lamppost in July, they didn't add a new idea to a phase that was finished. Three QR codes on lampposts. Three lampposts, Óscar.

The long sheet is the ideas report. The idea was that the draft grows with the cycle instead of me writing everything in July. So after each session I generated a new version. From mid-April reports could take our own instructions, and ours were: list proposals by neighbourhood, keep proposals separate unless residents themselves said they were the same, quote residents, say which session. Then I read it against the sources. Then it went to the delegates. Except the first time. Tell them, Maite, it's your sticker. It's everybody's sticker.

The first version was published before anybody read it. With report notifications on, publishing emails everyone who left an email, so two hundred people. And one line merged two proposals: shade sails for the playground at the El Carmen school and trees along calle Tejares became "shade for children on the way to school". Two groups of parents, two different things, both angry the same afternoon. The publish button even says how many people it will email. I just didn't think. Now nothing is published until someone has read every proposal and every quote against the sources.

And the drafts after that, I copied the report content into a document and sent it to the delegates only, from our own list. You can only download the PDF once it's published, and publishing emails everyone. That's where we still disagree. I think all 340 should see the draft growing, that's the point. And I think 340 people getting a long email every two weeks is how you lose them. They unsubscribe, and then they don't get the one that matters, in September. Write that down for next year, it isn't settled.

May, the two deliberation evenings. We had no Monitor then, it arrived in the summer, so I walked round looking at phones, and one table's phone was locked for twenty minutes before I saw it. At the closing evening in September we had the Monitor on a laptop, it said screen locked at table four, and Óscar was there before I'd read it. And the dog park. Oh, the dog park. A fenced dog area on the strip of park between San Roque and La Estación.

San Roque wants it badly. La Estación says that strip is where their children play. In the deliberation report I asked for disagreements with reasons from both sides, with quotes. Ramón wanted the report to say which side was more feasible. I wanted it to help, Nuria. I know. But it doesn't decide, that's the vote's job. So it went to the ballot with both sides' reasons, in residents' words. It lost, narrowly. And a man from La Estación said, at least they wrote down why.

June is the vote, on paper and on the city's own voting system. Not in dembrane, and we said that every time. dembrane is how we listened, the ballot is the ballot. Then the follow-up, the "what happened to your proposal" document. I made it as a report in the ideas project, where the proposals and most emails were. I typed the council's decision sheet in as text, named "council decisions after the vote, not residents".

The instructions: for each of the 31 proposals, the outcome, funded, merged, not feasible or lost the vote. One or two residents' quotes showing what people wanted and why. And the reason for anything not funded. Twelve funded, five merged, six not feasible, eight lost. Then I read every line against the transcripts and copied each quote from the transcript itself, not from the draft. And here Ramón and I had our big argument. Not big. Medium.

Because, Nuria, quotes next to proposals that lost reopen the argument. You put a lovely quote next to the losing dog park and people say, why did that lose, it's so reasonable. And Ramón, leaving them out is exactly what made people stop coming last time. Years ago the council put a list of winners online and the rest disappeared. My neighbour's proposal just vanished. She never came again. So we settled: quote, plus the reason, plus a line saying it can come back in the next cycle and how. I still think it reopens things. Maybe that's allowed.

The bad sticker. We promised the document for July. It went out at the end of September, nearly four months after the vote. Because the technical checks took until August, Nuria, and I wasn't going to publish "not feasible" without the engineer's reason in writing. Next time we promise a date we can keep, or send a short note in July saying where it is. We published it, so everyone who left an email got it, Maite printed it for the market stall, and we read it aloud at the closing evening. Óscar read Los Pinos.

Including the health centre. I said, this budget can't pay for it, we should have told you on the first day, and we didn't. Sorry. People clapped, which I didn't expect. The last sheet is the evaluation evening, in the follow-up project, where residents judged the process itself. I asked one thing in the chat: what did people say about the process, including complaints. You have to ask for complaints, otherwise you get thank yous. They came: weekday vote, school gate too short, too many sessions in Las Huertas before.

Okay, one thing each to next year's team. Maite? Never publish what nobody has read. Ramón? Read the scope aloud, and keep the reason next to every no. Óscar? Bring them their old words first. People come back when they see you kept them. Nuria? Promise a date you can keep. And keep the wall. Okay. That's the corridor. I'll stop it.

name: Crèche forum facilitators, supervision call on letting groups sort
summary: Synthetic sample. Thandeka, a senior facilitator, and Lwazi, her mentee in his first year with dembrane, hold their monthly supervision call about recent workshops for a crèche forum in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, recorded into Lwazi's private learning project. In June Lwazi showed seven themes from the chat on the projector after lunch; the room went quiet and the afternoon only agreed with them. In August groups clustered their own cards on the floor while recording, Lwazi typed the clusters in as one labelled text conversation, and asked what was said in the recordings but appears in no group's clusters. Four points came back; the room revived two, found a duplicate and dropped one with its reason on the record. Only then did the assistant merge the groups' clusters into a draft the room corrected, and each group checked a printed summary for what it got wrong. In September a power cut meant everything ran on paper, which Thandeka calls the real test. They disagree about merging at a 200-person meeting, counting who talks (there are no speaker labels, and equal time is not fairness) and when to mix owners with officials. Two practitioners will train as table hosts.

chunks.text: Okay, it's recording, Thandeka. Record yourself on the laptop, you're on speaker. This goes into my learning project, the private one, only me, not the forum's projects. So you can be as rude as you like. I'm never rude, I'm accurate. Good morning. How is your mother? Better, thank you, she's back at church. Good. So, supervision. I want to go through the three workshops, June, August and last week. I think I learned more in these three months than in the whole year before.

Start with June, then. Because you still don't like talking about June. No. Okay. The June workshop, forty-five crèche owners and practitioners, six groups, each with a phone recording. Each group had a QR card, and when they scanned they picked the workshop and their group as tags. The question was what support people need from the forum this year. Registration paperwork, food, training, children with disabilities, all of it. And over lunch I was excited.

I selected the six recordings in the chat, I asked for the main themes with quotes, and it gave me seven themes. Very clean. And after lunch I put them on the projector. And the room went quiet. Properly quiet. One of the older owners, from the crèche by the taxi rank, said, "so the phone has already decided". Everybody laughed, but not a happy laugh. And the afternoon was flat. Each group picked one of my seven themes and agreed with it. I got very tidy flip charts.

And what did I say to you in the car? You said the sorting is where people think. Yes. When a group stands over its cards and somebody says, no, that one doesn't go with food, it goes with the municipality, because the food grant comes from the municipality and it's never on time. That sentence is the thinking. If you sort for them at lunch, you've taken the most important part of the day and done it in the back room. And seven neat themes on a big screen look finished. Nobody argues with finished.

So, mid-August. We changed the order. Each group writes cards first, one idea per card, and then clusters them on the floor, because the tables were too small and people can walk around the floor. And the phone keeps recording through the clustering. That was your idea. It was a guess. A good guess, because when I read the transcripts that evening, the clustering was the best part. Every time someone moves a card, they say why. "These two are the same, it's the same clinic sister who never comes."

I didn't get that in June. In June they talked and I sorted. Then at tea, Nomvula read each group's clusters off the floor, the cluster names and the cards under them, and I typed them into the portal's text option on my laptop, one conversation for all six groups. I named it "groups' own clusters, typed at tea, not a recording", and I put the same line in the project context, so the assistant treats it as the groups' sorting and not as a conversation. It took twenty-five minutes. Tea is twenty minutes. Nomvula's tea was cold. She told me.

And then I asked one question, only one, on the six recordings and the typed clusters together. What was said in the recordings that does not appear in any group's clusters? Give the quotes. Four points came back. For each one I opened the source and read that bit of the transcript, to be sure it was really said and not guessed. Some passages are rough where a group switches into isiZulu, so Nomvula reads those. She's faster than me anyway.

The first point was from a practitioner in group five, a very quiet woman, maybe three sentences all morning. She said children with disabilities get turned away, because crèches don't know how to register them and they're scared the inspector will close them. Nobody picked it up, it never became a card. The second was transport money to get to training. The third, a landlord problem. The fourth, that the food grant forms are only in English. And how did you read them back?

Like you said. Not "here's what the analysis found". I said, these four things were said this morning and then dropped. Do you want them back? I read the quotes without saying who or which group. And the room did three different things, which I loved. Two they revived. The disabilities one, an owner said, "that's my crèche too, I've turned away two children", and suddenly it was a new cluster with five cards. Transport money they revived as well.

The landlord one, they said it's already there, in group two's cluster about premises, just in different words. So the assistant missed that it was a duplicate. And the forms one they dropped on purpose. An owner said yes, the forms are English, but the forum already has volunteers who help fill them, it's not our priority this year. Everyone agreed, and that reason is on the recording. That's what I want. Dropped with a reason, not lost on the way.

And then the merge. Only then. After the room had revived or dropped things, I asked Ask to merge the six groups' clusters into one draft, because six groups overlap a lot and merging is boring work. That's the tool's kind of work. I read it out as a draft and the room corrected it. They split "training" into training for owners and training for practitioners, because they're different people with different problems. That's the right job for it, merging what they've already sorted.

And each group got a one-page summary of its own conversation, printed, with one instruction on top: find two things this got wrong or made too tidy. Group three found it said "participants agreed", and they had not agreed, they had shouted. Anonymise was on, and the context says don't name children or crèches, because they talk about children by name all the time. It held. Only one summary said "the crèche next to the church". Everyone knows which that is. That's a small-place problem, not a software problem. Take that line out before you print.

Then September, which you keep calling the real test. Because it was. Tell it. A power cut, and then the whole area went down, no signal at all, the hall dark until eleven. No phones, no Ask, nothing. I panicked inside. And the groups just did it. Cards, floor, clusters, the read-back of what was dropped, which Nomvula and I did from our notes. On paper, by the window. Honestly, maybe better than June.

And that's the test I care about. If they couldn't have done it without the phones, then we'd have made the forum depend on us, and on something that needs electricity and signal. They could. So I'm not worried about the tool, I'd only worry if September had failed. Afterwards I typed our paper notes in as text, one conversation per group, labelled "paper notes, typed by facilitators". So the record is complete, but I know it's our words, not theirs. It's thinner.

And Explore, I tried once, in August, group four. The ECHO button on the phone. It asked a fair question, something like, who else looks after these children during the day, and were they asked? And the group talked about fathers, and grandmothers who run crèches informally in their houses and never come to the forum. Good question. But it couldn't bring them. It can ask about the people who aren't there, it can't put them in the room. So what did you do? Nothing yet. It's on my list. Put it higher.

Okay, the first thing I'm stuck on. In February there's the regional meeting, two hundred people, thirty tables. You can't cluster thirty tables on one floor. So there I think merging across tables is fair. Let the assistant merge. I agree, but only if every table clusters its own first. On paper, on the floor, wherever. Then you type their clusters, and the tool merges thirty sets of clusters, not thirty conversations. That's a different thing. And you still read back what got dropped. Thirty tables of typing. Then find more typists.

Second thing. I wanted to count who talks most, from the transcripts, to show the forum that the same five owners speak every time. You can't. The transcripts don't say who's speaking, there are no speaker names, it's one stream of words. And even if you could, I wouldn't want the number. Equal time isn't fairness. The older owners tell long stories, and the story is the point. Some practitioners come in once, at the end, and say the thing. So how do you know who's quiet?

I read. After every workshop I read two transcripts properly, start to end, two different groups each time. And I listen for who never comes in, by what's missing. Nobody from the crèches with babies said anything. Or the three young practitioners in group one, I hear them laugh but never speak. Then I talk to that group's host, privately, not in front of anyone. It's slower than a number, yes. I think you're half right. I still want something faster. Then find it and tell me.

Third. I want to put the municipal officials in a room with the owners and have the hard conversation. Registration delays, the food grant, the inspector, face to face. And I want same-role groups first. Owners with owners. Because some owners already feel small in front of a man with a lanyard. If you mix them on the first morning, the official talks and the owners nod. But if we always protect them, they never get that exchange, and the officials never hear it straight.

Yes. That's fair. And honestly, I don't know where gentle turns into keeping them out. Twenty years and I still don't know. My rule is same-role first, then mixed, with their own clusters in their hands, so they don't start from nothing. But I could be wrong for this forum. Try one mixed group in November and we'll read that transcript together. Okay. Deal.

My question, I ask it after every workshop. Will the forum be more able to run its own meeting next year than it was this year? Not, will the report be better. Will they need us less. In June the answer was no. In September, yes. And what are you doing about it? Two practitioners from group five, including the quiet one, actually, want to be table hosts. They come to the training in October. I'll show them the QR cards, how to stop the phone, and how to read back the dropped points.

Good. And write in your notes that June wasn't a disaster. It was a lesson that cost one afternoon. And that people sort better than you. I'm not writing that last bit. Write it. Okay. Same time next month? Same time. Greet your mother. I will. Stopping it now.

name: Development agencies podcast, four rounds and a fourth line
summary: Synthetic sample. An episode of a European network of regional development agencies' internal peer podcast, recorded with record yourself. Saskia, the host, talks to Zuzana and Radek from an agency in Moravia, Czech Republic, about an evening with about forty machine shop owners, vocational teachers, apprentices and two regional officials on what would make young people stay after vocational school. Four twenty-minute rounds at five tables, rotating, each recording named by round and table and tagged by round. Between rounds a seven-minute screen: three lines heard across tables and a fourth line, the strongest objection in the speaker's words, attributed to a table and checked with it first. Radek runs a saved template on the round's tag and checks two sources per line; Zuzana never touches the laptop. A teacher's objection that the screen turns everything into brochure language made round three franker; an apprentice showed that wages, rent and the bus were one question. Things went wrong: a slide built from the wrong round's tag, a line overstated from one table, a last round that only argued with the screen, an online edition dropped. They still disagree about how strict the objection rule should be. The report goes screen by screen and admits what was never answered.

chunks.text: Welcome to episode eleven of our peer podcast, for colleagues across the network. I'm Saskia. Today, two people from a small development agency in Moravia: Zuzana, who facilitated the evening, and Radek, whose job title, Zuzana tells me, was "screen keeper". Self-appointed. We're recording this in the browser into the network's podcast project, so if you'd rather read than listen, the transcript is in there. Zuzana, start with the evening itself.

About forty people, two weeks ago, in the old cultural house in our town. Owners of small machine shops, vocational teachers, apprentices, and two officials from the region. One question all evening: what would make young people stay after vocational school? Because they finish, they get the certificate, and they leave for the big city or for Germany. Five tables of eight, four rounds of twenty minutes, and people rotate every round so you always sit with new faces.

And between rounds, the screen. Seven minutes of screen, the same shape every time. Three lines, things we heard across the tables in that round. And a fourth line, which is always the strongest objection raised in that round, in the speaker's own words, attributed to a table, never to a person. "Table 3, round 2." That's why we call it the fourth line. Then people rotate and go again, and they can pick up the screen or argue with it.

Radek, how do you physically do that in seven minutes? Okay, setup first. Every recording is named by round and table, so "round 2 table 3", and when people scan, the portal asks for the round as a tag. Conversation language is Czech, the evening is in Czech. And in the project context we wrote that "a region of skilled hands" is our agency's slogan, the organisers' words, not something participants said. It's on every poster, and people repeat it, mostly ironically.

During the round I have a saved custom template, written and tested before the evening. I run it only on conversations with that round's tag. It asks for three points raised at more than one table, each with the tables, and then the strongest objection raised this round, in the speaker's words, with the table. Then I check two sources for every line. I click, I read that bit of the transcript. If I can't find two, the line doesn't go up. And I type the lines onto a plain slide myself.

White slide, black text, big. Zuzana never touches the laptop. I don't want to. My job is the room. If I'm looking at a laptop, I don't see that table four has gone quiet because the official just sat down. And the objection line, how do you avoid embarrassing someone? Before it goes up, I walk to the table. "Happy for this to be on screen as table 3?" Twice they changed a word. Once they said no, and I used the next strongest.

Tell the round two story, I've heard about it. Round two. One of the vocational teachers, thirty years teaching, objected to the method itself. He said, more or less: this screen turns what we say into brochure language. It keeps the polite version. "Better cooperation between schools and firms. We have said that for twenty years." And Radek put it up as the fourth line. His exact words, table 2. I asked him first, and he said, put it up, I'd like to see you do it.

The room laughed, and then something changed. Round three got franker. Nobody said "better cooperation" again. They started on why it never happened. Firm owners said the schools change the curriculum every two years. A teacher said firms take apprentices as cheap labour and don't teach them. An apprentice said her master doesn't let her touch the CNC machine. That was the real evening, round three. Did you expect that? I hoped. I didn't expect.

Same screen, round two, the three lines were wages, rent and the early bus. Three neat lines. And an apprentice at table five said out loud, while people were moving, "those are one thing. Can you live here on an apprentice wage? That's it." And she was right. Wages, rent, the bus to the industrial zone at six in the morning. For an eighteen-year-old it's one question. So I changed the round three question on the spot. I asked tables to re-cut the screen itself. Is this three things or one? What's missing?

And for the next screen I changed the prompt. Not "list the main points", but "what connects the points raised at different tables, with quotes". What came back was much closer: living on an apprentice wage, with quotes from three tables, wages, rent and the bus all in one line. I'm careful with the list version now. It makes things look separate that people live as one thing. And the room had told us that before the template did.

You also had Popcorn running, which some of us haven't tried. It's an early beta, you switch it on per project. I had it on a side screen by the coffee during rotations, as ambience. Half phrases from the conversations coming up. People stood with a coffee and pointed, "that's ours". I like it. I don't trust half phrases. A half phrase can mean the opposite of the whole sentence. So it stayed on the side screen, never the main one. We agree on where, not on whether.

What went wrong? My favourite. The screen after round three. I ran the template on the round one tag, picked the wrong one in the list, under pressure. The slide went up and someone at the back said, "we already said that. An hour ago." They were right. I stood up and said, sorry, that's round one, my mistake, three minutes. Which he did very well. People liked him more after. Now the round is in the slide title, big. If the title says three, the tag had better say three.

Round four, partly because of that and partly not, was the weakest. It had no new question, just "go deeper on what's on the screen", and they only argued about whether the screen was right. Nothing new came in. So next time the last round gets a fresh question, something like, what would you personally do in the next year. And the screen goes dark. No screen after round four, just the closing. Dark is a nice idea.

One more honest one. A line in the first screen said "firms are willing to pay towards apprentices' housing". I had two sources, but both were from the same table, two moments in one conversation, one owner saying it twice. A teacher caught it. She said, who said that? That's one man. She was right, and it had gone up as if the room said it. That's when the rule got stricter. Two sources from two different tables, or it says "one table".

And this is where Radek and I still disagree a bit. I think the objection should always be on the screen. Every round. The moment you skip it, people learn the screen is the polite version. And I worry one loud voice gets amplified. If the same man objects every round, he gets the fourth line four times. That's not the room, that's him with a microphone. So what's the rule now? Strongest objection, raised at more than one table where possible, checked with the table. Where possible. I wanted "must". I still want "must".

Some colleagues in the network read the round back aloud instead of projecting. Why the screen? People need to see their own words. Written, big, with their table. When the teacher saw his sentence up there, that's different from me repeating it. And to be honest, the other half is that people read the screen silently and nod. Seven minutes of forty people reading and nodding. It's not always a discussion. That's why the rotation matters. They take the screen to the next table and argue there.

Did you try it online? Once, for people in the villages who couldn't travel. A video call with breakout rooms, and in each room one person had the portal open on their laptop. And the screen was never ready inside the break. The breakout rooms close, everyone's back, and Radek is still checking sources. Twice we just looked at each other. So we dropped the screen online. Online we do the rounds and send the report afterwards. It's not really the tool. Online the break is two minutes, not seven, and I'm not skipping the checking.

And afterwards, the report? A report with our own instructions. One page per screen, in order. The screen as it was shown, and then what the next round did with each line: picked up, pushed back, or ignored, with quotes from the next round attributed to tables, never to people. So you can follow the evening as it moved. And at the end a section called "what we did not get to". That's the most important page for the region.

Because there's a question the screens never answered. Who moves first. Every round, the firms said the schools should, the schools said the firms, and the two officials said the region is waiting for both. Four rounds, nobody answered it. So it's written down as not answered, not as "broad agreement on the need for cooperation". Which is exactly the brochure sentence. Then I read the whole report against the sources. A whole afternoon. Two lines changed, and one quote replaced because it came from the wrong round.

Then we published it, so everyone who left an email at the end got it, about half the room. The officials got it the same day as the apprentices, which mattered to the apprentices. What would you tell a colleague who wants to try this next month? Two people. One for the room, one for the screen, never both. Save the template before the evening, test it on a rehearsal, put the round in the slide title. And walk to the table before the objection goes up.

So, did it make anyone stay? Ask me in five years. Two firms and the school are meeting about apprentice wages in November. That's not staying, that's a meeting. But it's a meeting about the real question. Can I add one thing? The tables were too big. Eight people around one phone, and there are bits in the transcript where two conversations run over each other. Next time six. Noted. Zuzana, Radek, thank you. That's the episode.

name: Heat plan lead and workers' centre organiser, phone call on who was missing
summary: Synthetic sample. Dana, who leads a county public health department's extreme heat plan in the south-western United States, phones Lupe, an organiser at a workers' centre for day labourers, roofers and landscapers; Marcus, the county analyst, joins halfway. After two public listening sessions with about ninety residents, Dana separated three questions: who is talked about but did not take part and whose concerns appear only in other people's words, both asked of the assistant with sources, and who was present but quiet (renters at tables with landlords), answered by reading transcripts and asking table hosts. Marcus explains that portal tags are picked at scan time by whoever holds the phone, count conversations rather than people, and that the first tag list had no option for outdoor work. Before session three, the centre ran its own sessions at a 5:30 am hiring corner and a Sunday football league, in a private Spanish project with anonymise on, read by the centre first by agreement. They tell how a fluent, invented answer about outdoor workers reached a draft slide and was pulled, compare the two projects by hand with the same saved question, disagree about merging projects, plan a homeowners' association session at its clubhouse, and keep a section on who they have not heard from yet.

chunks.text: Okay, I've hit record. Lupe, can you hear me alright? You're on speaker, I'm in the small conference room with the door shut. Just so it's on the recording: this goes into our team notes project, not the listening sessions project, so it never ends up in a report. And you're recording on your side? I am, the phone's on my desk. Good. We both keep a copy, so nobody has to trust the other one's notes.

Ha. That's kind of the whole thing, isn't it. Marcus joins in about twenty minutes, after the budget meeting. So, where we are. Two public listening sessions done, the branch library on the fourth and the high school gym on the sixth. About ninety residents, fifteen tables. Then your two sessions. But first, why I called you last week, because I think I explained it badly.

You did it fine. You said, we asked the computer who's missing and it said you guys. More or less, yeah. But it was three questions, not one, and that matters. After the gym I asked the assistant, with sources, who is talked about in these conversations but doesn't seem to have taken part. And it came back with three groups. Outdoor workers, so roofers, landscapers, people waiting for day work. Older people living alone in mobile homes. And people who are unhoused.

And every one came with sources, so I clicked through them. Table after table of people saying things like, my neighbour's husband does roofing and he comes home grey. Or, there's an old man in the park off the highway who won't run his AC because of the bill. People talking about them. Not them talking. That was question one. Question two I asked separately: whose concerns show up only in other people's words. And that's a slightly different list.

The unhoused residents, for example. They're in there, but only through the library staff and a pastor at the gym. Every quote is somebody speaking for them, kindly, but for them. And the third thing I couldn't ask the assistant at all. Who was there and stayed quiet. The transcripts don't say who's speaking, there are no speaker labels, so there's nothing to count. I read them myself, and I asked the table hosts what they saw.

Table six at the library. A woman, a renter, starts, well, in our unit the AC has been out since June. And a landlord at the same table says, you have to put in a work order, and talks for about four minutes about work orders, and she doesn't say another word for the rest of the hour. You can read it happening. The host saw it too. So renters at tables with landlords. That's a third kind of missing. They were in the room.

Yeah. And that's the corner too, you know. Some of my guys came to the library. Three of them. Did they? I didn't know that. Because your list didn't have a box for them. What list? When they scanned. Where do you live, how does the heat affect you. At home, caring for someone, a health condition, other. No I work outside. So they picked other. Oh, no. Yeah. So in your project they're just other. Hidden.

That's on us. We copied the tag list from an old air quality project and nobody read it with outdoor work in mind. Now the part I care most about. I didn't want to call you after the report and say, sorry, we missed you, here's a survey. Session three is the twentieth. I wanted to change who's in the room before anything gets written. Which is why I said yes. With a finished report I'd have hung up.

So tell me about the corner. Tuesday, five thirty in the morning, the hiring corner by the lumber yard. It's already eighty-something degrees. We brought coffee and pan dulce, and three of our phones, the centre's phones, not anybody's own. Groups of four or five, standing, phones on the tailgate of my truck. One question to start: tell me about the worst hot day you had this summer. Everybody has one. Everybody has one ready.

I said the consent part out loud, in Spanish, before anyone scanned. What's recorded, that names get taken out, that the county sees nothing until we've read it, that you can stop and walk away. Two men said no thanks, fine, they talked with me off to the side and I wrote nothing down. Then at six fifteen the first contractor's truck pulls up and half of one group just leaves. Mid sentence.

It's in the transcript. A guy is explaining how he hides water in the shade of the truck so the foreman doesn't see him stopping, and then it's just, ya llegó, and car doors. I love that. It's true to the place. And Sunday? The football league, between games, under the canopy by the snack stand. Families, kids running around, older men who don't get picked up for work any more.

Very different talk. The apartment at night, the kids, the power bill, who in the family can't take the heat. And technically? I know Marcus sent you notes. He did. Its own project, private, three people in it. Me, Chayo from the centre, and Marcus, for if something breaks. Conversation language Spanish. Anonymise transcripts on before the first recording.

No names asked, no email asked. And the deal, which I want on this recording too: Chayo and I read every summary first. The county works from the report we approve, not from the transcripts. Marcus can open it, and he tells me the county's workspace admins can open any private project, so that part is an agreement between us, not a setting. Marcus doesn't read anything until I say. Agreed. Completely. And Marcus is just walking in, hang on.

Hi Lupe, sorry. Did I miss the part where you say I can't read anything? You just missed it. You can't read anything. Understood. I watched the Monitor at both sessions, so I knew every table recorded, but it can't tell you who's at the table. And the tags thing. You're right, and it's worse than missing a box. The tags are picked at scan time, by whoever is holding the phone. One phone per table. So the tag describes one person's choice for a table of six.

And they count conversations, not people. If I say twelve conversations tagged at home, that's twelve tables or twelve phones, not twelve residents. So for the library, where the outdoor workers were hiding under other, I opened a Specific Details chat on just the conversations tagged other, eleven of them, and asked for every passage about working outside, with sources. Three tables. Your three guys, I think, spread over two tables, plus a woman who does landscaping.

Did it get them right? Mostly. One passage was a guy talking about his yard, not his job, so I took it out. I like Specific Details for this, I know exactly which eleven it's looking at. Can I say the thing now, Dana? Which thing. The slide. Somebody at your office told me about a slide. Okay. Yes. It's mine to tell.

Before I called you, Trevor, he's new, he's good, was building the draft deck for the board briefing, with a gap where outdoor workers should be. So he asked the assistant what outdoor workers would probably say about cooling centres. A very fluent answer. Transportation is a barrier, people need rides to the cooling centres, more bus passes. It sounded completely plausible. He put it on a slide with a little heading, outdoor worker perspectives.

I caught it the night before and pulled it. I sat with him the next morning, not to tell him off, it's the easiest mistake in the world. You ask a question, it answers. It doesn't say, I wasn't there. And here's what makes it worse. Lupe, tell Marcus what your guys actually said about cooling centres. Nobody said rides. They said the cooling centre is open nine to five, and we work nine to five.

By the time we're off the roof it's closing. And some people won't walk into anything with a county seal on the door, for reasons you can guess. And mostly they don't want a cooling centre, they want shade and water at the job, and to stop for ten minutes without losing the day. So the made-up version was wrong in a way that would have sent money to bus passes. Yeah. That's what scares me. Not that it was rude. That it was believable.

So two things changed. There's a line in the project context now. Something like: do not speculate about what groups who did not take part might think. If a group is only described by others, say so. And the rule for the team, which I said out loud at the staff meeting: nobody asks the assistant to speak for anyone. We ask what people said. If they didn't say it, we go and ask them. Which is what this whole call is.

Can I do the comparison bit? Because I think that's the useful part for the plan. Go ahead. So Ask works inside one project, it can't look across two. So I wrote one question, saved the exact wording, and pasted it into Ask in each project. What makes a hot day dangerous for the people in these conversations, what do they already do to cope, what would help. Quotes with sources. Don't generalise beyond these conversations. Then I pasted both answers side by side in a document and compared them by hand.

And they barely overlap. Power bills, both. Older relatives, both. But the public sessions are about cooling centres, trees, library hours. Yours is water on the job, rest breaks, the foreman, the hours, and the county building thing. Which I'd have told you, Marcus. Sure. But now it's in their words, with sources. That's not the same as me saying it. That's the part I want.

Here's where we disagree, so let's have it on tape. I still think the Spanish sessions should go into the main project. One Ask, one report. No. Lupe, hear me out. I heard you last week. Our people said things on a tailgate at five thirty in the morning because I told them it stays with us until we've read it. If it moves into your project, it's yours.

And there's the boring reason that wins anyway. Language is set per project. The transcript follows whatever people speak, but in an English project the summaries and the screens people see come out in English. So two projects, compare by hand. I lose, gracefully. And the report? Lupe, what do you want for the workers' section? Published the way we approve it. Not cut down, not reworded so it sounds nicer for the board.

I don't trust the county not to pick the three quotes it likes. No offence, Dana. None taken, I've been in the county long enough. So, yes. The workers' section goes in as the centre approves it. And before anything goes to the board, you get the full draft with every quote checked against the transcript, so you can see where your section sits next to everything else. Not just your part. And the quotes stay in Spanish, with our translation under them. Chayo and I do the translation.

Agreed. Two more things. The homeowners' association, the one against the shade tree requirement for new subdivisions. They didn't come to either session, they sent a letter. I've offered them their own recorded session, at their clubhouse, on a weeknight that suits them. Same deal as you, their arguments in their own words, they see their section before the board does. You'll go to their clubhouse. My guys had to stand in a parking lot at five thirty.

Your guys chose the parking lot. Their terms. Their clubhouse is theirs. Same principle. Hm. Fair is fair. Better their arguments in their words than someone at the county guessing what they think, like the slide. That's exactly it. Last thing. The report has a section called who we have not heard from yet. Right now it still says older residents alone in mobile homes. And unhoused residents, only heard through staff and a pastor.

Next week two community health workers go door to door in the two parks off the old highway, in the mornings. Short conversations, one per household, consent said at the door, on the portal on their phones. With an I live in a mobile home tag this time. Marcus read the tag list twice. And an I work outdoors one, before you ask.

So, for my notes: three separate questions. Change who's in the room before session three. The centre's project stays the centre's. Same wording in both, compared by hand. Nobody asks it to speak for anyone. And the gap stays in the report until it's filled. I'll send the draft when the quotes are checked. Send it to Chayo too. Will do. Stopping it now. Thanks, Lupe.

name: Nature park charter revision, scoping what earns its place
summary: Synthetic sample. Before anything is set up, Claire, participation lead at a regional nature park in France, director Bernard and independent facilitator Yasmina scope fourteen autumn sessions for the park's charter revision, recording into a sandbox project to share with the steering committee and a twinned park abroad. At a whiteboard they go through dembrane and switch on only what earns its place: recording everywhere, because the 2015 flip charts are lost and the regional council asked how outcomes traced back to residents; Verify only at village evenings, after the first round rather than at the end, with three custom topics; Explore off at facilitated, contentious tables; nothing projected live; Ask for merging across tables, what was missed, and disagreements with reasons from both sides. Wolf management follows national rules, so they will say plainly it is not being consulted on. They explain why recorded tables replace a 2019 comment form full of two-line opinions, keep a short form in its own project, offer the hunters' federation a session in its own hall, refuse a university's request for transcripts, and turn anonymise on everywhere with a rule not to name farms or hamlets. Bernard wants one recommendation per chapter; they agree the board decides with the split on record. Project structure stays open.

chunks.text: Right, it's recording. This is going into the sandbox project, so nothing here gets mixed with real sessions. Hello to the steering committee, and hello to our colleagues in the twinned park, which is why we're doing this in English, sorry Bernard. It's fine, I need the practice. So. Twentieth of August, the three of us at headquarters, the charter revision. Fourteen sessions planned this autumn and nothing set up yet. Which is the point. We decide what we use before we use anything.

Claire, you have the whiteboard. I have the whiteboard. Three columns. What it does, on or off, and where. And I want us to go through every part of dembrane and only switch on what earns its place. Not everything because it's there. Yasmina, you said that to me in June and it stuck. Because I've seen the opposite. A client turns everything on, the participants press buttons all evening, and nobody actually talks. Start with recording, then. Recording is easy. Yes, everywhere.

Every session, every table. And I want to say why on the recording, because the twinned park asked us. Two reasons. One, the flip charts from the 2015 charter consultation are gone. Gone. They were in boxes in the old building in the valley and when we moved, nobody knows. We have a twelve-page summary written by a consultant and no way to check a single line of it. Two, the regional council asked us last time, quite politely, how the outcomes traced back to residents.

And we couldn't answer. I couldn't answer, I was the one in the room. I said, well, it's in the summary. And the councillor said, and where does the summary come from? So recording. The transcripts are the record, and every claim in the report points back to one. Okay. Next column. Verify. This is the five minutes where the table picks a topic, hears what was drawn from its own conversation, and revises or edits it until they can approve it. Or they don't approve it. I want it only at the village evenings.

Not at the stakeholder sessions? Not at first. The village evenings are where trust is lowest. People have been consulted before and they think the park already knows what it wants. Seeing their own points and being able to say no, that's not what we said, is worth five minutes there. With the farmers' union or the tourism people, they're professionals, they'll correct the report anyway. And early in the evening. Not at the end. Why not at the end? Bernard, you've been to a village evening.

At half past ten people want to go home and feed the dog. If Verify comes at the end it's homework, they'll approve anything. I'd put it after the first round, maybe forty minutes in, while they still have energy and before the second question. And I'd set the topics myself. There's a setting for custom Verify topics. I'd use three: what we agree on, where we disagree and why, and what we want the park board to know. So the disagreement has its own place.
