Writing that down. Verify, villages only, after round one, three topics. Explore? Explore is the button that asks the table one question based on what it's been talking about. For our tables, off. Off? I thought you liked it. I like it at tables with nobody facilitating. Walking pairs, self-run groups. But at the stakeholder sessions I'll have a facilitator at every table, and those are contentious. Hunters, walkers, a farmer, a gîte owner at one table.

A question popping up from a phone in the middle of a tense moment, I don't want it. My facilitators are trained to hold those moments. A clumsy question at the wrong second and it feels like a gimmick, and you've lost the table. Off. And nothing on a screen live, before you ask, Bernard. No projected results at the evenings. Fine by me. I don't want the mayors reading a screen. Okay. And Ask, the assistant. That's the big one.

That's where I'll spend my time. But for three things, specifically. First, merging across tables. Each table writes its own points on paper at the end and reads them aloud into the recording, and afterwards I use Ask to merge and de-duplicate across all the tables, as a draft. Second, what have we missed. What came up once and disappeared, who is talked about but wasn't there. Third, disagreements, with reasons from both sides. Not the majority view. Why people disagree.

Can I stop you there. Because this is the part I want to talk about. Of course. I need, at the end, one recommendation per chapter. Landscape and farming, water, access and tourism, energy, biodiversity. One recommendation each. That's what the board can act on. If I bring them a document that says, well, some villages think this and the hunters think that, they'll say, so what do we do? And the consultant last time gave them exactly that. One clean line.

Can I tell the story? Because the twinned park should hear it. Go. Last time, the consultant presented at the mayors' meeting. Slide, big letters, the analysis says residents want to limit motor traffic on the forest roads. And one mayor, from one of the small communes up on the plateau, stood up and said, nobody in my village said that, where does it come from? And the consultant said, the analysis. And he walked out. He's still angry about it. He'll be at the first evening.

And that's why I won't write the split out of the report. Bernard, I understand what the board needs. But if the forest roads split the villages and the walkers, the report has to show the split, with quotes from both sides and their reasons. The decision is the board's, and that's how it should be. But the record has to show what they're deciding between. Otherwise you get another mayor walking out, and this time he'll be right.

So who writes the recommendation? The board. Not me, not the assistant. The board, in its meeting, with the split in front of it. Hm. Bernard? I'm thinking. It's slower. It's slower, but it's yours. You decide, and you say why. And then the report gets a third part later: what the board decided and the reason. Okay. I can live with that if every chapter starts with what people actually agree on. So the board isn't drowning in disagreements. Yes. Agreed first, always.

Let me write the report shape, then, so we have it agreed today and not in December. Per chapter: what people agreed on. Live disagreements, with reasons and quotes from both sides. Then, added later, what the park board decided and why. And every output we share is called a draft and carries quotes. No more the analysis says. Never. Next. What we don't ask about. Wolves. Ah. Wolves. Wolf management follows the national rules. The charter cannot change it.

So we don't consult on it. And we say so plainly, in the project context and in the opening of every evening. I'd rather say it on day one than pretend it's open and disappoint everyone in March. But they'll talk about wolves anyway. Of course they will. Especially on the plateau, the sheep farmers. And we won't stop them, it'll be in the recording. But the opening says: wolf management is decided nationally, this charter can't change it. What the charter can do is support herders.

And that we'll pass on what's said, without promising anything. And the context says it too, so the assistant doesn't write a chapter recommendation about wolf quotas because people talked about it at every table. Context. While we're there. What else goes in? Who we are, what the charter is, the five chapters, the two series of sessions, what's fixed and what's open. Then the names. Key terms: the hamlets, the rivers, the species. Grand tétras, sabot de Vénus, the Lirande, the Combettes.

Without key terms the transcripts will be full of nonsense, I tested one in July and it turned a hamlet into a brand of cheese. And conversation language French, of course, for all the sessions. Only this meeting is in English. And anonymise. Anonymise transcripts on for every session. Every one. Even the stakeholder ones? Every one. People in the villages name their neighbours, they name farms. Old Mr whatever's field by the bridge. It's how people talk here.

And we lose the audio. With anonymise on, you can't play it back or download it. I know. I'm accepting that. I'd rather lose the audio than have a transcript where someone's neighbour is named next to a complaint about his dogs. And one more rule in the context: do not name farms or hamlets in any output. Wait, you just put the hamlets in key terms. Yes, both. Key terms so the transcript spells them right, for us. The context rule so the summaries and reports don't attach a view to a hamlet.

With forty people in a hamlet, saying the hamlet is saying the person. Clever. Annoying, but clever. And the legal basis, I've set it with our data protection contact, she's happy, that's done. Now. The form. I know you want to drop it. I don't want to drop it, I want it in its place. In 2019 the park ran an online comment form on the draft management plan. Over a thousand comments. And almost all of them were two lines. I want more walking paths. Stop the quads.

No reasons. You can't learn much from a thousand quick opinions. You learn something from people giving each other reasons around a table and changing their minds a little. That's why recorded tables. But there are people who can't come. Shift workers, the old lady with no car. Yes. So a short form stays. Three questions, one of them why. We paste the answers in through the portal's text option, label every one clearly as a written comment, and analyse them separately. Not mixed into the tables. Its own project.

Otherwise a hundred two-line comments outweigh a two-hour conversation in every summary. Fine. Its own project. The hunters. Ah. The federation said no to the mixed evenings. They said they'd be outnumbered and shouted down. Which, in one valley, is not wrong. So I've offered them a session in their own hall. On their terms, their evening, their coffee. Their arguments in their own words, in the record. Not paraphrased by us, not by the walkers. With Verify on, so they sign off on their own points.

Won't they just use it to make speeches? Some of it will be speeches. But I'll have a facilitator, and the questions are the same as everywhere. And when the report says the hunters' federation argues this, there's a quote and a transcript behind it. Which is more than the hunters ever got from us before, to be honest. Then the university. Yes. The university in the city wrote last week. They want the transcripts for a research project on rural participation. Very nice letter.

The answer is no. Not without the participants' separate consent. People are agreeing to talk to the park about the charter. Not to be research data. If the university wants to do something later, it's a separate question, with its own consent, and exporting anything would be a decision for the park and the participants together. Not a button I press because they asked nicely. Agreed. I'll write back. Now, our open question. Projects. One or several. I want one project.

For the whole revision. Tags per chapter, tags per series. One place to ask everything. And I'd rather one project per series. The village evenings and the stakeholder sessions. Each gets its own report, for different readers. And the settings are different. Verify on at the villages, and Verify and Explore are switched on per project, in the portal settings, so the stakeholder series needs different settings anyway. Hm. That's a real point. But I lose asking across everything in one go. You do.

You'd compare by hand. I know. Let's not decide it today. We test both in the sandbox next week with a dummy evening and see. Leave it open, then. Open. Okay, I think we have the whiteboard. Recording everywhere. Verify at the villages, after round one, with our three topics. Explore off. Nothing projected. Ask for merging, what we missed, and disagreements with both sides. No consultation on wolves, said plainly. Anonymise on, no farms or hamlets in any output. Form in its own project.

Hunters in their own hall. University, no. Report: agreed, split, then the board's decision and why. And everything is a draft with quotes. And the board decides. The board decides. With the split in front of it. Good. Bernard, you look almost happy. I'm thinking about the mayor from the plateau. If he reads his village's words in the report next spring, I'll be happy. Okay, I'll stop it there.

name: Teacher college, peer observation after a trainee deliberation
summary: Synthetic sample. Meera, a senior lecturer at a teacher education college in southern India, gives peer observation feedback to Farhan the day after he ran a deliberation with 48 trainee teachers in twelve groups of four on whether continuous assessment should replace end-of-year exams in practice schools. Recorded with record yourself into his private portfolio project. Three groups opened with chatbot-generated pros and cons and stayed general, so the next pre-task is one question and one memory from their own schooling, no position. A table card asking what experience or value a view comes from brought reasons into the transcripts. Farhan's two-minute timer cut off a story and a fast exchange; they drop it for a short opening go-round, noting nobody can count airtime without speaker labels. Two quiet trainees used type instead and a second QR on the door tagged "added afterwards"; five entries held the most candid points, about fear of the inspector. Meera worries this turns deliberation private, so the points go back to the groups next week. Also: Explore helping once and repeating itself, Ask on reasons rather than majorities, a summary calling a split group a consensus (fixed with a context line), a locked phone missed on the Monitor while Farhan took notes, and Verify used as reflection. Meera proposes one session without phones.

chunks.text: Is it recording? Yes, red dot. Okay. Farhan, this goes into your teaching portfolio project, the private one, so it's only you unless you share it. For the record: peer observation debrief, Farhan's session yesterday afternoon with the second-years. Forty-eight trainees, twelve groups of four, deliberating whether continuous assessment should replace the end-of-year exam in their practice schools. I'm Meera, I observed from the back, under the fan.

And I'm Farhan, who was observed and did not sleep much. Good news or bad news first? Neither. Tell me what you think happened, then I tell you what I saw, and then we look at the transcripts, because I read four of them last night and they don't fully agree with either of us. Fair. Okay.

The setup I was happy with. One project, portal in English because that's our medium, a QR card on every table with the group number on it, the host guide folded beside it. I went through consent and the legal basis with the data officer two weeks before, she wanted to see the welcome cards. And at the start I said recording is optional and any group can stop the phone. Nobody said no out loud.

Nobody said no out loud. Hold that, we'll come back to it. Then the pre-task, which is where it went wrong first. I told them, come prepared, think about both sides. And three groups out of twelve opened by reading pros and cons that a chatbot had given them. Off their phones. In bullet points.

I saw. Group two, group five and the one by the window. Nine, Divya's group. They read the list, everyone nodded, and then for ten minutes it was general. Reduces exam stress. Holistic development. Burden on teachers. Like a guide book. Nobody said I, nobody said my school. Group five's first ten minutes, I could have written that transcript without being in the room.

It wasn't wrong, that's what annoys me. Every point on those lists is real. No, it wasn't wrong. It was finished. They came already decided, and someone who has decided doesn't need anybody else at the table. So next time? Don't ask for positions at all. Ask them to bring one question they really don't know the answer to, and one memory from their own schooling. A test, a teacher, a result. No position.

And say please don't look it up. As a request, not a rule. If they look it up anyway, they still have to bring a memory, and the chatbot doesn't have their memory. One question, one memory, no position. I'll put it on the sheet. Good. Now the card, because that worked and I want you to know it worked.

The reasons card. I put it out about fifteen minutes in, when I saw how flat it was. A half sheet on each table: what experience or value is this coming from? That's all. I watched group nine read it, and Divya turned it face down, which I thought was a bad sign. Then Rohan said, okay, my experience is my uncle failed the tenth standard board and never went back. And the table changed.

It's in the transcripts. Before the card, the list. After the card, people. Group four, Pradeep says continuous assessment is just more chances for a teacher to have favourites, someone asks him where that comes from, and he talks about a teacher in his village who gave internal marks to children whose parents brought him vegetables. The group spends ten minutes on what would stop that. That's a reason, not a pro or a con.

Should I give the card out from the start? Maybe. Or keep it for when it goes flat. Fifteen minutes of guide book talk isn't wasted if they feel the difference afterwards. I'll try both, morning batch and afternoon batch. Fine. Now the thing I wrote most about in my notebook. Your notebook? Your notebook, Farhan. You wrote the whole time.

Habit. Twelve years of writing everything down. You were taking notes on a session being recorded twelve times over. And while you were writing about group three, group seven stopped talking. I timed it, six minutes. Phone still on the table, nobody went over. I thought they were thinking. They were stuck on whether internal marks count for college admission, and nobody knew.

So that's my main feedback. The recording is taking the notes. You watch the room. Walk, listen for silences. The transcripts will tell you what was said better than your handwriting. And honestly the notes are for me, they make me feel I'm doing something. Watching the room is doing something. It just doesn't leave a page behind.

The timer. Go on, you first. I gave everyone two minutes per turn on a phone timer, to make it fair, so the confident ones didn't take over. At group eleven Lakshmi was telling a story about her younger brother and his board exam, the timer went, and she stopped. Mid sentence. She never came back to it.

And group six had a fast exchange, four people going back and forth, really useful, working out what a portfolio would look like for a class of sixty. The timer kept cutting it. So it was fair on paper and worse in the room. Equal time isn't fairness. Stories need room, a quick back and forth needs no timer at all, and quiet people often come in late, after the timer has given their turn away.

So drop it. Drop it. Keep a short go-round at the start, everyone says their memory in a sentence or two, so everyone has spoken once. Then let it run, and you watch. I wanted to count, actually, who spoke how much, from the transcripts. You can't. There are no names on the lines, it's one block of text per group. You can read it and get a feeling. There's no number.

Which is fine. A number would tell you who talked, not who was heard. Okay, the quiet ones, and your "nobody said no out loud". Two trainees came to me at the break. One said the phone in the middle made her quieter. The other, I won't say who, didn't want her spoken English recorded. She's shy of her accent. She writes beautifully.

So I told her she could use type instead, scan the card on her own phone and type. And I put a second QR on the door, a link that sets a tag, added afterwards, so anyone could add something alone after the session, spoken or typed. Five did, out of forty-eight. And those five are the most candid material in the whole project. Three are about the inspector.

The fear that continuous assessment means the inspector checks your registers every month instead of results once a year. One of them typed, and I copied this from the transcript, not from a summary: in the group I said it is good for children, but really I am afraid every mark I give will be checked and I will be the one who failed. Nobody said that in a group.

Here I disagree with you a bit. Those five are valuable. But a deliberation is people working something out in front of each other. If the honest points go out the back door into private recordings, the groups never have to deal with them. It turns into a suggestion box. The inspector fear never met the group that says it's good for children.

But they would never have said it in the group, Meera. Maybe not yesterday. The week after, if they knew someone else felt it, some might. So bring it back. Next Thursday, start with: here are points someone added afterwards, not who, just what, do you want to take any up? And if they don't, they don't. That I can live with. Then it's not a side door, it's a way back in.

Explore. Did you see group nine again? Stuck on the list a second time, after the card wore off, and Rohan pressed the ECHO button and chose Explore. It only appears after about a minute of recording, they had forty. It asked something like, which of these points have you seen happen in a real classroom? And it came down to the ground at once. Divya told the story of her practice school's weekly unit tests.

Then group two pressed it twice, a few minutes apart, and the second time it was more or less the same question back. There's a wait between presses as well, they found that out. They laughed and stopped. So, once, when they're going in circles, not as a toy. It only works with what they're already half saying. Group nine had something there. Group two didn't, yet.

And afterwards, what did you ask? The actual question. I did not ask what the majority thinks, because forty-eight trainees in twelve groups is not a vote. I asked, which reasons did groups give, and what experiences were they based on, with the sources open. Then a separate question, only on the added afterwards conversations: what appears here that doesn't appear in any group conversation?

The first answer grouped reasons by experience: own schooling, practice school, family. Every point had sources. I opened all of them, and two quotes were cut in a way that shifted the meaning, so I copied from the transcripts instead. The second answer is where the inspector came from. In three of the five, in none of the groups. Which I checked by reading, because I wasn't going to trust a no.

And group four's summary? I saw it this morning. It says the group reached consensus that continuous assessment should come in gradually. Two of the four never agreed, Pradeep and the girl beside him, it's plain in the transcript. I've put one line in the project context: do not describe a group as having reached consensus unless everyone in it said so, and name the disagreement. Regenerated, it now says two for, two against because of favouritism. Which is what happened.

And Verify. You gave them five minutes at the end of a long afternoon. I was nervous. And it was the best five minutes. They picked a topic, read out what it drew from their conversation, revised or edited it, and most approved in the end. One group wouldn't approve theirs at all. Group eleven changed exams are unfair into exams are unfair to the ones who freeze. I heard, did we actually say that? And, we said it, but we didn't mean it like that.

That's reflection, Farhan, don't sell it as checking the tool. They're trainee teachers, hearing what they sounded like is the most useful thing they did all day. Last thing. The phone. Group ten. I had the Monitor open on the laptop and didn't look at it for twenty minutes. Because you were writing. Because I was writing. It said Screen locked. Someone had laid it face down, and they lost about twelve minutes.

I told them screen on, once, at the start, along with ten other things. Put it on the card: screen on, face up, in the middle. And glance at the Monitor every few minutes, which you'll have time for, because you won't be writing. Okay, I hear it. Let me say what I'm changing so it's on the recording. One question and one memory, no position. Reasons card. No timer, a short go-round. I watch, I don't write.

The door QR stays, and on Thursday I read those points back as points someone added. Screen on, on the card. Explore once, when they're stuck. The consensus line in the context. Ask for reasons and experiences, never majorities, and copy every quote from the transcript. Verify as reflection. Good list. One more from me. Next term, run one session with no phones at all, paper only.

Without the tool? If the reasons only appear when there's a card and a phone, we haven't taught them anything, we've built a nice room. Most of them will teach in schools where nobody puts a phone on the table. That's annoying and right. Stop the recording? Stop it. Then go and eat something, you look terrible. Thank you, Meera.

name: Community radio, resident hosts on the drains conversations
summary: Synthetic sample. On a monthly community radio programme in Ghana, Kwesi interviews Abena, a community development officer at a municipal assembly, and Efua, a 19-year-old lead host, about community conversations on market drainage and sanitation that youth and women's groups in three neighbourhoods now host themselves. Residents host with printed QR cards and a host guide they rewrote; two lead hosts per neighbourhood have member access to their neighbourhood's private project to read summaries, tidy names and tags and lead Verify, while Abena stays admin and they decide together what is published, one project per neighbourhood. Twi-only sessions stay on paper, typed in as notes, as Twi transcription is untested. Efua's first session skipped a spoken consent explanation; she now opens in her own words and stops the phone when asked. A listener asks whether recordings could be used against traders, and Abena explains anonymise and who can open the project without promising more. Failures: a chat-drafted letter that "sounds like us, but is not ours", rewritten aloud, quoting the recording; one neighbourhood recording into the wrong project; a month that depended on one host. They settle on one shared question plus one of the hosts' own, report monthly on what the assembly did and did not do, and celebrate by reading chosen quotes aloud with the speakers' agreement.

chunks.text: Good morning, good morning, and welcome to Community Hour, last Saturday of the month, when we talk about our own town and what is being done about it. I am Kwesi. Small announcement first: Madam Abena from the assembly is recording this programme on her phone, with the station's agreement, for the programme's own record. So if you call in, you are on the radio and on her phone. Madam Abena, good morning.

Good morning, Kwesi, good morning everybody. Yes, it is only our record of the series, so next month we can check what we promised today. And beside me, Efua from Ekyir Ridge. Good morning, Uncle Kwesi, good morning everyone. Efua is nineteen and she is one of our lead hosts. Efua, somebody stopped me at the lorry park and asked, so now Efua works for the assembly?

No, no, I don't work for the assembly. I'm a host. Since June the youth and women's groups in three neighbourhoods are running the community conversations on the drains and sanitation ourselves, after the assembly staff ran the first two rounds. So I bring people together, eight or ten, at a shop front or under the tree by the chapel, and we put the phone in the middle. You scan the card with the code, and the phone records. Nobody needs an account.

And there is a printed guide that goes with the card. The first one was written for a meeting hall, so I edited it with the hosts. Ours says put the phone on a stool, not on the floor where the gutter is loud, keep the screen on, and when a car with music passes, wait. Those were Efua's lines. Then the lead hosts, two per neighbourhood, get more. After one Saturday morning of training I gave them member access.

So we can open our own neighbourhood's project and read the summaries, and correct the names and tags of the conversations. Madam Abena stays the admin, she sets things up. Each neighbourhood has its own project in the assembly's workspace, three projects. And what gets published, the hosts and I decide together, not me alone. Efua, tell them about the tidying, people think it's boring. It is a bit boring, Madam. But it matters.

The first week every conversation was just called conversation and I didn't know which was where. Now we write the place and the day. Fish section Tuesday. Chapel tree Thursday evening. And tags, women's group, youth, traders, so we can see who we have talked to and who not yet. And at the end of each session we do the checking, Verify. We pick a topic, the phone writes up what it heard, I read it out, and people edit it or press revise until they can approve it. Or they don't approve it.

The market women like that part. One of them said, at last somebody writes down what I said and asks me if it is right. Now Efua, I have my sources, I heard your first session was not so smooth. Uncle Kwesi! Okay, it's true. In June I was so worried about the phone working that I forgot to explain anything. The phone shows some cards about recording, and people pressed yes, yes, yes, like installing an app.

Nobody said it aloud. And afterwards an auntie asked me, so where is this going? And I didn't have a good answer, and she had talked about her stall, her husband, everything.
